en: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā Tattvārthā*, Chapter Nine:
A Record of the Textual Exegesis by the Śramaṇa Yuanyu.
Commentary on the Twelfth Fascicle of the Treatise.
"Among the formless dharmas... [up to] the nature of aggregates, acquisitions, and so forth. Commentary:

The following clarifies those dharmas that are neither form nor mind. Question: Previously, at the beginning of the section on mental factors (*caitta*), four types of conditioned phenomena were raised;
two were concluded there, while the remaining two logically ought to be concluded here. Why, then, does this not conclude the previously mentioned non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)?
Therefore, herein, regarding the two types of formless fetters (*ārūpya-saṃyojana*) that produce one [result], the underlying intent is not yet fully detailed.

The commentary explains that because the subsequent section on "summarizing alternative names" also clarifies the mind (*citta*) as well as mental factors (*caitta*), it can be understood that the citation concerning the formless fetters applies here.

Within the formal explanation, there are three parts: first, the initial presentation and enumeration; second, the restatement and interpretation; and third, the differentiation of categories. This [passage] constitutes the initial presentation.

The first phrase provides a general heading, while the subsequent three phrases list them individually. According to the masters of the Sarvāstivāda school, since they establish "factors dissociated from mind" (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), there is no fixed number;
it varies according to the different treatises, with some adding or omitting elements.

Now, this author of the present treatise, because he maintains that there exists a "conjunction-nature" (*saṃyoga-dharma*) in addition to the fourteen [dissociated factors], includes it within the category of "equality" (*sabhāgatā*). Furthermore, there are other masters who...

Beyond "acquisition" (*prāpti*) and so forth, one further conceptualizes "acquisition of the aggregates," "acquisition of the elements," "acquisition of the bases," and so on; it should be understood that these are simply varieties of acquisition.
Or, beyond "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*), one conceptualizes "non-conjunction" (*asamanvāgama*) and "regret" (*kaukṛtya*) and so on;

it should be understood that these are simply varieties of non-acquisition, because they do not possess a separate substantial entity. Furthermore, because the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used, it includes other such categories by way of analogy.
Regarding the term "differentiation of essence" (*bhinnasvabhāva*), the word "essence" (*svabhāva*) here refers to a synonym for the very substance itself.
Thus, these various phenomena arise in association (*saṃprayukta*).

[The commentary] states: This explains the general name; it is not like the mental factors (*caitasika*) which, while associated with the mind, have a substance that is further classified as formations (*saṃskāra*).

Because they are included within the aggregates (*skandha*), the term "dissociated from mind" (*cittaviprayukta*) excludes mental factors (*caitta*), while the term "conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) excludes matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*);
for all of those latter categories are not subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Regarding the statement "speaking of mind" (up to) "therefore it is further called 'mind-utterance'":
the commentary states that this second explanation uses the term "mind" to clarify the attainment [of meditative states] and so forth;

since the mind belongs to the same category of formless phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*), and because the mind is of a homogeneous nature, the expression "mind-utterance" (*citta-vāda*) serves to exclude the single category of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).

All mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise formless (*arūpin*), and since they are similar to the mind in being of the same class and associated with it (*samprayukta*), the term "dissociated" (*viprayukta*) is used to distinguish them from those.
Furthermore, because all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are formless, they could be termed "mind";

however, to distinguish them, [it is specified that dissociated factors] are not included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) or do not involve flux (*pravṛtti*). Thus, [the term "dissociated"] serves to exclude these.
For that reason, it is further stated:
"This has already provided a general indication [extending] to the two cessations within one's own continuum.

The commentary states: From here below, the explanation follows the meaning through a series of analogous correspondences, which is divided into seven sections in total. The first section is as follows:

The first elucidation concerns acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); within this, the first two lines clarify their essential nature (*svabhāva*), while the latter two clarify their distinctions (*viśeṣa*). Regarding the clarification of their essential nature, the first two lines define their substance (*tattva*). [The text continues: ...the second elucidation concerns the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*);

the third elucidation concerns the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*); the fourth elucidation concerns the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); the fifth elucidation concerns the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); the sixth elucidation concerns the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and the seventh elucidation concerns designations (*nāman*) and so forth. Regarding the first elucidation, acquisition and non-acquisition:

first, the essential nature is clarified; subsequently, the distinctions are clarified. Within the clarification of the essential nature, the upper two lines clarify its substance, and the lower two...

The phrase "total indication" refers to the basis upon which this general name is established; it indicates that one merely attains the first level, while "obtaining" and "accomplishment" refer to the subsequent stages.
The treatise states: "Attainment, obtaining, and accomplishment... [up to] not obtaining the noble dharmas."
The commentary states: First, the verse is explained; subsequently, there is an extensive determination.

Regarding the explanation of the first half-verse, it concerns the arising of two dharmas, the single nature of their acquisition, and the meaning of "attainment. Among these, the initial acquisition of what was previously unobtained is termed "acquisition" (*prāpti*), while the repeated acquisition of what has already been obtained is termed "possession" (*samanvāgama*).
In summary, although they are essentially one acquisition, they are distinguished by the two meanings of "acquisition" and "possession."
This is because the initial primary gate of the general and specific categories differs in this way; it differs slightly from the explanation in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
In the *Kośa*, that which was never previously obtained, or which was obtained and subsequently lost, but is now obtained for the first time, is called "acquisition" (*prāpti*).
From the second moment onward, as long as it continues in a series without being lost, it is called "possession" (*samanvāgama*). That which is contrary to this is called "non-possession."

Regarding "acquisition" (*prāpti*): that which was previously lost and then reacquired is not termed "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*); rather, it is only the very first moment of loss that is called "non-acquisition.
From the second moment onward, the continuity of this non-acquisition is termed "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*).

Thus, both acquisition and non-acquisition are initially produced as a single momentary characteristic; they are called "acquisition" and "non-acquisition" respectively, while their subsequent continuity is called "possession" (*samanvāgama*).
In this treatise, "acquisition" (prāpti) refers solely to obtaining what was not previously attained;

thus, that which was not previously obtained is called "non-acquisition" (aprāpti). If something was previously attained but was subsequently lost, and is now regained, it is merely termed "possession" (samanvāgama), because it is a re-attainment.
Therefore, that which was already lost is called "non-possession" (asamanvāgama). Question:

Thus, this would contradict the fourfold formulation of acquisition (*prāpti*), relinquishment (*tyāga*), accomplishment (*siddhi*), and non-accomplishment (*asiddhi*). To explain the resolution: acquisition refers to the initial attainment;
"accomplishment" is merely a distinction according to the convenience of the commentator’s intent. This text and that [other] cannot be treated as identical.
How is their meaning to be understood? Here, the meaning of attaining accomplishment is explained by means of relative distinctions through different perspectives.
Because the distinctions between acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are explained, the entities of their respective attainments (*samanvāgama*) differ.

Among those four propositions, the intention is to adorn the meaning through various methods: "acquisition" refers exclusively to new acquisition, while "attainment" applies to both new and old acquisition.
It should be understood that acquisition includes non-acquisition, whereas attainment does not include non-attainment. This can be easily discerned through reflection.
Regarding which phenomena [one should reflect] according to reason... [The commentary states:
This explains the latter half [of the verse], providing a general indication of the bases. There are two types of bases: conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, among the conditioned, acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exist only within one's own continuum. That is to say, conditioned phenomena that fall within one's own personal continuity [possess these].
It is not [a possession] of another’s continuum, because there is no such thing as a dharma that accomplishes the body of another;

nor is it [a possession] of what is not a continuum, because there is no such thing as a dharma that accomplishes insentient things. Among unconditioned dharmas, acquisition (*prāpti*) exists only for the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), because it is induced by mental factors and because it opposes internal arising.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) does not exist for space (*ākāśa*), because it is not induced by mental factors and does not oppose internal arising.

Therefore, it is asked: "How is the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of insentient matter and so forth established? The answer is: "It is also by virtue of this very fact that [those things] do not arise as dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*);

they are likewise established by many people in common, just like analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This should be carefully considered: all sentient beings possess the non-analytical cessation of those states;
this applies to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), as well as to those who have entered [the path] while still bound by all fetters."

At the stage of *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), only these two types of persons do not achieve cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); all others achieve it.
Although it is stated that those "bound by all fetters" (*sakalabandhana*) are excluded, this principle should logically apply to all.

The two gates are taught because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) are distinguished separately. For whoever possesses an attainment (*prāpti*), there is necessarily a non-attainment (*aprāpti*); in reality, attainment and non-attainment are established as being mutually exclusive.

Therefore, to prove this meaning, the root treatise cites the statement that the two aggregates of matter (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) share a single acquisition (*prāpti*). The phrase "the two aggregates of matter and formations" refers to matter and the ten acquisitions;
since these are all acquired by a single "great acquisition," it is said that they are acquired by one acquisition. Question:

Are the other characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) acquired by the same acquisition or by separate acquisitions? If so, what fault is there in either case? Both [positions] have faults.
If one were to argue that a single *prāpti* (acquisition) serves as the model for all associated dharmas (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For if a separate *prāpti* were required for each *prāpti*, there would be no end; since the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of a dharma each have their own *prāpti*, this chain of acquisitions would continue indefinitely.

The explanation states: There is indeed a separate *prāpti*, yet it does not result in an infinite regress. This is because multiple [acquisitions] do not arise for a single dharma. Thus, [the system remains coherent].

It may be argued that there are four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and these four characteristics are called "existence" (*bhava*). If this "existence" exists, even if its characteristics were distinct from the dharma they characterize, what fault would there be?
Since they do not obstruct one another, there should be no error. Furthermore, one understands that the "attainment" (*prāpti*) is that which is attained;

however, the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be cited as an analogous objection. How could one, on the grounds that the characteristic and the characterized share the same characteristic, thereby cause the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) [to be affected]?

If one were to raise an objection based on the analogy that the mental concomitants (*caitta*) must share the same characteristics because they are obtained by the same attainment as the mind-king (*cittarāja*), this is not correct.

It is not stated that the four aggregates are obtained by a single attainment; furthermore, there are cases of deficiency and cessation, and it does not apply to all [phenomena]. Therefore, this should be reconsidered.
The Master of the Sūtras [Vasubandhu], in this section [extending to] "a distinct entity called acquisition" (*prāpti*), states:

"The following provides a detailed explanation and resolution of the first response. It cites authoritative scripture (*āgama*) and subsequently raises objections through formal inference (*anumāna*).
This is the opening passage. Within it, he first sets forth the question posed by the Master of the Sūtras in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
One should answer him as follows: [up to] "and unwholesome dharmas.

The commentary states: This master of the treatise answers by citing a sūtra which refutes the idea that a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, or one who has not severed the roots of goodness yet has committed the five heinous crimes, can be fully endowed with wholesome [dharmas].
If it is argued that the scriptural passage [from "if one says" up to] "there is the fault of over-extension," the commentary states:

this restates the opponent's objection. According to these scriptures, there would be the fault of having to admit that [the wheel-turning king] possesses non-sentient objects such as wheels and jewels, as well as things belonging to other continuums such as elephants, horses, soldiers, ministers, and women; thus, the fault of over-extension is established.
This objection is not valid, because [the term] is established as a name.

The commentary states: This is the Master of the Treatise’s explanation; when other masters speak of "establishment" (*siddhi*) in their sūtras, it means "mastery," and is not the same as this [usage].
If it is argued that other sūtras should also be interpreted in this way, [the author] replies:
This restates the objection of the non-Buddhists; since the Cakravartin [is already established], he should not be considered as attaining [this state] separately.
This is also not the case... [up to] ...it is designated as "attainment" (samanvāgama).
The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains that "mastery over speech" means the present subject possesses power over the present;

that those seven treasures are all comprised within the fruit of dominance (*adhipati-phala*) and constantly manifest before one; and that they revolve according to whatever vehicle of the King of Sūtras is mounted.
Thus, it may be called "accomplishment. It does not mean that wholesome and unwholesome dharmas of the past and future do not coexist in their manifestation. One.

If there were no acquisition (*prāpti*) for that which does not currently function when something else is functioning, how could it be established? It is already difficult to establish the existence of a past entity even without acquisition;
how much more so, then, can you establish the establishment of a non-entity according to your own school?
"If it is said that [the seed] is 'accomplished' (siddha) with respect to the future," the commentary states:

this restates the previous position; although there is no substantial entity (*bhāva*) in the present, even though it is not separately acquired, it still possesses the functional capacity to produce [the result] in the future, and is thus termed "accomplished."
This reasoning is also incorrect... [it] should be the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
The commentary states: This master of the treatise raises an objection: if it were as you understand it, there would be the fault of non-concordant karma.
For when one simultaneously attains the final body of a Bodhisattva and is certain to give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, this is precisely the accomplishment of the outflow-free state.
If it were already the case that this is the final mind of a noble Arhat, then this would be distinct [from the preceding state].
Since the mind characterized by arising and ceasing cannot subsequently give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*), one would not possess the untainted; thus, one would be a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, since the afflictions to be abandoned through mundane patience and vision no longer arise, one would not possess them; thus, one would be a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

According to this text, it appears that upon entering the stage of *kṣānti* (receptivity), one immediately attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision.
However, the "unexcelled receptivity" (*anuttara-kṣānti*) should further be examined in light of other passages.
Moreover, if one grants that [this occurs], what would be unreasonable about it?
The commentary states: From here below, there are six sections: first, raising objections to challenge the established inference (*anumāna*) and pointing out subtle faults in the initial thesis;

second, external objections demonstrating the lack of validity; third, clearing away those objections through reasoning; fourth, citing the opponent’s thesis to extensively refute what they cling to; fifth, [the section on] the extensive refutation of their attachments; and sixth, concluding by determining right and wrong.
This [section] specifically examines the faults in the opponent’s own thesis as they raise it for scrutiny.
"In this way, it is unreasonable (up to) 'this is unreasonable.

[The Commentary] states: This second external objection clarifies that the existence of a substance (*dravya*) as held by the ancients is not known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), unlike the five consciousnesses which directly apprehend objects such as visible form and sound;
nor is it apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds regarding states such as greed and hatred, as is said to be known through auditory perception.
That which is not a present object must be established through inference based on its functional activity, as in the case of the eyes, ears, and so forth.
However, the "acquisition" (*prāpti*) that you postulate lacks both essence and function; to claim it exists beyond what is established by perception and inference is irrational.
When establishing an inference, the "acquisition" that is the probandum must necessarily be non-existent in essence and function, because it does not exist, just like a rabbit's horn.
This is certainly not the case (up to) "stating that this is non-existent.
The commentary states: This third proponent refutes [the opponent's] position through reasoning.

That which is accepted as having a great functional efficacy—namely, "acquisition" (*prāpti*)—is such that by virtue of acquisition, once the various dharmas have been obtained, they are not lost; it is established as their mark, and by means of this, one knows them.

When that subsequent discriminative knowledge (*pṛṣṭhābhiniveśa-jñāna*) arises, it does not lose its status as the cause for the arising of the preceding knowledge; these two constitute its great function. What further function could there be beyond this?

To claim otherwise—that such a measure of meaning is non-existent—is untenable. It must be admitted that [this subsequent knowledge] has a distinct substantial entity and possesses a great function, just like the eye and other faculties.
Because they possess a function, one knows they have their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this demonstrates what exists externally.
There is the fault that the three-dimensional [nature] cannot be established without a cause.
If this is so, what is the purpose of the "mark of wisdom"?
The commentary states: This fourth opponent raises the tenets of his own school to refute the preceding position, citing scriptural authority.
Thus, these two functions do not require effort for their attainment; rather, they exist within the basis [the ālayavijñāna] when the seeds of affliction have not yet been uprooted,
the seeds of innate virtue have not yet been impaired, and the seeds of applied virtue have increased and become sovereign—
therein lie the aforementioned two functions.
Furthermore, what is meant by "called abandonment"? [The commentary] states: This is a re-explanation of the preceding meaning.
Although two gates were opened, for now we explain the meaning of "unimpaired" with respect to that which is acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).
That is to say, the power of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is able to impair the seeds of innate wholesome factors within the body, rendering them incapable of producing manifest wholesome states.
The mind is said to be "severed" because it is not utterly destroyed such that it is entirely non-existent; rather, because it is rendered useless, it is merely called "impaired.
Thus, when it is impaired, it is not accomplished, whereas when it is not impaired, it is called "accomplished."
"Peace [attained] through effort" (up to) "is called non-attainment.
The commentary states: This refers to the ease of application (*prayoga*).

It means that although one has seeds from previous practice since beginningless time, one lacks mastery; or, regarding virtues not previously practiced, some say they are "innate" (*prakṛtistha*). Or...
It is said that those things produced through habituation all arise from the growth of seeds once they have been activated;

because one has mastery over the production of the manifest state (*samudācāra*) through that growth of the seeds, it is called "attainment" (*samanvāgama*). This is similar in meaning and force to the Mahāyāna concept of "mastery-attainment" (*vaśitā-samanvāgama*).
If [the seeds] have not yet arisen, or if wisdom has already declined, such that one lacks mastery, it is called "non-attainment" (*asamanvāgama*).
The unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified [afflictions] would thus become useless.
The commentary states: This explains that through the paths of seeing and cultivation, the basis (the body) undergoes a transformation different from its original state;
consequently, among the afflictions abandoned by those two paths, these [unwholesome and obscured-unspecified afflictions] no longer possess the capacity to manifest.
The arising [of such seeds] is called "cutting off" (*prahāṇa*); that which is contrary to this is called "not yet uprooted.

If the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) suppresses those seeds so that they lack the capacity to produce manifest activity (*samudācāra*), this is also called "cutting off"; that which is contrary to this is also called "not yet impaired.

Regarding one's own pure (*anāsrava*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) states, or those lacking the capacity to produce manifest activity—such as those pertaining to craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and the like—[the same applies].
Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that are not yet clear or sharp are the opposite of this and are termed "unmastery" (*vaśitā*).

All such categories are established solely by way of the distinctions among the seeds (*bīja*) upon which they depend; thus, their two functions are accomplished without the need for laborious recourse to "acquisition" (*prāpti*). Therefore, those two functions do not depend on acquisition.
Otherwise, the Master [Vasubandhu] would incur the fault of his reason for establishing "great function" being unestablished.
"Such various [factors]... are called seeds. The commentary states:
From here below is the fifth section, the extensive refutation of what is clung to. Within this, first the seed is refuted, followed by the specific refutations of each phenomenon;
this is the initial passage. Therefore, he first provides a general negation, for all that has been stated by them [is as follows]:
Because branches and leaves naturally lean when planted upon seeds and roots that are not upright, one first examines the essential characteristics of the seed,
namely name-and-form (nāmarūpa) through to its transformation and differentiation.

The commentary states: Within the Sautrāntika school, there are two positions regarding the establishment of seeds (*bīja*). One position holds that they depend upon name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), while the other holds that they depend solely upon the mind (*citta*).
Following the refutation of these two views, the text is divided into two parts; this first section describes the [position] concerning seeds.
That is to say, within name-and-form, there exists either a successive capacity for inducing its own fruit or an immediate one.
The "arising capacity" (janana-śakti) is called "transformation" (pariṇāma) because, based on the supporting body, the capacity arises in the subsequent two moments;
that is to say, it is the successive capacity that gradually increases until the stage of the arising fruit, wherein the increase and decrease of the capacity is termed "differentiation" (viśeṣa).
Differentiation is the immediately preceding capacity; thus, through the continuity [of the stream], there is transformation and differentiation.
Regarding the statement that "there are distinctions in their functions due to their mutual proximity," what are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)?
The commentary states: this inquiry concerns the essential nature of name-and-form.
This refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The commentary states: "This identifies the substance of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
How is this grasped? (Up to: By what is it the seed?

The commentary states: This master [Vasubandhu] correctly refutes you by showing that the reasons for asserting the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as having the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their essence do not exceed three types.
If the five aggregates collectively must be present to be called the "cause," then it would necessarily be a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

If each individual aggregate could separately serve as the cause, then according to your Sautrāntika school, since they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), how could that which is indeterminate give rise to the two other natures? If...
If wholesome [states] of their own kind produce only wholesome [states], then what serves as the seed for those of a different nature that arise in alternation?
"O Beloved of the Gods (Devānāmpriya)," it is not the case that you [hold] that unwholesome natures arise [from them].
[The author] comments: This second teacher’s thesis is once again addressed by the Master as "Beloved of the Gods," for such a person is inferior.
Those who are weak are pitied by Heaven; because their intent exists in mutual contempt, they are called "Heaven’s favorites. Those of inferior intelligence cannot understand the seeds.

As for the "ancient seeds," they are perfumed upon the subsequent mind by the excellence of the preceding moment's volition (*cetanā*), causing that subsequent mind to give rise to a distinct functional capacity.
This refers to the fact that the volition currently manifesting possesses excellence, which differentiates its capacity.

Since activity is a specific differentiation within volition (*cetanā*), it is termed a "differentiation of volition. It causes the functional capacity (*śakti*) in subsequent moments of mind to undergo transformation;
furthermore, as a specific differentiation within that very capacity, it constitutes the seed (*bīja*).

Thus, one should understand that the capacities produced by the three natures of mind each universally depend upon the minds of the three natures. By means of these seeds, they cause their respective bases (*āśraya*) [to transform].
The transformation of the mental continuum consists of successive functional distinctions;
because of these proximate functions, they acquire different natures and mutually induce one another.
Now, that which you maintain [to be the self] has no distinct substance.
The commentary states: This inquiry investigates whether the seeds grasped by outsiders are distinct from the substance of the mind as its cause;
[the answer is that] these have no separate substance. The commentary states: These outsiders reply that they are simply the functional capacities of the mind and possess no separate substance.
"Is it not granted that there is the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) regarding wholesome [states]?
[The author] comments: From this point on, he formally refutes [the opponent's view].

If the seed and the mind do not have distinct entities, then a wholesome mind, like a seed, would be able to produce the unwholesome, and the unwholesome, like a seed, would be able to produce the unwholesome; in both cases, this is because they are not different in essence from the seed.
Fearing that the Śākya might say, "An unwholesome seed can produce an unwholesome [result] within a wholesome mind, but it is not the wholesome mind itself," the following objection is raised:
"One who is insane or without mind could entertain such a thought; however, there is no such statement regarding one who possesses mind.
Is this not like [the relationship between] heat and its function? Since they are not distinct, one should establish an inference based on the reduction of the cause [to explain] the result."
It is said that a wholesome mind ought to be able to produce unwholesome results because there is no essential difference between it and the seeds of the unwholesome;
just as those seeds are manifestly unwholesome, a wholesome seed cannot be established within them.
As for "Naraka" (the hell realms), there are two Western [Indian] interpretations: one states that *naraka* is named after *nirartha*, meaning "that which is not to be desired."
Because they cannot be compared [to anything else], they are called *naraka*. Second, *nara* means "human" and *ka* means "evil";

thus, those who commit evil deeds fall into them, and for this reason they are called "places for evil persons. Ancient translators translated this according to its meaning as "Hell" (*dīyù*) and so forth;
"and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the animals (*tiryagyoni*) and hungry ghosts (*preta*). Furthermore, even a presently arisen wholesome mind cannot induce what is undesirable [in these realms].
The fruit cannot contain the seeds of unwholesome states. *Manuṣya* is the Chinese translation for "one who gathers the mind.
At the beginning of the kalpa, King Mahāsaṃmata—the supreme ancestor of the Śākya clan—exhorted the great multitude:

"You sentient beings should gather yourselves in meaning; you should [strive] for nirvāṇa in the human realm. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "A 'human' (*manuṣya*) is one capable of reflecting upon much meaning."

This is precisely its meaning. If one were to plant both unwholesome and wholesome seeds within a mind that is either desirous of the unwholesome or the wholesome—just as a seed of goodness might instead bring forth evil—the Tathāgata would know only that obtaining a wholesome fruit from wholesome [causes] is a possible case (*sthāna*), while obtaining an unwholesome fruit [from wholesome causes] is an impossible case (*asthāna*).
He would not permit that the wholesome could ever bring about the unwholesome; such is not within the knowledge of the Buddha.
This is precisely why, because the Tathāgata’s flavor is the wisdom that serves as the locus of accomplishment, [denying it] constitutes slandering the Buddha.
Furthermore, one would have to admit that [the position of the opponent] is an extreme delusion.
The commentary states: herein, it is further proven by the absence of a separate entity that the seeds and the mind attain a single fruit together.

If [it were argued that] attaining the same fruit serves as the cause for realizing the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) capable of inducing the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*), then it would follow that the uncontaminated could also produce afflictions (*kleśa*), because the seeds of affliction would be established within the uncontaminated mind. Fearing such an interpretation, [the opponent] might say:

"Because the uncontaminated is either the elder brother or the direct antidote [to affliction], the seeds of affliction are not established within the uncontaminated mind. To this, the following objection is raised: "Or..."

If, within the body of an Ārya, the afflictions resulting from the cultivation of merit were to arise spontaneously without seeds, then this would mean that the untainted (anāsrava) arises from the tainted (sāsrava).
Alternatively, if the mind of an affliction were to possess untainted seeds, then the affliction itself should be able to produce the untainted.
Fearing that such an explanation would contradict the sequence of the obstacles, [the opponent] says that the untainted does not rely on the mind; thus, the following objection is raised.
If it is argued that once an Ārya has already given rise to afflictions, they would be reborn with outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states without seeds, [the opponent] might offer this explanation:
"Just as the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) arises without seeds, what fault is there in this? Therefore, the following objection is raised:
"If it were produced without a cause, it would at that time be categorized as the very first outflow-free state; thus, what is called a 'moment' (*kṣaṇa*) is not merely a single thought-instant."

Thus, if one were to raise an objection based on the *śaikṣa* stage—that there should be seeds of the cultivation of the three realms for those of the *aśaikṣa* stage who are of the "nature of falling away"—this objection would not hold for the Sautrāntika school, as they maintain that there is no falling away from the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, [the text] points to the following passage regarding falling away from the afflictions.
Fearing that [the opponent] might explain it thus: "Although seeds and the mind do not have separate entities, there is a distinction between them."
Because they are differentiated, they each produce distinct results; because they are dependently originated, they lack separate substantial entities. Thus, the following objection is raised:
"I have never seen it stated that things are distinct while being identical, nor is this something the wise would find pleasing."
Furthermore, regarding the previously raised point up to the meaning of mutual correspondence, the commentary states:
This passage interrogates the preceding thought and the subsequent mind; since they do not exist simultaneously, how can they constitute cause and effect?

The commentary states: This presents a dilemma. If the power [of the roots] is diminished, then once they have been exhausted through hearing, what further use would there be?
If their function is diminished but not yet exhausted, then it should not be called "severing the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, as for that which he says [up to] "is said to be possessed":
The commentary states: This second [point] refutes the notion that within the context of preparatory virtue (*prayoga-kuśala*), those dharmas have already arisen;
this is a restatement of what was previously asserted. This, too, is irrational... up to... the conceptualization of categories (*prakāra-parikalpa*).
The commentary states: This directly refutes your Sautrāntika position that there is no future dharma.

It is illogical for the seeds of previously unarisen preparatory wholesome dharmas (*prayoga-kuśala-dharma*) to exist within the present mind. Furthermore, as previously refuted, seeds cannot be established because they lack a cause for their arising;

thus, the principle of arising is necessarily absent at its inception. Since even the first arising does not exist, how could there be a "previously arisen" [seed]? Moreover, the future is non-existent.
Regarding what [is it that] has mastery? Fearing that they might be questioned as to "for what cause and condition was it originally not produced?", the following explanation states:

"Because the cause of production does not exist. Since it is not the case that there is a non-existent cause of production, and since the causal power is fundamentally non-existent, how could it exist?
By this very principle, one simultaneously refutes the speculative categories of the school’s tenets concerning the dharma that severs the afflictions; such is the meaning.
What are the categories? They refer to the nine grades and five classes, as previously refuted. Since seeds are not established, the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) does not arise.
There are no afflictions (*kleśa*) present in the present; as for their future and past states, their substance is non-existent.
What afflictions could there be such that one speaks of "categories"? Even if seeds were to exist, upon what would they depend? The present untainted mind is not a basis [for them].

Therefore, if [the seeds] were based on the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) substance, since their substance would not differ, they should have the same fruit and should not be subject to abandonment (*aprahātavya*), just like the uncontaminated mind.

If it is argued that the seeds do not exist as long as they do not rely on the manifest [defilements], and that making them non-existent constitutes the meaning of "abandoning delusions" (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), then since the substance of the seeds is already non-existent, there would be nothing to be abandoned.
How, then, can one say that "afflictions are abandoned"? Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: [text omitted].

It is said that if there were no seeds for the [pure] precepts, they would have no essence; yet if one allows them to constitute the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), that is illogical because those two [seeds and essence] do not exist.

For the transformation of the basis consists either in the absence of those seeds or the absence of their essence. When the supramundane mind is actually present, how could it be said that its seeds are absent or that its essence has been severed?
It is impossible for them to be found at that time. Therefore, the claim that there is a transformation of the basis despite the absence of those two is unreasonable.
If cessation were defined as non-existence in the present, it would be called "annihilation," and since all things would thus be non-existent, the mind should be severed instantaneously;
how then could one speak of there being various categories [of afflictions]?
As for what was said [up to the point] regarding that which is not yet severed:
The commentary states: This third section concerns the meaning of what is abandoned by the two paths within the refutation of all afflictions;
this is a restatement of what has been taught. This shall now be explained [up to] "because it lacks the function of arising."

The commentary states: This inquiry into the distinction between those two paths arises from the concern that one might object, "If the functions of these two paths are different, why do you harbor such doubts?

This restates their explanation. Although [the seeds] are damaged, they have not yet been destroyed;

they are like seeds that have already been moistened and are about to sprout, but suddenly encounter the condition of fire which causes them to dry out again, so that although they do not sprout at present...

It is called "impairment" because it is not a permanent destruction; thus, that which arises later through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) for the purpose of suppressing afflictions (*kleśa*) should also be understood in this way.
Although it cannot presently produce various fruits, it is termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*).

Yet, at a later time, just as before, it still gives rise to the various fruits of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), namely the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) and so forth, as well as the various afflictions, namely the fruits of conditions (*pratyayaphala*).
"How is it said [that the seed is damaged], up to: how is it called 'cut off'? The commentary states:
This master of the treatise refutes the error [of those who claim] that when fire dries the seed, it is merely the absence of the conditions for production; it does not constitute damage to the seed.

this restates his explanation of the preceding meanings of "successive" (*pāramparya*) and "proximate" (*sāmantaka*).
That is to say, the transformation of prior and subsequent moments within a continuum is the "successive function," while the differentiation [of that transformation] is the "proximate function."
"Thus, Venerable One... (and so on), as will be explained later.

The commentary states: This is a direct refutation of your Dārṣṭāntika school, which maintains that only the present exists while the past and future are non-existent, and which asserts that the present consists only of a single moment without the distinction of a preceding or succeeding continuity;
[the opponent's claim] regarding "preceding and succeeding" contradicts their own accepted tenets.

The discrepancy between their words and their intended meaning is as follows: they claim that past and future phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet they assert that the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) throughout the three time periods is an eternal principle;

thus, their words are contradictory. Furthermore, since the subsequent fruit does not exist, from what could its activity arise? At the stage when the fruit is produced, the cause no longer exists—so who produces it?
To designate that which produces a fruit immediately after [the cause] has ceased as the "seed" is also contrary to reason; therefore, this is called a discrepancy.

This is because the mind is admitted to be exclusively present, whereas the present lacks differentiation while verbal expression possesses differentiation;

thus, they contradict one another across the two time periods [past and future]. Since both are established as the phenomena of seeds, it is said that their seeds are also distinct. Furthermore, this is explained as being simultaneous.

this concludes the thesis regarding establishment and destruction. Since the seeds cited by the Master of the Sūtra are not established, and there being no seeds...

The masters of the Abhidharma (up to this point) have thus established their own position.
The commentary states: This section establishes the intent of refuting [the opponent's] positions. According to those various doctrines, the true system is corrupted;
specifically, the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that the capacity within the differentiation of the mind to produce an effect is what is called the "seed" (*bīja*).

Teachers of other schools either claim it is named the "concomitant element" (*anugata-dhātu*), meaning it is the cause because it exists in accordance with the body, or they claim it is "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), based on its dependence [upon the substrate].
Because the preceding thought perfumes and forms a habit-energy (*vāsanā*), some say it is a "functional capacity" (*śakti*), for it possesses the power to produce a result.
The Saṃmitīya masters say it is "unshared," because due to its existence, the future fruit necessarily arises, just as in the case of a "meaning.
The Mahāsāṃghika masters call it "accumulation by the Sangha" (*saṅghabhṛta*), because it is accumulated by prior volition (*cetanā*) and is able to augment subsequent moments of mind.
Therefore, regarding such [views] as these, some masters within various schools maintain that there are distinct entities, as explained in the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*.
Because of these and other such [theories], the noble ones are confused; thus, this present work provides a definitive analysis to establish the correct understanding.
Thus, [the two types] that are already accomplished up to those not to be abandoned have been explained.

The commentary states: From here below, the distinctions are clarified; first, the distinctions of acquisition (*prāpti*) are explained, and subsequently, the distinctions of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are explained.

Within the section on acquisition, first there is the formal analysis, followed by a further detailed examination; this [present passage] constitutes the formal analysis. [The first phrase contains] three [points].
The second phrase concerns the distinction of the world; the third and fourth phrases concern the distinction of the three natures;
the fifth phrase concerns the distinction of the four bonds; the sixth phrase concerns the distinction of the three trainings; and [the seventh] concerns the distinction of the three abandonments.

Regarding the actual substance of attainment, it extends across the three times, the three natures, the four bonds, the three trainings, and the three abandonments; however, in this present text, the discussion is made from the perspective of that which is attained.
Therefore, there are distinctions.
The *Śāstra* says: "The acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the three time periods [will be] further explained later.

The *Commentary* says: This explains the first gate; regarding the three types of past [acquisition], that which is "past prior to the dharma" refers to the acquisition that arises before the dharma itself.

Whether it be obtained subsequent to the dharma (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) or obtained simultaneously with the dharma (*sahaja*), regarding these dharmas heard in the present or future, there are three [temporal states] among them;
those in the past and present are all the dharma itself, and they also obtain the future.

Because there is no sequential order [in the future], its textual position cannot be fixed; this should be further considered later. Regarding the present dharma, there are the three aforementioned faults.
That which has passed consists solely of past dharmas; that which is yet to come consists solely of future dharmas; and the present consists solely of dharmas simultaneous [with their acquisition].
This applies universally to all cases where such is possible. There are indeed certain dharmas that lack these three types of acquisition, as will be explained later during the detailed analysis.
Furthermore, there are three types of acquisition (*prāpti*) for wholesome and other dharmas, up to the indeterminate.
The commentary states: This second section clarifies that the acquisition and the acquired share the same nature, such as being wholesome and so forth. Question:

Since the distinctions among various acquisitions cannot be treated by a single rule, do the acquisitions of conditioned dharmas necessarily share the same nature—wholesome and so forth—as the dharmas themselves? Answer: They do. Regarding the acquisitions of conditioned dharmas...

The attainment of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) associated with whatever dharma is acquired is virtuous (*kuśala*), because it follows from its counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).

The attainment of non-deliberative cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because it is a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*) that follows the basis, the realm, and the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Furthermore, other passages should also be examined accordingly.
Furthermore, there are dharmas that are bound (up to) those that are exclusively unbound.
The commentary states: This explains the third gate, namely that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) pervades all three realms.

This means that the acquisition of the non-analytical cessation of all dharmas universally extends across the three realms. Why is this so? It is asked: if one attains [it] within a body belonging to the desire realm...

All these are included within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) according to their respective bases; the rest should be inferred by analogy. As for the acquisition (prāpti) of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), if it follows a contaminated path (sāsrava-mārga), it is bound to the two upper realms;

if it is the acquisition of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) via a desire-realm path that lacks the [contaminated] path, it is not bound. If it follows an uncontaminated path (anāsrava-mārga), it is then non-bound (apratisaṃyukta).
All other cases follow the nature of the dharma itself; this should be reflected upon according to its meaning.
Furthermore, there are those who possess the dharmas of training (*śaikṣa*) up to those who have attained only the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

The commentary states: This explains the fourth category. The possession (*prāpti*) of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) follows the nature of the dharma and is thus outflowing (*sāsrava*).

The possession of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) follows its basis and is thus outflowing. Since the possession of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) which is realized follows the path and is thus outflowing, none of these are [unoutflowing].
Since it can be known that the learner (*śaikṣa*) is not the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), one may ask:

when a noble one (*ārya*) has already abandoned the afflictions of the three voids (*trivimokṣa*) during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), do they further cultivate the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths?

Furthermore, regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) obtained through the cultivation of the contaminated path during the stage of the non-learner, how is it explained that both paths obtain it? The explanation is as follows: that single unconditioned [is obtained by both].

Regarding the attainment of the limit realized by the two paths, it follows that which is empty: the attainment of the limit realized by the Noble Path belongs to those who are in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa);

the attainment of the limit realized by the contaminated path (sāsrava-mārga) belongs to those who are neither in training nor beyond training (naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa), following the contaminated path.
Furthermore, one sees that what is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) [is considered] up to what is not to be abandoned (aheya).
The commentary states: this explanation of the fifth section may be understood by analogy with the preceding.
As for the previous statement regarding the three times [up to]: "In the desire and form realms, there is no prior arising."

The commentary states: This is a further clarification and explanation; other categories can be understood by extension. Because there are doubts regarding the existence [of dharmas] across the three time periods, they are analyzed separately here.
Within this verse, all [dharmas] are cited that lack acquisition (*prāpti*) across the three times; those that possess it are not discussed.
The *Śāstra* says: "Unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) ... up to ... the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

The commentary states: This explains the first half [of the verse], clarifying that among the unobscured-neutral states, there are only two types—the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
Although the four aggregates (*skandha*) co-arising with these are themselves neutral, they are all produced by the power of superior preparatory effort (*prayoga-bala*).
Regarding those with powerful influence whose conduct (*iryāpatha*) is exemplary: because the mind is the basis upon which such conduct depends, it is called a "path.

As for those who have cultivated even a single aspect of this to an extreme degree—for example, when Kāśyapa saw the Buddha’s deportment and his heart was filled with joy, or when the Venerable Aśvajit and Śāriputra beheld him and were moved by admiration—such cases likewise constitute the accomplishment of the *śailpasthānika* (artistic or technical) attainments through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, because the mind is the basis for craftsmanship, it is said to "dwell in the midst" of its objects.

For those who have cultivated this to an extreme degree—such as Viśvakarman (in the language of Tang, "the Maker of All Distinctions" or "the Maker of Various Works"), the deity of supreme craftsmanship whom no artisan in the Western Regions fails to worship—these examples are likewise established through preparatory application (*prayoga*). Such dharmas are therefore [included].

There are three types of acquisition (*prāpti*) pertaining to the remaining all other resultant (*vipāka*) five aggregates, as well as the five aggregates of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*);
and one portion of deportment and craftsmanship that consists solely of mental factors (*dharma*). These are acquired simultaneously with the phenomenon itself.

Regarding those acquired through temporal cessation (*adhvan-viccheda*), they are accomplished in only one time period (*adhvan*), because they are accomplished in a single moment (*kṣaṇa-viccheda*), being achieved in a single instant. The four aggregates of the paths of deportment and craftsmanship [are likewise so acquired].
"One part possesses it in the world"—is this the correct meaning? If not, why was it not stated in the verse?
If it were not so, why would the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* not refute it by stating that this is the correct meaning? Thus, the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* says:

"One who possesses a wholesome mind of the desire realm, an unwholesome mind, or a concealed-neutral mind, necessarily possesses [the seeds] of the desire realm. Why does it not say "necessarily possess" [the mind itself]?

If the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) before one has entered a higher meditative absorption (*samādhi*), since the two types of unspecified minds do not exist prior to that attainment, how can it be established as fixed?
It is not mentioned in the verse because it is not exhaustive; it shall be further analyzed later regarding the subsequently attained mind (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-citta*).
"Although there are acquisitions (prāpti) preceding and following unobscured [neutral] dharmas...
[The commentary states: This explains the third phrase. In the desire realm, obscured [neutral] states cannot initiate karma;

the two meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) do not initiate karma because their minds lack vitarka and vicāra. Furthermore, they do not initiate karma [in the higher realms], except for the three great afflictions and deceit (*śāṭhya*) in the first dhyāna.

It should be understood that because the power of the obscured form arising from deceit and pride does not produce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), it is only the acquisition of the factors themselves;
thus, all four obscured aggregates have acquisitions belonging to the three time periods.
"Regarding the various forms (*rūpa*) of the desire realm...

up to and including those subsequently known and acquired. The commentary states: This explains the fourth phrase. It means that the wholesome and unwholesome forms of the desire realm—comprising both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter—are of a determinate nature (*vyākṛta*).

Therefore, there are dharmas whose acquisition occurs subsequent to them; because they do not coexist with the mind, there are no dharmas whose acquisition occurs prior to them. One should know this to apply to all cases.
The four aggregates of the unwholesome, the four aggregates of the wholesome in the desire realm and the formless realm, the five aggregates of the wholesome in the form realm,
and all uncontaminated four or five aggregates— all possess acquisitions (prāpti) belonging to the three time periods.
Having thus explained [the acquisition of dharmas] up to their being easily obtained and abandoned by others, the commentary states:
from here below, the distinctions of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are clarified. The first line is the analysis according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);

the second line is the analysis according to the three time periods (*tryadhvan*); the next three lines are the analysis according to the realm-attachments (*dhātupratisaṃyukta*); and the final line clarifies the timing of their abandonment.

The essence of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and it pertains to all three time periods and all three realms. However, in this present text, because the discussion is based on the dharmas that have not been acquired, there are distinctions.

If one follows the analysis of acquisition (*prāpti*), it should likewise be categorized as belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Nevertheless, when considering the initial statement—that it is exclusively indeterminate—it belongs to that which is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*) and is to be abandoned by cultivation.
Since the meaning is self-evident, it is not explained separately.
The *Śāstra* says: "As for the distinctions of nature (from...), they are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.

The *Vyākhyā* says: This explains the first phrase, clarifying that the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of all phenomena belonging to the three natures is invariably non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

As for their nature, all non-possessions (aprāpti) follow their respective bases; they are not produced by attention (manasikāra), are not objects of knowledge, and are comprised within the same category as the realms (dhātu), the homogeneous class (sabhāgatā), and out-flowing nature (niṣyandaja).
Regarding the distinction of time, it is because their nature is incompatible with [the nature of] the world.
The commentary states: This explains the second gate. Because one first knows the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of future dharmas that have not yet been attained, it pertains to all three time periods.
Because one knows past dharmas that have not been attained both before and after [their occurrence], they likewise pertain to the three time periods.

As for present dharmas, because they are currently being acquired, there is no non-acquisition in the present; this is because it is logically impossible for there to be a "non-acquisition" of what is currently being acquired.

Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) likewise does not exist [as a substantial entity], though there are two theories; their words differ but their meaning is the same. Before one has acquired [a dharma], there is past non-acquisition;
for those who have already been born, there is future non-acquisition. Although non-acquisition is intermingled with other factors, it exists as a nature that is not presently perceived.
"The distinction of realms (*dhātu-viśeṣa*) may be termed 'the nature of an ordinary person' (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Commentary: This explains the third point. Because non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) follows its basis, the non-acquisition of each individual dharma extends throughout the bonds of all three realms.
One might raise the objection that "leaked" (*sāsrava*) dharmas are not themselves leaked or bound to the three realms, whereas "unleaked" (*anāsrava*) dharmas [are].
Since non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) should be untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*aniyata*), it is explained by means of two propositions.

That is to say, the *Abhidharmakośa* accepts that the non-acquisition of the noble state constitutes the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). The essence of this nature of an ordinary person must certainly not be untainted;

this serves as scriptural proof that the essence of non-acquisition does not conform to the dharma that is not acquired, but rather conforms to its basis, because it arises dependently upon common conditions.

It cannot be said that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through wisdom is either untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*). Some might raise this objection:
"If the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of a noble one (*ārya*) by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) were tainted, then the non-acquisition of an ordinary person by a noble one should be untainted.

Likewise, if the non-acquisition of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) by one belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) were not included within the desire realm, then the non-acquisition of the desire realm by one belonging to the form realm should be included within the form realm."
All such difficulties should be resolved by considering the basis upon which they depend; thus, one’s mind may be said to have attained them.
This applies from the point of not yet having acquired any noble dharma up until the stage of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
The commentary states: This question concerns the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) up to the point of not attaining the dharmas.
Some say it refers to the non-possession of all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
The commentary states that there are three masters who explain this; this is the first. [It means that] within the ear of an ordinary person, all noble dharmas are...
Because they have not yet acquired [these qualities], the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is defined in relation to all [of them].
If this is so, does it not follow that [the state of being an ordinary person] would extend to all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*)?
[The author] replies: This is an objection raised by an outsider; since not all noble dharmas constitute the state of being an ordinary person, [the fault does not apply].
Since every sentient being possesses the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), they would all consequently be ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
However, there is no such fault, because there exists [a specific case of] not having obtained [them].

The commentary states: To resolve this objection, [it is explained that] if, within the continuum of a person, there is merely the non-acquisition of the various noble dharmas, this pure non-acquisition constitutes the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*);
however, if it is mixed with [other factors], it is not so. Therefore, there is no fault in the aforementioned [position].
If that were so, the root treatise should have used the word "exclusive" (*kevala*).

[The author] comments: This objection implies a further inquiry; if it were only the non-attainment of the exclusive [noble qualities] that constitutes the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), then the root treatise should have stated:
"What is the distinct nature? It is the exclusive non-attainment of the noble dharmas."
It is not so; it is called "unmixed" because it is not mixed with anything else.
The commentary states: This explanation clarifies that although the word "pure" (or "exclusive") is not explicitly used, its meaning is already evident.
For example, when it is said, "This person eats water," it is clearly understood that he does not eat anything else.
Some say: "Because one has not yet attained that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).

[The author] comments: This second explanation refers only to the case where the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering) has not yet been established;

it anticipates the objection that if it were produced by subsequent inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), then one who has abandoned the initial untainted state would still be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, he preempts this by stating: "But it is not so."

Regarding the first [type of] non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*), there are two kinds: first, that which depends on the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); second, that which depends on the body of a noble one (*ārya*).
That which depends on the body of an ordinary person is necessarily not conjoined with untainted knowledge; this is termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Since that [nature] has been permanently destroyed, even though it exists at present, it does not constitute the nature of an ordinary person when it depends on the body of a noble one, because it is conjoined with the untainted. If...

If there is a subsequent question regarding the first untainted [attainment] of the three vehicles, it should also be resolved by applying the principle of "pure non-attainment," as in the previous case;
the meaning can thus be understood by analogy with the explanation concerning all noble dharmas.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra), at this point, further states as follows.

[The author] comments: Since what follows is a detailed determination, he first cites from the *Abhidharmakośa* the explanation by the Sautrāntikas regarding the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is a provisional designation for a specific state within the continuum of the body of one in whom the noble dharmas have not yet arisen.
Regarding the definition of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), its intended meaning is explained as follows: the state of being an ordinary person has no real entity whatsoever.

The commentary states that this is because the intention of the Sūtra’s author is that the state of being an ordinary person lacks any distinct, substantial reality; therefore, he [the author] explains it in this way.
[The author] explains: If that is so, whose state is it that continues? The commentary states:
This inquiry asks, since the Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrāntika) has stated that this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), upon what is it established, and whose state is it?
This refers to the states within the continuity of the eye, ear, and so forth.
The commentary states: This explains the intention of the Sūtra’s author; it concerns the states of the eye and other faculties.
How could it be [the case that] a single moment [is the basis], for that would entail the fault of it not being real?

The commentary states: This is precisely to address the objection that there is no distinct nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) other than the non-arising of noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) such as the eyes and ears.
If the non-arising of noble dharmas were itself the nature of being an ordinary person, then at the very first moment [of arising], one would immediately be an ordinary person.

Conversely, if at that first moment one were not an ordinary person, then at that same moment one should have produced the noble dharmas. Yet, since the noble dharmas are not produced at that first moment, [the nature of being an ordinary person must be something distinct].
To claim that the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) exists only during the stage of continuity is certainly not the case;

for it seems they [the opponents] offer the explanation that form (*rūpa*) and so forth possess continuity within each moment. Therefore, [the author] refutes this by stating: "The term 'continuity' has the sense of a mutual relation between two [entities], whereas a moment is merely conventional (*prajñaptika*);
it would follow that the moment is not real, which contradicts your own school's tenets, since the Sautrāntikas assert [this]."
Because each moment (*kṣaṇa*) is a real dharma (*dravyadharma*).
This is not merely [the case] because it can be transcended. [The author] states:

this further surpasses [the objection that it is] merely a continuity; the statement [that they are] "simultaneous" contradicts [the claim that they are] distinct moments. This refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "nature" (*gotra*) is not distinct from "birth-nature" (*jāti-gotra*). This does not contradict the *Bhūmi-vyatikrama-sūtra*, which states:

"If one of dull faculties, having heard the instruction of another, is able to practice according to the teaching and practice in accordance with the Dharma, reaching up to the stage of patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), such a person is called a 'follower by faith' (*śraddhānusārī*)," and so on at length.
One should not fear that this scriptural passage refers to the "stage of different birth" (*bhūmi-vyatikrama*).

Without explicitly stating "the nature of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*), the text below immediately explains: "This stage of an ordinary person is itself the nature of being an ordinary person.

Furthermore, a question is asked: "By what reason is it known that this is the nature of being an ordinary person? The text below immediately answers: "Because it speaks of acquisition and abandonment.

That is to say, there is a sutra which states that at the moment of the cessation of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), one abandons the state of an ordinary person and acquires the nature of a noble one (*āryatva*). Furthermore...
A sutra states that the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) perishes simultaneously with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*),
while the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises simultaneously with the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the nature of an ordinary being.

Since it is said at that time that one acquires the noble dharmas and abandons the nature of an ordinary being, and since it is also said at this very moment that one enters into right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and transcends the stage of an ordinary being.
Therefore, it is known that the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanabhūmi*) is itself the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Fearing that [the opponent] might explain it by saying, "The nature of an ordinary person is defined as not having attained the dharmas of an ārya," [the author] states that at that time, this does not contradict the sūtra; hence, the following objection is raised:

"At that time, there is nothing whatsoever abandoned regarding the eyes, ears, and so forth, such that they could be known [to have been discarded], as is the case when one attains the dharmas of an ārya."
Since the eyes and so forth are all established as they were originally, there is nothing to be abandoned; this would thus contradict the Sūtra.
If it is argued that those in the evil destinies (up to... should not be ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), [the author] states:
"This restates the alternative position that takes the evil destinies as the nature of an ordinary being," and subsequently refutes it by saying, "Regarding patience (*kṣānti*)."
If one has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the miserable destinies while still in this state, one ought not to be a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).
If it is argued that [this state] reaches the stage of a worldling regarding the eyes and so forth, the commentary states:
this restates the counter-argument; that is, by transcending the passage concerning the eyes and so forth, the meaning becomes clearly evident.
This reasoning is also incorrect (up to the point where it says) "transcending the eye and so forth.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise refutes [the claim that] the eye and so forth are as they were originally; how then could there be transcendence?
If one says it is like realization (up to the point where it says) "transcending the eye and so forth," [then...]

The commentary states: This restates the opponent's defense, which claims that there are scriptural passages proving that one who has attained the fruit of no-more-learning transcends all contaminated phenomena;
how could it be that the eyes and so forth are not as they were originally?
This reasoning is also incorrect (up to the point where it says) "therefore the analogies are not equivalent.

The commentary states: When this master [Vasubandhu] refuted the proof regarding the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), he did so on the basis of the severance of fetters (*saṃyojana*), and thus termed it "transcendence" (*abhisamaya*).
Since the present case involves the complete transformation [of the faculties], it does not constitute a valid precedent.
If it is argued that [the sūtra] says, "up to transcending the evil destinies," the commentary states:
This restates the opponent's defense. Just as it is said that a stream-enterer can transcend the evil destinies, does this mean they have severed their fetters?
This case should be understood in the same way.
This reasoning is also incorrect (up to the point of "transcending what eyes, etc.").
The commentary states: This sets forth the principle to refute [the opponent's view].

It is called "transcending" because at the stage of the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), one never again performs karma leading to the three evil destinies, never again proceeds toward their fruits, and never again engages in afflictions (*kleśa*), having attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Therefore, it is named "transcending. Now...

If one asks how the eyes and other faculties, which are present within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), can be said to have "transcended" [the ordinary state], and if it is argued that there must be examples such as the nature of birth (*jātidharma*) and so forth—[the author] states:

"The following section addresses the external objection; therefore, he restates the opponent's challenge by saying: 'Apart from the body of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), there exists something distinct.'"

The nature of arising (*jāti*) should likewise exist separately from the jar and so forth, because there is a "jar-nature" and so on; thus, he restates that objection and refutes it as being incorrect.
This is because if a jar is not broken, its jar-nature is not lost; therefore, one knows that it has no separate entity [apart from the jar].

Furthermore, since the eye and other faculties do not lose their distinct natures of arising when they cease, one knows that they do have separate entities. Fearing that the opponent might again raise the objection regarding the natures of cows, horses, and so forth, [the author] says:
The general rule for negation is that because [the quality] exists or does not exist simultaneously with its substance, one knows there is no separate substance [for the quality].
If it is asked why this is not the case for the nature (*prakṛti*) of a Brahmin and so forth, the commentary states:
this restates the opponent's objection, such as when various people of the world—whether Vaiśyas or those who transgress the conduct of Kṣatriyas—[are still called Brahmins].
If the conduct of a brahmin can sometimes constitute being a brahmin, and if the conduct of a brahmin who performs defiled and evil deeds can result in his becoming a vaiśya or others—
then this nature of a brahmin and so forth would not be coexistent with the body and ought to have a separate substance;
why is it that there is no such separate [substance]?
Just as with noble ones and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is no fault [in this].

The commentary states: This master of the treatise resolves the objection by establishing a definitive distinction—namely, that while noble ones do not perform, do not approach, and do not practice [rebirth] in the three evil destinies, ordinary beings do approach and practice them;
thus, one understands the Dharma through the skillful application of intentional restraint.

Regarding such matters as the capacity for various evils or the ability to practice virtue, since these capacities exist within every nature, what fixed distinction is there upon which to establish those specific natures?

Even if there were some slight difference between the central regions and the borderlands due to intermediate causes, one should know that this is based solely on the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneity of group); there is no separate nature whatsoever.
"Is it not like [the case where one is called] an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) because one has not yet attained the noble Dharma?
The commentary states: This cites the nature of the noble ones (*āryatva*) as an example to raise a difficulty against the opponent.
This example is not valid; [it is only] when one has not yet attained the noble Dharma that this is the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains that ordinary beings lack untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, yet they possess the nature of being noble (*āryatva*); noble ones possess tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas, yet they lack the nature of being ordinary (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Fearing that others might object that since the miserable realms (*apāya*) and so forth are absent in noble ones, they ought therefore to be of the nature of ordinary beings, he subsequently adds the qualification "universally accomplished by ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanasamavāgata*) to definitively exclude such a possibility. Fearing further that others might [misinterpret this] as...
Because the two meanings [of being born into the same class] cannot be fully established for those who have already been born, it must be the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Therefore, in the second section below, "attainment of that which is contrary to the Noble Path" is further added to distinguish it from the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Furthermore, if there is a dharma (up to... that constitutes the nature of an ordinary person...
