The commentary states: Here, an opponent might raise an objection, asking: "How is it known that the essence of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) exists, given that it is not like form and so forth, which are known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor is it like the eye and so forth, whose existence can be inferred from their function? To resolve this, [it is said]:
This nature of an ordinary person acts as the cause for the production of the bodies of all ordinary persons; because it possesses this great function, its existence is known.

[The opponent asks: "If there is a common substratum (*sabhāgatā*), why is it necessary to have a separate 'nature of an ordinary being' (*pṛthagjanatva*)? [The text continues from] 'Are not karma and afflictions...?
The commentary states: The outsider objects that since karma and so forth are the causes of the body, what business has the nature of an ordinary being with them?"
This criticism is unreasonable... [up to] ...it can arise.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise replies that while the eyes and so forth arise from karma, they necessarily depend upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*);
likewise, the arising of this body depends upon the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*). Furthermore, through the power of mutual dependence, how could it be due to karma alone?
"Therefore, there is a distinct dharma" (up to) "it has great significance. The commentary states:

This [dharma] is known to have a distinct substantial entity because it possesses utility; that is, by transcending this [state], one is designated as being in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This interpretation does not contradict the scriptural teachings. If the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) did not exist, it would contradict the characteristics of the Noble Teachings.
The digression is concluded. [Question: When shall it be abandoned? [Response:
This section below explains the fourth [point], namely the reason why the preceding conclusion cited the inquiry regarding knowledge.
This dharma is non-acquisition; [the rest] should be considered by analogy with this.
The commentary states: Herein, there are initially two distinct ways in which non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is abandoned: first, it is abandoned because it is contrary to acquisition;

that is, at the moment one acquires a dharma, [the prior non-acquisition] is abandoned. Second, it is abandoned because it follows the body; that is, at the moment one changes planes of existence (*bhūmi*), [the prior non-acquisition] is abandoned.

Regarding this, the explanation of abandoning the non-acquisition of dharmas refers to the specific instances observed: when one attains the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), the non-acquisition of the three realms is abandoned for those who were previously ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the three realms.
Because one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding their nature, it is called "abandonment," though this does not mean abandoning the three realms all at once.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "abandoning" refers to abandoning the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) within the three realms—just as it is said that one cuts off the roots of goodness in the three realms—and so on, up until the stage of Arhatship.
Regarding those who attain liberation at an improper time (*asamayavimukta*), they transcend two types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*) during the interval.

Therefore, it is said "up to" (*yāvat*) because the explanation also includes those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) with sharp or dull faculties; thus it says "up to," as the rest is easy to understand.
Furthermore, how is this non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) termed "abandoned"?
The commentary states: This explains the abandonment of dharmas.
If it is not the acquisition (*prāpti*) that is severed, then [the question arises] how one abandons non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
The commentary states: This explains the function of abandoning dharmas. [Objection: Since non-acquisition is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it would only exist for a single moment.
Regarding the second moment in relation to the prior non-acquisition (*aprāpti*): since one no longer possesses it, there is a non-acquisition of that knowledge.
Because this non-acquisition is abandoned moment by moment, how can it be said that "one acquires the dharma and only then abandons the non-acquisition"? The explanation is as follows:

what is here called "abandoning" refers to the total exhaustion of a particular category [of non-acquisition], not the abandonment of a mere portion; it is the non-acquisition that is abandoned when its acquisition is severed.
This means that there is no further continuity of such knowledge as there was prior to entering the state of a noble one;

because the continuity of the acquisition of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) has ceased, it is called "abandonment. This refers to the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of this entire category of non-acquisition, not merely a partial non-acquisition—this can be understood by reflecting upon it.
Acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) do not necessarily arise simultaneously.

The commentary states: Fearing that there might be an objection—namely, that acquisition itself would possess a non-acquisition, which would result in an unobscured [neutral] state—he now uses the mutual acquisition of acquisitions and non-acquisitions to dispel the infinite regress of acquisition, non-acquisition, and the negations thereof; how much more so for those who are not [subject to such].

If the innate *paryavasthāna* were [itself] non-possession (*aprāpti*), there would be the fault of infinite regress. Why? Because one does not possess what is presently manifest, yet it is currently accomplished.

Furthermore, regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a craft, there can be no further non-possession; rather, it is only at the second moment that the non-possession of knowledge is lost and its possession is attained.
Therefore, while it is conventionally termed "non-possession" because it is the non-possession of non-possession, in reality, it should be understood as being like the subsequent moment.
Regarding the attainment of attainment (*prāpti-prāpti*): although it is attained by means of attainment, it is still called "attainment" because it is not the case that it is not attained;

therefore, it cannot be designated as "non-attainment. For example, when a single dharma possesses [attainments], at the first moment there are three dharmas, at the second moment there are six dharmas, and at the third moment there are eighteen dharmas. It is thus.

When one attains [the first], one loses one dharma; at the moment of the first thought-moment, there is one non-possession-knowledge (*aprāpti-jñāna*); at the moment of the second thought-moment, there are two non-possession-knowledges;
at the third thought-moment, there are [three]—one should reflect upon this accordingly as it truly is.
Furthermore, because [non-acquisition] shifts from a lower stage [upward].
The commentary states: This explanation also allows us to see the meaning that [non-acquisition] is abandoned upon changing stages, as it follows its basis.
Thus has been explained [the categories] up to "homogeneous character" (*sabhāgatā*) and "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
The commentary states: From here below begins the second major section, which clarifies the "homogeneous character" (*sabhāgatā*).

"Homogeneous character" is the heading of the chapter; "sentient beings," etc., indicates its essential nature. This means that the homogeneous character has only the categories of sentient beings and so forth as its nature.
The term "sentient beings" is used to exclude non-sentient things; this excludes those that are not of the same category. Such is the meaning of the phrase "sentient beings," etc.

Furthermore, if one considers both the object and the agent as identical, then "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is the essence of sentient beings, being a state of equality. If explained through the *samānādhikaraṇa* (co-referential) construction, then "sentient beings" themselves are the equality.
If the object of equality is the sentient beings, then the term "equality" indicates that homogeneity is the agent of that equality;

thus it is called "equal," and because it is similar, it is called "equal. This is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) construction: the meaning of "sentient beings" is designated as "sentient beings" by virtue of their equality.
"Equality" refers to the equality of sentient beings; that is, they are similar.
Thus, "sentient beings are equal," yet in this statement, one does not simultaneously cite their effects to clarify their cause within the same homogeneous class (*sabhāga*).
The *Śāstra* says: "There is a distinct, real entity (up to) called 'homogeneity' (*nikāya-sabhāga*). The *Vyākhyā* states:
Regarding this treatise, first the main doctrine is elucidated, and subsequently external objections are addressed. Within the elucidation of the doctrine, there are six sections:

first, showing the essence; second, stating the name; third, explaining the function; fourth, interpreting the name; fifth, identifying the basis; and sixth, determining the stage of abandonment. There exists a distinct, real entity.

Regarding the three interpretations of "things" (*vastu*) as "objects," "sentiments," and "successive categories," the second interpretation is superior and thus indicates the essential nature (*tattva*).

The *Mūla-śāstra* refers to this as the "homogeneous character" (*nikāya-sabhāga*). It is designated by the name "recollection" (*smṛti*). Because it is the cause for the similarity among many phenomena, it is called "homogeneous character."
Regarding "arising in a single destination and so forth" (up to) "because there are distinctions":
the treatise states that the function of arising in a single destination, a single birth, a single realm, a single stage, a single lineage, and so forth,
refers to the activities performed by the various faculties according to their respective common forms, sizes, and arrangements among those born therein.
The food they consume is all mutually similar; this serves as the cause [of their similarity] and acts as the formative cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the characteristics of that class.

If *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) did not exist, there would necessarily be no sense of mutual similarity or shared pleasure regarding these characteristics. Since similarity and pleasure arise through the power of *sabhāgatā*, one might raise the objection:
"Since birth in a particular realm (*gati*) and so forth occurs by the power of karma, what business has *sabhāgatā* with it? To address this, the following explanation is given:

For example, when a single sentient being is present, because it is produced by the four great elements induced by the present mind and is derived from the primary elements previously brought forth by karma, it possesses three types of causes;
therefore, although its physical form and so forth are identical [to others], it is also due to the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) that this is so.
How is this known? It is seen in the world that while the size and proportions of the bodies of those distinguished by similar karma are alike, their various sense faculties differ.

The distinctions between beauty and ugliness, the presence of superiority or inferiority, and the differences in food and drink— all these should be known to arise from the variations in the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class), due to the cause of karma.
If it is argued that this distinction arises from the *paripūraka-karma* (completing karma):

The commentary states: This passage cites the external explanation that because the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) is the same, the physical form is equal; yet because the completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) differs, the sense faculties and so forth are distinct.
It is not due to the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*).
Such reasoning would be untenable [if it were] as far as the distinctions in function and so forth are concerned.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise raises an objection regarding those with outflows (*sāsrava*).

Even if it were as you say, or even if it is only because the power of the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is superior that one is said to "receive" the fruit, how could the distinction between the projecting karma and the completing karma (*abhinirvartaka-karman*) not be due to the existence of the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
"If [the body and so forth] were [to perish], they should not exist.

The commentary states: This restates the opponent's thesis and challenges it with reasoning. It is clearly observed that there are people who first practice one type of karma and later abandon it to perform another;
if [karma] were to perish [simply by being abandoned], it would be impossible to reach such a state, as there would be no present possibility for modification.
It is clarified that because [beings] are similar by virtue of their *sabhāgatā*, *sabhāgatā* is known to be the cause of the karma that produces such similarity.
In this context, it is called *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) because the physical forms [of beings] are alike. The commentary states:

this explains the etymology; since the bodily karma is similar, it is termed "same" (*sama*), and because it is a portion (*bhāga*) of that which has the sense of being the same, it is called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
This can be understood by analyzing it according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
Thus, regarding "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) [up to] "the aggregates, bases, and elements" (*skandhāyatana-dhātu*).
The commentary states: "This explains the basis; that is, because 'devas' and so forth are spoken of in reference to sentient beings," and so on at length for the others.
Regarding these three realms of existence, if one considers their actual meaning, the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is not unitary;

that is to say, there are immeasurable distinctions such as the three realms, five destinies, four modes of birth, forty-two abodes, or the central and peripheral regions, male and female bodies, Brahmin and other castes, lay followers (*upāsaka*) and monks (*bhikṣu*), those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and so forth. If explained according to the Dharma, it corresponds to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so on.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable [factors] that all rely upon internal phenomena and do not pertain to insentient things. Within the *Abhidharmakośa*, regarding the single dharma of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) for one sentient being:
the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) and the homogeneity of dharmas (*dharma-sabhāgatā*). Furthermore, the homogeneity of sentient beings is of two kinds:
first, that which is without distinction, meaning that the homogeneity of sentient beings exists equally in all sentient beings; second, that which has distinctions...
The so-called "distinctive realm" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) refers to the fact that each class of sentient beings possesses it equally.
The *pṛthagjana-sabhāga* (the homogeneity of ordinary worldlings) is abandoned upon reaching *nirvāṇa*.
[Commentary: This refers to the stage of abandonment; two types have been briefly cited, and the others may be inferred accordingly. In summary, setting these aside—

Because those types [of beings] abandon their respective homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), the *Abhidharmakośa* establishes four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on the acquisition and abandonment of death and birth:
there is death and birth without abandonment; this refers to dying in one place and being reborn in that same place.
There are also cases where there is abandonment without death and birth, and cases where both occur together or neither occurs; these propositions can be understood through reflection.
"Is it not the case that the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is itself the commonality of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*)?

[The commentary] states: From here below, he addresses the external objections; specifically, he addresses the five successive difficulties established by the Master of the Sūtras (Vasubandhu) within the *Abhidharmakośa*.

This is the first difficulty: at the moment one attains the first untainted state (*anāsrava*), one abandons the nature of an ordinary being and the commonality of ordinary beings. At the time of such abandonment—
Since they share the same path yet possess distinct entities, this should not be so;
[the opponent argues that] one abandons [the former] but does not obtain [the latter].

The commentator states: This master of the treatise resolves the objection by noting that although the activity is abandoned simultaneously, the functions are distinct; therefore, we know there are distinct entities performing these actions.

Because their functions and causes are identical, they are termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*); yet, because one abandons the homogeneous nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and acquires the homogeneous nature of a noble one (*ārya*), and because this contradicts the establishment of the state of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) through the attainment of the Noble Path, one abandons the state of being an ordinary being and does not acquire the state of a noble one.
Since there is still the conception of being an ordinary being within the body of a noble one, and because their functions are distinct, it is clearly known that they are different entities.
"Non-material *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) has no distinct entity or category.
[The commentary] states: This Master of the Sūtras raises a second objection below: since non-material *sabhāgatā* cannot be perceived by the senses, how can its existence be known?
Previously, there was no distinct function; there is no distinct entity, namely the body and so forth; and there is no distinct category, namely the marks such as teeth.
Although the *Abhidharmakośa* states that [the effect] has no function, we have already demonstrated its function; therefore, it is set aside here without further discussion.
This is because one perceives its fruit and thereby attains direct realization of it.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise maintains that perceiving no distinct fruit while knowing there is a common cause constitutes inference (*anumāna*).

For the practitioner, however, this is also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), namely, the mind that perceives suffering and pleasure when one who has cultivated the tainted path (*sāsravamārga*) feels weary of their own homogeneous class and contemplates the truths.
"Why do you not allow that insentient things possess a commonality (*sabhāgatā*)?

The commentary states: This is the third objection: "If humans and others, who are similar [to one another], already possess a commonality, why do things such as manifest action (*vijñapti*), which are also similar, not possess a commonality?"
"One should not [hold] thus" (up to) "millet, beans, and so forth would arise.

The commentary states: This master of the treatise responds that if one were to object in this way, then even for those such as the gods who possess a homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), it would follow that they too must have birth and a realm of rebirth (*gati*), which would lead to a great logical error.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, [stated that] there is a distinct *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity).

The commentary states: This is the second explanation. Since the Buddha has not explicitly taught it, and because its principle lies beyond the reach of words, one must further investigate and discern the Buddha’s intention:
upon what basis does it rely solely on sentient beings, and by what reasoning is its actual existence known? Regarding this, there are five layers of explanation; first:
Regarding the two explanations of the first and last [categories], and the single combined explanation of the middle one: this refers to the first.

Because sentient beings each possess similar inclinations and desires, the "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) and so forth are established; since these do not exist among non-sentient things, there is no such homogeneity there.

However, according to the Sautrāntika masters in the *Abhidharmakośa*, [the term] is used because they give rise to similar cognition and linguistic conventions regarding phenomena and sentient beings.
It is said that even insentient things share a "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) because they are designated by a common cognition and awareness; thus,

by taking insentient things as the basis for the objection, this author of the treatise has already skillfully resolved that objection by establishing that homogeneity consists in the similarity of respective cognitions.
Furthermore, it is necessarily because of sentient beings [up to] that one speaks of "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
The commentary states: This second point is based on the fact that the external exists because of the internal; thus it is explained in terms of the internal.
Moreover, it is proven by prior karma that this is a real entity (dravya).
The commentary states: This third section establishes the existence of the fruit by means of two internal causes.

First, because there is diligence (*vīrya*) within that which has been acquired as a homogeneous class of rebirth (*nikāya-sabhāga*) through the influence of prior karma; second, because such diligence is not present in the aforementioned [non-existent] categories.
Thus, based on these two internal factors, it is proven that the fruit exists. Question: Are fragrances and so forth the dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*) of karma, and do they arise from diligence?

Regarding the question of whether [the fruit] arises from being planted and grown, the explanation states that both [the seed and the fruit] depend on the internal [conditions] and do not exist inherently of themselves. Furthermore, even if they were nominally present at a distant time, they would be non-existent;
moreover, it is through this process that the wood, lacquer, and so forth arise.

The commentary states: This fourth point holds that although images and actual forms are largely similar, because only the actual form gives rise to true speech, we know that within internal phenomena there must be real entities to serve as the basis for true speech; thus, it is clearly understood that they are distinct.
If they were not distinct, then since color and other qualities are similar, one would have to say that both are equally real.
Furthermore, because it was previously stated [up to] "because there is a distinction.
The commentary says: This fifth repetition refers back to the same explanation above; since there are differences, one knows that there is a distinct entity.
"Are these various *sabhāgatās* [the objects of] the designation of 'cognition'?
The commentary states: This fourth objection asks, since they are already *sabhāgatās*, how can they obtain the expression "cognition of a common awareness"?
"By means of the various *sabhāga* [factors]... the nature of matter (*rūpa*) is established.
The commentary states: Since this master [Vasubandhu] maintains that the cause is common (*sāmānya-hetu*), its essence is indeed common;

just as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves constitute the nature of matter, so too the "cause for the designation of cognition" mentioned here should be understood as the wisdom within the body, as previously explained.

The designation of "perception" (saṃjñā) may also be understood through mutual similarity based on the commonality of the object (ālambana-sabhāgatā), as well as through the single liberation resulting from the various aforementioned distinct causes.
Apart from these external factors, there is no such thing as "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā);
this [treatise] should clarify and establish the category of "similarity and difference" (sārūpya-vairūpya).

The commentary states: This is the fifth objection. Because you maintain that the *sattva-sabhāgatā* (homogeneity of sentient beings) pervades all sentient beings, it is identical to the Vaiśeṣika school’s category of *mahāsāmānya* (the great universal).

This corresponds to the fourth truth, the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*). Furthermore, all other [categories] that possess distinctions are identical to the Vaiśeṣika category of *viśeṣa* (particularity), which is the fifth truth.
If the Vaiśeṣika school holds [such views] (up to the point where they) should not be accepted, the commentary states:
This master [of the treatise] refutes the tenets of the Vaiśeṣikas, which differ from this [position].

They hold that a single dharma pervades multiple dharmas, its essence is eternal, and it only conjoins with dharmas when based upon the truth of combination (*saṃyoga*), and so forth—these are the differences. If...

If this distinct commonality does not exist, how could they encounter one another? How could the words of those outsiders—who claim that what is seen is form—compel the disciples of the Buddha to say it is not form?
In terms of logical correctness, which is right? To debate with outsiders is difficult for even the wise; it is something for which the intelligent feel ashamed.
The *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) has already been explained [up to] its maturation (*vipāka*) residing in the Bṛhatphala heaven.

The commentary states: From here below, the third major section clarifies the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*). First, it clarifies the place of birth, namely, among the gods who lack sense-faculties;
second, it clarifies its essential nature, namely, the cessation of mind and mental factors; third, it clarifies the five matters of analysis, namely, that it is exclusively a [result of] maturation.
The matured [state] of the four clarities (*caturvidha-vyākhyāna*) has its basis in the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
The treatise says: "If one is born among the sentient beings of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
The commentary states: This explains the place of birth; because within that heaven there is non-conception for a long period of time, it is therefore named "Non-conception," although...

Furthermore, the mind and its concomitants are also extinguished; because when one originally practiced meditative concentration, one was solely averse to perception (*saṃjñā*), it was established by the name "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*).
Fearing that this might be confused with plants and trees, the term "sentient being" (*sattva*) is used. Here, "sentient" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*);

although that state lacks the various sense faculties, it is the basis for the substance of consciousness, and thus it is described as a "sentient being" by way of analogy. Alternatively, those gods may possess both portions [of the two types of cessation].

The state of being without mind is called "unconscious" (asaṃjñika), while the state of having mind is called "sentient being" (sattva); taken together, that heaven is designated as their place of birth.
There exists a phenomenon capable of [obstructing] [the flow], like a dam blocking a river.
The commentary states: This explanation of its essential nature means that there is a distinct dharma capable of rendering the mind and its associates temporarily incapable of cognition;
because it causes perception (*saṃjñā*) to cease, it is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñika*), named according to its function.
This dharma extends exclusively [up to] what is called the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).
The commentary states: This explains that the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) is the maturation induced by the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*);

from the passage below, it generally describes the main point that those who cultivate the signless (*animitta*) all perceive the physical forms and exquisite features of the bodies of those gods through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

Perceiving that which is tranquil, unmoving, possessed of form, yet devoid of mind as being *nirvāṇa*, one conceives a longing for it and cultivates the concentration of the mindless state (*acittaka-samādhi*), hoping to realize it.
Therefore, that aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) along with its signless phenomena (*animitta-vastu*) is definitely produced solely by the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*);

because this [attainment] is not karma, it cannot project a common destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*) or the characteristics of life (*jīvita-nimitta*). Prior to entering the state of non-perception, [the practitioner] [cultivates this].
After emerging from the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*), for a long time there are the four aggregates of mind and mental factors;

there is no fault in their being the fruition (*vipāka*) and the common operation of determinate karma (*niyata-karma*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "The state of non-conception lacks meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and cannot produce the basis for receiving a body.

Why? Because it is not karma itself. Karma alone can produce the basis for receiving a body and can obtain the faculties (*indriya*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); the state of non-conception does not."

Regarding the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and other such states, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, these share the same faculties (*indriya*). It is argued that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), such as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), is also shared;
however, commentators differ in their interpretations. All agree that the five faculties are generally not produced by karma (*akarmaja*), yet there is no other precedent for this elsewhere.
Nevertheless, because the force of the meditative attainment of non-conception is so powerful, it is able to induce the five faculties, unlike the case of the life-faculty produced by karma.
Since the faculties mentioned above are both prolonged and simultaneous, although they are not collectively a maturation (*vipāka*), they are nonetheless the primary sustainers of the body;
therefore, they too are produced solely by karma. This is because it is taught that those gods possess many minds, and one might otherwise object to the name "Non-ideation" (*asaṃjñin*);
thus, the meaning of the name is explained by way of what is predominant.
"Sentient beings without perception" (up to the point where they are) called the Heaven of No-Perception.
[The commentary] states: This question-and-answer sequence clarifies that both [the body and the mind] have a common basis.
That [basis] arises through karma; thus, both types exist simultaneously.
The commentary states: One might raise the objection that, as the Buddhist sūtras teach, all sentient beings subsist on nutriment;
yet in that state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), all four types of nutriment are absent—how, then, can they remain? Therefore, it is now explained:

they subsist by means of the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) consisting of past karma, which is drawn forth by the mind at the moment of rebirth and serves as a support until they enter the state of non-conceptual mind without interruption.

Furthermore, both minds may serve as the "projecting" and "sustaining" conditions for the consciousness-food (*vijñānāhāra*), and since the contact associated with that consciousness constitutes the contact-food (*sparśāhāra*), in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*) there exist only the three past foods.

Since these foods are absent [in that state], it follows that in the state of possession of mind (*sacittaka*), there must also be present food; otherwise, the substance of the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) would not function as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Regarding the question of why this is explained here as "nutriment" (*āhāra*):

it means that the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) of the mind at the moment of rebirth draws forth the prior mind of the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) in that realm; thus, it is called nutriment.
If that [rebirth-linking mind] were absent, the entity of the non-conception of that heaven could not arise. Furthermore, one may also consider it from the perspective of its emergence.

Because the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñika*) serves as a nutriment and supporting condition through its immediate contiguity (*samanantara-pratyaya*), those sentient beings [experience] karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*).
The commentary states: This explains that because those gods rely on conceptual cognition (*saṃjñā-jñāna*), they mistakenly claim it is *nirvāṇa*, rather than the true ultimate goal.
When one realizes that the slander of cessation on that stage is a false view, one abandons that lifespan and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by the power of prior karma.
Since one no longer exerts further cultivation, like an arrow falling to the ground, one returns to birth in the desire realm.

Because there is no karma for the desire realm remaining once one has been born among those gods, there must necessarily be no karma to be experienced in subsequent lives; for it is certain that those born in Uttarakuru will be reborn in the heavens.

The karma for rebirth in heaven that was previously created as *anāgata-vedanīya* (to be experienced in a subsequent life) may instead give rise to *upapadya-vedanīya* (to be experienced in the next life);
the meaning of its being "fixed" (*niyata*) is the same, as it is similar to [karma] that is not *anāgata-vedanīya*.
The non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) has already been analyzed [up to the point that] it is not attained by noble ones and lasts for one lifetime.
The commentary states: From here below, the fourth major section clarifies the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). This consists of: (1) the summary introduction;

(2) the specific names; (3) the analysis of their characteristics; and (4) the basis of the body. The summary introduction and the specific names can be seen according to the text. Within the analysis of their characteristics, the non-conceptual attainment is explained first.

Following the section on meditative concentration, this explains the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by way of six points within the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*): first, clarifying its intrinsic nature, which is like the preceding mind and so forth;
second, clarifying its dependence on others, namely the subsequent dhyāna; third, clarifying its mental application, which is the seeking of liberation;

fourth, clarifying its inclusion within the categories of moral quality, which is exclusively wholesome; fifth, clarifying the results it attracts, which are exclusively to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*); and sixth, clarifying the practitioner who cultivates it.
That is, the seven types of clear realization (vidyā-samudāgama) attained by noble beings and ordinary beings are acquired for the first time in a single lifetime.
The *Śāstra* says: "As previously explained... [up to] it is the same as the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñin*).

The commentary (*Vivaraṇa*) states: This explains the essential nature (*svabhāva*), meaning that such a connection is an illustration of the preceding principle; it refers to that which can extinguish the mind and its mental factors.

It is the same for the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Because one enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) through the correct accomplishment [of the preparatory stages], it is so called.
The commentary states: This explains the name of the "attainment of non-conception. Here, the term "attainment" (*ding*, *ding*) is, in Sanskrit, *samāpatti*; in the language of Tang, it is...
The term "attainment" (*samāpatti*) is designated as "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*) for the sake of linguistic convenience;

that is, because the essence of the non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is a continuity of the true nature (*samyaktva*) capable of accomplishing great function, it is called an "attainment. This signifies the meaning of reaching great function through equality.

Alternatively, the word "equal" (*sama*) indicates the sense of ultimate limit, meaning that one reaches the furthest extent of hearing [the teachings]; thus it is named "attainment" (*samāpatti*). Or again—

Based on the meaning of "equilibrium" (*samāpatti*), it is explained as "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*). Other masters interpret it as follows: because it is "according to principle" (*yoniśas*)—being wholesome and correct—it is called "equal" (*sama*);

and because it proceeds in a continuous succession according to conditions, it is called "attainment" (*āpatti*). Among the mental factors, it causes the mind, the mental factors, and their basis—the primary elements—to proceed in equilibrium;
therefore, it is called "equilibrium-attainment. This non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is able to bring about this state.
Because it proceeds with the great elements in equilibrium, it is called "equipoise" (*samāpatti*); because this dharma possesses the aforementioned meanings, it is named "equipoise.

Because it is equipoise, it is called "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*). Why is it called the "attainment of non-perception"? Within the body of a person (*pudgala*) who has entered this state, there is no perception;
thus it is called "non-perception. This meditative concentration belongs to one who is non-perceptive; based on the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) analysis, it is termed "non-perception."

The established name for this is "the attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Alternatively, because perception (*saṃjñā*) is incompatible with that attainment, the attainment itself is called "non-perception";

this is an interpretation based on shared dependence. Fearing that there might be an objection—namely, that since both mind and mental factors are extinguished in that attainment, why is it designated specifically as "non-perception"?—the text below provides the explanation:
perception is the coarsest and most active [of the mental factors] and is what is to be shunned; therefore, [the attainment] is named after that which ceases first.

Because it is established as a name, it is merely called "non-perception. Since ordinary beings and others who have entered this meditative absorption do not yet feel aversion toward sensation (*vedanā*), and because sensation is associated with perception (*saṃjñā*), when perception ceases, sensation and the other [mental factors] also cease.
"In what stage does this meditative absorption reside? (up to) "it resides in the dhyānas and not elsewhere.
The commentary states: This explains the basis upon which it relies.
One should not say [that it resides elsewhere], for one cultivates that cause within those [dhyānas].

The commentary states: Furthermore, others raise this objection: "If it is intended to state that this absorption occurs prior to the maturation of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*), and yet later in the section it is said that the Non-Conceptual Abode (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) is within the Bṛhatphala heaven, and since the fruit of the higher dhyāna has already been revealed, its cause must necessarily follow;
why then labor to state here that it relies on the stage of the higher dhyāna?"
This criticism is not valid. [The opponent argues: "It serves as the cause for non-conception.
[The author] replies: This proponent of the treatise has never stated that it serves as the cause for non-conception.
Is it not previously stated in the verse that it is the fruit of the attainment of non-conception?
The commentary states: Furthermore, others raise an objection regarding the preceding verse’s explanation that "non-conception is the fruit of non-conception.
This very statement reveals that this meditative absorption (samādhi) is the cause of non-conception; thus, it has already been explained.
This is also not the case; it is only now that the explanation is established.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise answers the previous lack of a verse by stating that it is only now that [the meaning] is clearly established.
How could one take the subsequent text based on the previous explanation? That is to say, the subsequent text does not state [this] within the following verse.
Why is this concentration called the concentration of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-samādhi*)?
[The author] states: The following explains the mental application (*manasikāra*); thus, he cites the sūtra’s mention of the concentration of ordinary beings as a question to investigate its meaning.
It is called the concentration of ordinary beings because it seeks liberation [up to that point].
The commentary states: This explanation of the sūtra text clarifies the mental application (*manasikāra*) of seeking liberation.

It means that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) grasp the fruit of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-phala*) as the true truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), liberation, and nirvāṇa, and they reckon the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as the means of transcendence.

Since they are born [into that state], they must rely upon the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) to cultivate practice and realize the fruit of liberation before they can cultivate this meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The noble ones (*ārya*), however, are not like this.

Only the meditative attainments of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) are called "attainments of ordinary beings. This explains the verse’s statement that one enters [this attainment] preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of seeking liberation.
It was previously stated that the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
The commentary states: Fearing that there might be an objection—namely, why the aforementioned [state] was not excluded from the category of the neutral (*avyākṛta*)—it is now explained:
the previous statement that it is "ripened-neutral" (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) establishes this by itself.
"Is it not the case that this [is] the maturation (*vipāka*) of the five aggregates? [The author] comments:

This is an objection raised by an outsider; since it is clearly understood that the cause of maturation (*vipākahetu*) is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*), why is it necessary to laboriously state that it is "virtuous"?
"Not so," [it is argued]. [The verse] from "In the verse" up to "who else could prevent it?"—the commentary states:

This master of the treatise answers that because the verse has not yet stated [them] as being the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), he must state that the wholesome is the cause, so that the meaning may be made manifest.
Furthermore, although he does not explicitly say "wholesome," when he speaks of the cause of maturation, this excludes both the undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
As for the claim that the masters of the West also maintain that this text refers to the defiled-neutral being subsumed under the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), I say this is not so.
This is because [defilements] in the form realm are solely the fruits of one's own karma;
they cannot induce the causes and effects of the desire realm; and because neutral phenomena are not stable or substantial. Thus, it is stated in various treatises.

Since it is taught that only unwholesome and wholesome *sāsrava* (contaminated) dharmas function as *vipāka-hetu* (ripening causes), I privately maintain that the Master’s statement here deviates from his own tenet.
Alternatively, because all afflictions (*kleśa*) can nourish rebirth, they may be designated as *vipāka-hetu* by way of figurative inclusion;

thus, the present mention of "wholesome" is intended to exclude them. Furthermore, another explanation states: the subsequent phrase, "to be experienced in the next life" (*upapadyavedanīya*), clarifies what is being summoned [by the cause].

Since the maturation of karma moistened by afflictions follows along with it and likewise possesses the sense of being "conducive to experience," one must refute [the notion that such karma is not so].

Within this context, it is also clarified that the maturation produced by the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is the five aggregates of the gods who lack sense faculties (*arūpya-devas*).
If that were so, one should say here "exclusively wholesome" (*kevalakuśala*).

The commentary states: An external opponent objects that if it were merely said "wholesome," it would not exclude other natures; since the intention is to exclude them, the word "exclusive" (*kevala*) must be stated.
"Not so; by excluding [other categories], it is already shown that it is not anything else.

The commentary states: Although this master of the treatise does not explicitly state "pure," the meaning of "pure" is already implied, just as it was explained in the context of *pṛthagjanatva* (the nature of an ordinary person).

Furthermore, he provides the analogies of food, water, and wind. Moreover, when he simply says "wholesome" (*kuśala*), it is understood that he is speaking of the wholesome itself and not implying other natures.
It is understood from this that [this attainment] does not exist. Since this meditative absorption is "attained" (*prāpta*), for what kind of feeling (*vedanā*) is it conducive?
The commentary states: the following section explains the ripening of its fruit; therefore, it first raises an interrogative inquiry.
"Only to be experienced in the next life" (upapadyavedanīya), and so on, is not based on possession (*prāpti*).

The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains the statement of a certain class of Dharma masters as follows: "Only to be experienced in the next life. I have explained this according to reason to resolve the case of those born with indeterminate [karma].

That is to say, when various non-Buddhists, having attained this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), turn their minds toward the noble state and enter the Path; once the Noble Path has arisen, [the karma] is transformed.

It is certainly not the case that "certainly" (*avaśyam*) refers to the knowledge [of the fruit] based on what is practiced by those who are not noble ones (*anārya*), nor does it refer to the possession [of the fruit];

for once one enters the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), one will certainly not receive [the fruit] again. In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the Master of the Sūtras (Vasubandhu) did not adopt such a correct interpretation;

rather, regarding the previous master’s explanation that "knowledge is not simultaneous with the mind," he stated that this certainty refers to the attainment [of the fruit] through falling away (*parihāṇi*). It must be understood as referring to knowledge.
One who attains this concentration will certainly not enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*); to lack faith in this [teaching] may be called "cleverness.
Furthermore, it is permitted that one does not delight in entering this concentration.
The commentary states: This explanation concerns the practitioner; this concentration is common to both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those outside the Buddha’s disciples.
This dharma of the "attainment of non-ideation" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is something cultivated and attained in common by various non-Buddhists (tīrthika), but not by the noble ones (ārya).
Since it is contaminated (sāsrava), when the noble ones contemplate it, they feel only weariness and aversion; it produces the fruit of birth and death, and is likened to a sail.
Because one must cultivate it with the thought of seeking liberation, it is not practiced by the noble ones. This is what is stated in this passage.

Regarding this dharma, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) cultivates it and thereby realizes what was previously cultivated, they enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*). Those who possess "favorable but indeterminate" karma are all said to be ordinary persons;
as for the unwholesome [karma], the noble ones are explained as being only those who cultivate it while remaining ordinary persons.
The verse has already stated [up to the point where it says] "it would be useless.

The commentary states: This is the Master of the Treatise refuting the prolixity of the verse; having already declared that seeking liberation constitutes mental attention (*manasikāra*), there is no need to laboriously further explain that non-noble cultivation is not required.
Regarding the question, "When this is first attained, how many time periods (*adhvan*) are attained?
the commentary states that the following section explains the breadth and narrowness of the attainment of the time periods; thus, it first poses the inquiry.
This [attainment] occurs within various stages (*avasthā*) and is not obtained through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya*).
The commentary states: This is the formal explanation of the various stages.

In both the initial and final stages, because one either attains the *prātimokṣa* as in the Desire Realm or attains what was previously unobtained, one does not acquire the past [discipline] at the time of the first meal.

If one were to acquire the past, it would not be called "previously unobtained," for due to the absence of mind, one does not cultivate the future; thus, one acquires only one period [of time]. Regarding the second meal and so forth...
If the mind has not yet known [an object], it always possesses the present and also accomplishes the past, thereby constituting two time periods.
Once one has emerged from a state of non-cognition (*acittaka*), one abandons the former [past] and no longer possesses the present, but only accomplishes the past.

Fearing that there might be an objection—asking why the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) does not induce knowledge of the future—one uses the examples of the divine eye and ear faculties to provide a comprehensive explanation; however, because such a cause does not exist, [the objection is resolved].
Because it is mental, one does not cultivate it in the future; because it is wholesome, there is an attainment subsequent to its arising but no prior attainment;
and because it is acquired through a specific cultivation apart from the attainment through detachment from defilements, it is acquired solely through application (*prayoga*).
Next is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), up to thirty-four moments of thought. The commentary states:

from here below, the characteristics of the attainment of cessation are clarified. Within this, first, its essential nature is explained, meaning that as previously described, it is the extinction of the mind and so forth;

second, the mental application (*manasikāra*) is explained, meaning the seeking of abiding in tranquility; third, the basis of the stage (*bhūmi*) is explained, meaning it relies upon the meditative absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

1. Regarding the fourfold classification by nature (*svabhāva*), it refers exclusively to the wholesome as being the nature. 2. Regarding the fivefold classification by the attainment of results, it applies to all three types [wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral]. 3.

Regarding the sixfold classification by those who cultivate, it refers to noble ones (*ārya*) and not to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). 4. Regarding the sevenfold classification by initial acquisition, it means that both [the path and its fruit] arise through application (*prayoga*).
The *Śāstra* says: "As previously [stated regarding] the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñin*), it is called the 'attainment of cessation' (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The *Vyākhyā* states: In the commentary, first the verses (*kārikā*) are explained, and subsequently the meaning of the sūtras is addressed. Within the explanation of the verses, there are also seven parts;

this explanation of its essential nature uses the word "likewise" (*tathā*) as an illustration, meaning that just as the non-conceptual state can extinguish the mind and mental factors, so too does this.
[The practitioner] attains entry into these two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*). Commentary:

This explanation of *manasikāra* (mental attention) is provided to clarify its distinction from the previously mentioned absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Thus, it is explained in contrast to the former.
In the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), one clings to the fruit as liberation and, being weary of perception alone, clings to this meditative absorption as the path of deliverance.
In the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one seeks to dwell in present tranquility as *nirvāṇa* in the present life;

being weary of coarse agitation, one contemplates the cessation of mind and mental factors in the attainment of cessation as merely a state of stilled rest. Because it is a state of stilled rest, one attains freedom from distraction and movement.
"Abiding in tranquility" means the body is stilled; "the cessation of activity" means the mind and its associates are extinguished.
From the aforementioned "unconscious attainment" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) up to the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Commentary: This explanation concerns the basis (*bhūmi*). It is called the "Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*) because it is produced by superior karma and is the highest point of existence.
It is called the "Summit" (*bhavāgra*) because it is supreme within the realm of existence (*bhava*), or because its highest limit is the "summit.
For what reason do the lower stages lack this meditative absorption?
The commentary states: This objection intends to question why the lower stages lack the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
"Disgusted with and turning away from all [states] up to the middle limit, the mind is severed.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains that the attainment of this cessation-samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is due to the presence of two conditions:

first, being disgusted with all minds of the lower stages; second, not being averse to the upper limit of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*). That is to say, one severs the extremely superior mind of the lower stages, yet the lower stages cannot sever the superior [minds].
Therefore, among the three natures (it serves as) a dwelling in tranquility. [The commentary] states:
This explanation of the inclusion of the nature means that it is exclusively wholesome, because the defiled and the indeterminate are both states of distraction.
The Noble Ones loathe it and would not again take it as a basis for peaceful abiding.
Regarding the statement that "the prior non-ideation [attainment] results in the maturation of the four aggregates," the commentary says:

This explanation accords with the correct principle regarding the attainment of the fruit; therefore, it is said that the prior non-ideation is a non-determined [attainment] conducive to rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*).

Since it is admitted that those who fall away from meditative concentration can still undergo rebirth, [the statement] applies to future births. This is said in order to show that all these cases involve the experience of the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*);

therefore, it says "in terms of the ripening fruit. When it says "the lower stages are exhausted and fulfilled," meaning they are not experienced at all, we see that this is stated as a distinct case of total non-experience.
Thus, we know that the three types [of falling away] are spoken of merely in terms of time; here, however, it refers specifically to the ripening fruit.
Concentration (*samādhi*) may also be included here; furthermore, it is subsumed within the "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).

Its fruit is precisely the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) experienced as the maturation (*vipāka*) within the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which distinguishes it from the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).
[The practitioner] first enters the attainment of non-ideation (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and so forth, up to attaining the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
The commentary states: This explanation regarding those who practice means that only noble ones (ārya) attain it, not ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

This is because the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) must be extinguished by wisdom; since ordinary worldlings have not yet severed these obstacles belonging to their own level, they lack the capacity to enter [this attainment].
Other masters say: [up to] "it is not for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The commentary states:

This recounts a divergent opinion; that is, according to the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati), because ordinary beings fear the cessation [of existence], they can only enter this state through the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life.
Therefore, while noble ones do not fear cessation, ordinary beings possess the resolute conviction regarding nirvāṇa.
Because they are contradictory, only the noble ones attain it.
That [explanation] is irrational because there would be no distinction [between them].

The commentary states: This master of the treatise refutes the Sūtra-master’s interpretation; if ordinary beings were terrified of annihilation, they would not have the excellence of attaining nirvāṇa.

One’s resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) should likewise lack the concentration on signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*). Why is this? Because in both mindless concentrations (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the mind is entirely extinguished;

furthermore, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also take the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) as their object, regarding it as *nirvāṇa*. Thus, there would be no distinction between their resolute conviction regarding *nirvāṇa* and the principle of extinction.

Since the principle of extinction is one and the same, by this logic, those who do not cultivate the concentration on cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) should likewise lack the concentration on non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This explanation is unreasonable.
Regarding this, some say that because [the practitioner] has attained [this state], they do not fear annihilation.

[The author] comments: This recounts the interpretation of the master Vasubandhu and the master Manoratha regarding the preceding meaning—namely, entering the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).

In this scripture, although the coarse mind has ceased, there still remains a subtle mind of a higher stage as its support; because it does not cause [the mind] to be utterly extinguished, one does not fear annihilation.
That too is irrational (and) is not a valid reason.
The commentary states: This master [Vasubandhu] refutes the error of those who take the cultivation of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as the basis for extinguishing the mind.

He clarifies that since they do not fear annihilation, yet seek liberation, their notion of "the ideation of renunciation" is flawed; this is because they employ the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in *nirvāṇa* as the means for the outflowing of the outflows (*āsrava*).

Therefore, the objection raised—that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) fear annihilation and thus lack the resolute conviction in *nirvāṇa*, which renders them incapable—is not valid. This is not the case.
The primary reason:
Do all noble ones [attain] up to the attainment of cessation?
The commentary states: The following explains the initial attainment; therefore, it first poses an interrogative inquiry.
One should say that it is not obtained [until] because it is obtained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-prāpti*).

The commentary states: This treatise explains that the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*) is not obtained through the abandonment of defilements; therefore, at the time of reaching the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one has not yet attained it.
By what means is it obtained?
The commentary states: this inquiry concerns the time of attainment;
it is obtained through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), and upon reaching [the state], it also becomes past.

The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains that [the attainment of cessation] is acquired through application (*prayoga*), just like the attainment of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
[An opponent asks: "Does the Blessed One also acquire it through application?

The commentary continues: "Furthermore, others object: 'All qualities of a Tathāgata are acquired through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya-labdha*); if you say that the attainment of cessation..."
Is it also the case that the World-Honored One attains [the fruit] through preparatory effort? No.
The commentary states: "The author of this treatise has briefly contradicted [the established position]."
How so? The commentary states: This is an external objection.
[It asks whether it is] attained at the time of becoming a Buddha, or attained at the time of reaching the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

The commentary states: This passage describes the Master of the Abhidharmakośa’s (Kośakāra) interpretation, namely that [the knowledge] is attained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Is it not the case that even the knowledge of exhaustion has its own faults?
The commentary states: Herein, the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) refutes the Kośakāra’s explanation as being inconsistent with reason; the phrase "attaining" (*prāpti*) refers to...

This is the initial attainment; "initial attainment" refers to reaching the moment of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*). If it reaches the present, it is called "maturation" (*paripāka*) and not "attainment" (*prāpti*).
When one considers the time of attaining Buddhahood, this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) reaching the present.

At this time, even the knowledge of exhaustion is not an "attainment," let alone the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). When the knowledge of exhaustion is attained, it is at the moment of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), which exhausts [all defilements].
When wisdom abides in the state of arising, it is then called the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

At the moment of its arising, it may simply be termed "the five established active manifestations. Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s qualities are attained through freedom from defilement (*vairāgya-lābha*):

the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) is what is meant by "freedom from defilement. Because of that freedom from defilement, the attainment of the Buddha’s qualities reaches the state of arising; this is termed "attainment through freedom from defilement."
It is not that one only attains [this] at the time of becoming a Buddha; therefore, there is no fault in the statement that "whatever desire or pleasure arises momentarily all appears before one.
However, there is a fault in the statement that "one attains this at the time of becoming a Buddha," for while it does not entirely contradict reason, it nevertheless possesses a deficiency.
Thus, it is said that this [latter] statement also has its own errors.
[This is] for the sake of establishing that they will ultimately attain Buddhahood according to their capacity.

The commentary states: This is the Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) providing a resolution on behalf of the Master of the Sūtra (Asaṅga). In reality, the term "attainment" refers to being in the stage of a Bodhisattva;

however, because the matter concerns the maturation of one who is close to Buddhahood, it is spoken of as the Bodhisattva at the distant [beginning] first attaining the voice [of a Buddha]. Thus, it is explained in terms of the state of a Buddha.
There is no fault in this; furthermore, since one attains Buddhahood immediately following the vajra-samādhi, it is designated as "becoming a Buddha" with reference to that specific stage.
To say that one "attains Buddhahood" in this sense is likewise without fault.
Let us set aside this matter for now [until we reach] the section on liberation through both parts.

The commentary states: This provisional explanation for the sake of transition shall cease here. Regarding the question of whether one attains [the absorption] at the time of becoming a Buddha or not:

since the absorption of cessation is without mind, there is no cultivation of it in the future. Furthermore, since one has never previously arisen in the absorption of cessation prior to the moment of the Buddha’s *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion), how can one be called "liberated by both" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*)?
"Because they are eternally free from the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*), they become those liberated-in-both-ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

The commentary states: Regarding this master’s explanation of the "obstacles to meditative concentration," he refers to the lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*) within the tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*).

Because one is eternally free from this, prior to attaining Buddhahood, there may be instances where one fails to attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) when it ought to be attained, or where one regresses from having previously attained it.

When he attains Buddhahood, he does not rely on that body; thus, the "abandonment" [of the body] is not established as an abandonment. Furthermore, regarding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there is a class of beings who cannot rely on a body whose obscurations have not been severed.

Since they have already permanently abandoned it—just as one abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) upon attaining the state of an Arya—and because the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the Path of the Aryas is not something that can be satiated or exhausted, nor is it something that can be acquired by a Path of the Aryas that has not yet been attained, [this applies] when he attains Buddhahood.
There are those who, relying on the Buddha-body, have entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and are not dependent on the non-elimination of hindrances;

because they have permanently eliminated them, they are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). Furthermore, although one has not yet attained mastery over what is to be attained, an inference may be established:

the Tathāgata, possessing the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), is named "liberated in both ways" because he has attained mastery over the arising of the meditative attainment of cessation, just as in the state when it has already arisen.
The masters of the Western regions say (up to) "attaining enlightenment later.
[Commentary: This refers to the Sarvāstivāda masters of the country of Kaniṣka, who provide this interpretation:

that bodhisattva, having perfected the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and generated the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*), enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and only then enters the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Because it was accomplished in the past, it is called "liberation through both.
In the kingdom of Kaśmīra, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises only later.

[The commentary] states: This cites the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā*’s explanation that during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), a Bodhisattva does not give rise to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
For what reason does this country know that [the cause] had not previously arisen?
[The author] replies: This criticism is directed at the Northern Masters regarding the "prior non-arising" of the cause;
why then do you not criticize the Westerners regarding the "arising" of the cause?
The commentary states: This is the statement of the masters of the North regarding the reason why [the mind] does not turn toward the West.
Their intention is also to investigate the previously arisen cause.
This is because we, the Kashmiris, maintain that the mind is touched by tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).

The commentary states: The masters of the North explain that "not having yet aroused the intention" means that when those [Bodhisattvas] enter meditative absorption during their time as Bodhisattvas, they make a vow that this task remains unfinished and will never again be aroused;
thus, throughout the intermediate state, no different mind arises. If such a mind were to arise, it would constitute the fault of transgressing this resolve.
Therefore, one should know that Bodhisattvas do not enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
In reality, [this extends] from the Bodhisattva up to the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-ārya-mārga*).

The commentary states: This is the explanation of the Western masters regarding the *Abhidharmakośa*. It says that the foreign masters—that is, the Sarvāstivāda masters of the various Indian countries—hold the same intent;
therefore, whichever [master] is cited, it is all their teaching, even when [the Bodhisattva] has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

[The opponent asks: "If one temporarily transcends the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), yet in reality does not transcend it because the mind remains directed toward it, then how is it that this mind itself does not transcend?
[The author] replies: This is a difficult question from the North. A tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) is precisely what is called "transcending"; how could it not be transcending?
It means: "Because I have not yet attained [the goal] up to the ultimate perfection of all matters.

The commentary states: Since this Western interpretation necessarily implies the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the statement that one does not transcend the intermediate stage of knowledge—how could this possibly contradict the principle?
Is it not because [these]—up to being non-antecedent causes—are so designated?
The commentary states: The masters of the North argue that those afflictions to be abandoned through seeing can serve as causes for other afflictions, and are thus called "roots" (*mūla*);
or they are termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*); or because they are not abandoned through cultivation, or because they draw in external objects, they are called "enemies" (*ari*).
When a bodhisattva intends to cultivate the path of cultivation, they must eliminate various doubts and views;

although the time for the fulfillment of the path of seeing has arrived, the matter is not yet finalized. Since beginningless time, there have been the deceptions of tainted concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*).

As for the "extinction concentration" (*nirodha-samāpatti*), because it is indeed tainted, it is capable of deceiving or [falling under the sway of] the various types of worldly concentrations shared with the śrāvakas.

Since this is so easily attained, how could it be permitted that a Bodhisattva’s fundamental [mysterious] potential (*gotra*) remains unfulfilled while yet being able to honor and delay the Great Matter?

If that matter were to arise, his concentration would immediately [manifest] the mysterious mind; since the mysterious mind does not transcend [this state], we know that the analogy refers to what has not yet arisen.
Because he attains Bodhi in thirty-four moments of thought, it is proven that the principle of its prior non-arising is established with supreme certainty.
As it is said in the Sūtra (up to): "One touches these three contacts. The commentary states:
The following explains the meaning of the Sūtra. As asked in the Mahākauṣṭhila Sūtra:

"When emerging from the attainment of cessation, one should touch [the contact] spoken of by the Buddha. [The Buddha said: "Venerable sir, one should touch three contacts," and so forth, as explained at length. What [is meant]?
Regarding these three types of contact, what is their essence, and how do they contact that which is contacted?
Some say that the cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) contacts [the object] through these three types of contact.
The commentary states: this explanation of the previous sutra’s question contains three points; this is the first. The three liberations are...

Regarding the three types of contact corresponding to their respective order, what is the meaning of their names? "Agitation" refers to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātma-ātmīya-grāha*) and to mental restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Because the practice of the contemplation of emptiness and non-self (*śūnyatā-anātman*) serves as their antidote and is able to destroy such agitation, it is called "immovable.
Contact associated with the immovable is "immovable contact. When a mind of craving clings to an object and appropriates it as its own, there is "grasping."
Therefore, it is called "that which is grasped," and it is called "samādhi. It is able to sever all names and all that remains is as previously explained.

Regarding the ten characteristics of birth-and-death, the five objects, arising, abiding, and ceasing, the realms, women, and nirvāṇa—within these, there is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*).
Because it takes the signless as its object, it is named "signless. The rest is as previously explained. This is the third.
The essence of contact (sparśa) exists even when one is in a state of mindlessness; it is that which suddenly emerges upon arising.
This is like encountering a wall while walking in the dark. This is the meaning of the third [aspect] of contact.
Other masters say: [up to] "because it manifests before one. The commentary states:

This second master explains that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) contemplates only consciousness, while the preparatory stage for the sphere of space (*ākāśāyatana*) likewise contemplates only space;
because there is no difference in their conceptualization, it is called "immovable" (*aniñjya*). The contact associated with that is therefore named "immovable."

Although the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) involve diverse perceptions (*nānātvasaṃjñā*), they are conventionally termed "immovable" (*aniñjya*) from the perspective of their preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

In the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there is no prior pervasive consciousness; and in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because there is no diversity of perception and no two distinct characteristics, it is called "signless" (*animitta*).
Furthermore, since everything below the Peak of Existence may be described as signless, these are the four formless [attainments].

All are termed "possessing perception"; this is called the essence of the three contacts. Regarding the knowledge of the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mind may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

If it is contaminated, entering the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) in reverse order is called the contact of the signless (*animitta-sparśa*). If one enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by skipping levels in reverse order, it is the uncontaminated [contact];
entering the sphere of nothingness in reverse order is the contact of the knowledge of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya-jñāna-sparśa*). As for the sphere of nothingness... [text ends].
There is a contact that, if it is untainted (*anāsrava*), is called "contact of immovability" (*āneñjya-sparśa*) when one enters the stages by skipping over them.

Although one may not enter the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) [from such a state], both spheres are termed "immovable contact"; thus, the first [sphere] also possesses that name. Furthermore, this master’s interpretation is not the orthodox doctrine;

it is the view of a teacher from another school who maintains that one can enter the sphere of infinite space and so forth from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and thus he offers this explanation.
Furthermore, there is another master [up to] named "Signless" (animitta).

The commentary states: This third master’s interpretation takes a single moment of untainted (*anāsrava*) mind focused on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is Nirvāṇa within the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Because its essence is untainted and not tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called "Immovable" (*āneñjya*); it is designated by way of its stage (*bhūmi*).

Because it is "nothing whatsoever" (*akiṃcana*) with respect to its object, it is called "signless" (*animitta*); the contact associated with it possesses these three aspects and is thus called "contact of the three [aspects].
When that mind enters [into meditative absorption], it is called "contact of the three contacts.
Although the two meditative absorptions have already been discussed, [the third] up to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) begins among humans.

The commentary states: Below this, the fourth section clarifies the Buddha’s body. Within the preliminary analysis of its characteristics, if one considers its essential nature, it consists entirely of the cessation of [defiled] mind and mental factors, being comprised solely of wholesome states.
At its initial attainment, it belongs to a single lifetime; this is called "many sharing the same basis" (*ekāśraya*), as it is produced by the attention (*manasikāra*) of the meditative stage.
When including the long prose section, it also encompasses maturation (*vipāka*); this is called "many having different [bases]," which is what is clarified here.

Regarding the basis of the body, both meditative attainments (samāpatti) rely equally upon the desire and form realms for their initial arising; thus, they are said to be identical in this respect. However, regarding the first person [who attains them], the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is common to both [realms], whereas the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) belongs only to humans; this is what is meant by "having differences.
The Treatise says: [The passage from] "the two attainments" [up to] "this is called their common characteristic" [is as follows].
The commentary states: In the *Śāstra*, the verse is first explained, followed by the resolution of objections.

Regarding the explanation of the verse, the first section explains the basis of the two attainments (*samāpatti*) by way of their common characteristics—that is, their general characteristics—stating that both are based on bodies belonging to the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*). However, regarding the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), there are three different views among the schools.
