The principle by which the Dharma draws [the object] from the distant to the near and from the external to the internal is as follows:

with respect to the aspect (*ākāra*) of the object, it becomes "internal" within the mind; with respect to the meaning (*artha*) of the object, it becomes "internal" within the mind as its comprehension.

Through these two meanings, it is able to summon the establishment of the meaning, for the name and the meaning are extremely close to one another; this is explained according to their mutual proximity.
Therefore, it is called "name" (*nāman*).
If that were so, [it would follow that] there is nothing to which it reaches, because there is no object of cognition (*ālambana*).
[The author] states: This is an objection; among the four aggregates, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are able to cognize objects, and thus they designate them.

Because it is capable of establishing various meanings that are dissociated [from mind], it is called "dissociated" (*viprayukta*); thus, there is no fault in its inclusion within the dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), even though it does not encompass the mind.
This is because it functions as a designation (*saṃjñā*) that points toward [the object]. There is no error in this.
The commentary states: This refers to the pervasive [element]. Within the initial category of "dharmas," it is divided into the material and the immaterial;

since there is no manifesting [form] within the immaterial realm, and because it does not exist within the aggregate of matter, there is no fault. The explanation of the meaning of "matter" (rūpa) can be understood from the text as it appears.
Furthermore, because it is subtle... [up to] ...because it is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The commentary states: This second explanation—in the Sanskrit manuscript, the second explanation says *namo namaḥ*—is "taking refuge" (*śaraṇagamana*), hence it is called *nama*.
Regarding the explanation of the name: it refers to that which is able to follow, that which is able to follow.

This refers to taking refuge. For example, just as a disciple takes refuge in a teacher and may be called the disciple of such-and-such a teacher, so too these four aggregates, because they are subtle, have names established according to their respective objects and principles.

For instance, regarding visual consciousness and the consciousness of forms, various characteristics—such as "form," "person," and "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*)—are all established by way of other phenomena.

Regarding the designation that follows reason: "reason" has the sense of a cause, just as the reason for naming it "eye-consciousness" (cakṣurvijñāna) is its dependence upon the eye-faculty (cakṣurindriya).
Thus, because there is a basis in the object and a cause, the four aggregates are established by following another;
they are not like form and so forth, which are known through direct perception, nor like the great elements (mahābhūta) which are the causes of the five faculties and the unmanifest (avijñapti).
That which is apprehended by direct perception has a coarse and manifest characteristic and should therefore be established by its own name;
thus, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is designated as "name" (nāman) in the sense of being dependent on others and in the sense of taking refuge.
Furthermore, because it resembles this [name] in relation to all [objects], from the point of arrival [at the senses].
The commentary states: This third explanation [of the Sanskrit term] says that *namo* means "to go toward" (*namana*), thus it has the meaning of "inclination.

Because the four formless aggregates are able to incline toward rebirth within the three realms, the nine stages, the five destinies, and the four modes of birth—meaning that the mind and mental factors are capable of linking to a new birth—the four aggregates travel everywhere throughout [existence].

Because it applies to all instances, if that were so, then the four aggregates belonging to the untainted (anāsrava) and the non-seeking realms (apranihita-dhātu), etc., would not be included under the term "name" (nāman).

This is not the case; this objection is also logically consistent with the categories [of the system]. What is being discussed here as "name" refers exclusively to the tainted and untainted four aggregates, which are not what is being elucidated in this context;
nevertheless, they are still "names" and belong to this same class.
Furthermore, regarding the formless [realms]... [up to] there is no need for further inquiry or interrogation.
The commentary states: "This fourth explanation follows the intention of the speaker.
The intention of the Elder (Sthavira) is that... [up to] it conforms to and establishes that meaning."

The commentary states: These two refute divergent explanations. First, it refutes their interpretation of the meaning; second, it refutes the evidence they cite; and third, it refutes their definitive resolution.
Within these three, there are two parts each, and this [section] presents those very points to refute their interpretation of the meaning.

The intention of the Venerable (Sthavira) is that names are explained in accordance with [their referents]; for example, as in the case of a "person," the four aggregates accord with the continuity of the person, and that continuity is conventional (prajñapti).
The four aggregates are real, and because they are established based on reality, they are called "names.
If this were so, then material phenomena (*rūpa*) would have nothing to rely upon. [The author] states:
This is a refutation; by using material phenomena as an analogy for the objection, it is shown that there is no basis [for names].
"Is it not so that the Buddha taught [from] 'all follow the movement of mastery'?
The commentary states: This is an instance of citing that [scripture] as proof. The intention of the Sthavira is this:

the "name" (*nāman*) mentioned in this verse refers to the formless aggregates (*arūpaskandha*). Since it is described as "superior" and not identical to form (*rūpa*), it is therefore specifically said to be capable [of acting as a basis].
The characteristics of establishment are superior.
Herein, that [preceding argument] is cited as the probans (*sādhana*). The commentary states:

from here below, the initial concession is refuted in its entirety, while the subsequent denial is refuted in detail. Within the concession, there is first an inquiry based on a hypothetical assumption.

If it is granted that these four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*), and it is said that "name alone" can establish the continuity [of existence], this inquiry is intended to demonstrate the preeminence of name.
By citing this verse as proof that it is "name alone" which establishes the continuity, the underlying meaning is clearly revealed:

since it is stated that other phenomena proceed according to the power of name, it is evident that "name" is taught as that which draws forth (*ākṣepaka*) matter and the other aggregates. Is this not so?
This is reasonable.
If it is argued that everything up to the formless realm (*ārūpya*) serves as the cause, [the author] comments:
this cites the opponent's defense. Since the formless realm pervades all sentient beings, yet there are sentient beings who...
To claim that because form (*rūpa*) is accomplished, it is known that only the name "sentient being" is established, is logically incorrect; [if so], it would lead to a great error.
[The author] states: This objection is invalid because, since there is no mind, the meaning of "pervasive" is not established, for according to that school’s tenet, there is no mind [in such states].
Since even in states such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*) there still exists a subtle mind, [the author] cites the preceding passage to prove that the mind is not non-existent.

Fearing that the opponent might claim that dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) constitute those sentient beings in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), [the author] states that "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth do not exist in their school’s tenets.
Thus, if one were in any of the mindless states, then according to what they themselves maintain, there would necessarily be no basis for the prior path or the mind.

Furthermore, since there is no attainment [of a self] and so forth, and they [the opponents] maintain that there is only form, the four aggregates would all lack [a self], and the statement "pervading all" would not be established.

Fearing that they might further argue that for each sentient being born in a single location, all their aggregates constitute a single continuum, and that there is no such continuum that possesses form but lacks a name—since this does not refer to a single moment—it does not constitute a valid objection. Thus it is said in the treatise: [this is not a difficulty].

According to the Master [Vasubandhu], since each and every sentient being’s aggregates within the three realms constitute a single continuum, there would likewise be no such thing as a formless sentient being.
If one were to be born in a different location, it would constitute a different continuum;

thus, when one is born from the realm of form into the formless realm, the cause of form would have to perish, yet when subsequently returning to be born below, it would not have been produced [previously]. Furthermore, this would mean that death occurs in all places simultaneously.
Since being born there constitutes a different continuum from this [world], these faults all arise.
If it is argued that a single sentient being’s form (*rūpa*) is not omnipresent, the commentary states:
This restates the opponent’s defense; in reality, the three realms (*traidhātuka*) constitute a single continuum, yet each individual location is distinct.
Because their stages are not identical and because form is not omnipresent, they are merely called "formless.
The same applies to the formless [realms] themselves.
The commentary states: This refutation concerns the non-omnipresence of form in terms of its stages; the absence of form in terms of temporal stages is likewise the case for the formless.
Because in the state of non-conceptualization (acittaka), there are no forms (rūpa).
Furthermore, one should carefully consider [the passage] up to the words "based on names, it is called 'name'.

[The commentary] states: From here below, [the author] refutes [the opponent's position] by means of a separate analysis; therefore, he first raises this inquiry. That which is described in the verse supersedes all [other views].
It is said that "name" (*nāman*) refers to the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*).
However, within this context, [the text] extends to encompass the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
The commentary states: the author of this treatise intends to definitively resolve and refute divergent explanations.
"If it is claimed that [all four aggregates] are names (nāman), as well as their associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*)," the commentary states:
"This restates the opponent's explanation that the four aggregates constitute 'name' (*nāman*) because they pervade everything.

If it is further claimed that 'investigation' (*vitarka*) takes everything as its object, this is immediately refuted by stating: 'It should belong only to the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), for only the mental stage is capable of universally taking objects as its domain.'"
If it is argued that [the name-base] exists because it pertains to the remaining [factors] up to the mental continuum of sentient beings, the commentary states:

this restates the opponent’s defense; the verse properly explains that the "name-base" (*nāma-dhātu*) is so called because these [remaining factors] are of the same category and are subsumed under the term "name.
Below, the refutation states that citing the verse is useless, as there are further probative reasons available outside of the verse.
How could one not know that "name" is also subsumed under form?
Furthermore, how can it be said that there is no fault in the term "name"?
The commentary states: This again investigates and refutes [the claim that] the four aggregates are subsumed under "name"; why, then, is it said that "name" is free from fault?
If it is argued that names do not exceed [the scope of] form, the commentary states:
this restates the opponent's position;
since the number of aggregates (*skandha*) is many, how could names possibly exceed what is designated within form?
The commentary states: This is an analysis based on the *dhātus* and *āyatanas*.
If it is argued that "name" (*nāma*) also extends to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the commentary states:
This cites the opponent's defense, asserting that because it extends to all three realms, it is predominant.
"Those things that do not communicate [their meaning] should not be called 'names' (nāman).
The commentary states: This raises the objection that [names] such as "sighing" (tāna) and so forth do not communicate [their meaning].
If one were to claim that there is no such fault because they do not communicate [to a distance], [the following applies].
The commentary states: To cite external objections and attempt to resolve them by classifying them according to their common characteristics is also logically untenable...
because they are equal to those that are pervasive. The commentary further states:

This Master [Vasubandhu] refutes the verse’s claim that what is pervasive must be so while the rest is not; he argues that if this were the case, the verse should have stated that [the other factors] are likewise non-pervasive.

Regarding form (*rūpa*), there is further form in other states of meditative concentration; moreover, a verse is cited to prove its preeminence, which is why it is specifically designated as the "characteristic that establishes continuity" (*saṃtati-saṃdhāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Since it is admitted that the name "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*) applies to what is not preeminent, it follows by logic that it should be the same for form; thus, it cannot be subsumed under the category of "name" (*nāman*).
This should be examined in detail.
"Excluding the name that is grasped... all follow according to the sovereign [mind].
The commentary states: This objection asks, "Excluding the name, what serves as the agent of following?
If it is claimed that this name... matter follows the transformation of the name."
The commentary states: This passage cites the externalist's position, termed "following the name" (nāmanuvartin), and refutes its partial meaning by means of successive dependencies.
If it is claimed that names are pervasive because they extend from form (rūpa) up to sentient beings without consciousness (acittaka).

The commentary states: This passage restates the externalist position that wherever there is a material base (*rūpāyatana*), there must be a name (*nāman*), and wherever there is a name-base (*nāmāyatana*), it is not necessarily material.
The following section refutes this by stating: "In non-sentient things and in those without mind, the four material bases do not exist."
Nor is it outside of name-and-form (up to: there is no third).
The commentary states: This clarifies that apart from these two, there is no "name" capable of following [the conditions].
Furthermore, logically it should not be so (up to: it certainly does not accord with reason).
The commentary states: This is a general refutation of the claim that [the four formless aggregates] should be spoken of as a single dharma.
Even if it were a single dharma, it would still lack accompanying factors (anucara). Therefore, a verse says: "What are the characteristics of all [dharmas]?"
"The Elder [states] regarding this... (up to) 'but takes only the remaining name-and-form' (*nāmarūpa*). The commentary says:

this is an instance of citing that [position] to provide a definitive explanation. That is to say, since he himself admits that the four aggregates constitute 'name,' the term 'name-and-form' is said to fully encompass all five aggregates.
Furthermore, a sutra states that consciousness depends upon name-and-form; according to his own school's tenet, past and future [dharmas] do not exist."

Because there exists the intrinsic nature of phenomena, doubt arises immediately within a single moment; below, [the author] himself explains this by saying, "based on others, excluding consciousness.
Now, upon close examination, both that objection and its response are unreasonable.

The commentary states: This is a refutation. [The opponent argues that] distinct moments of thought may serve as the basis for consciousness, since it is commonly accepted that consciousness has a basis;
however, this objection is invalid because feeling and so forth cannot serve as the basis for consciousness. Thus, their explanation is also unreasonable.
"Now, within this [passage] (up to the point where it says) 'for the sake of [discussing] co-arising'...

The commentary states: "From here below is the third section, which cites sūtras to provide a comprehensive reconciliation. This consists of two parts: first, reconciling the sūtra on consciousness and name-and-form acting as mutual conditions;

second, reconciling the sūtra on the progression of the cycle of existence up to the reversal of consciousness. Regarding the first of these, there is first the question and subsequently the reconciliation."
This is the question. [The text states:
"Consciousness conditions name-and-form" (up to) "it is taught that they are mutually conditions.

The commentary says: From here below is the explanation, which consists of two parts: first, the correct explanation; second, the refutation of divergent explanations. Within the correct explanation, there is first the actual exposition.
This is the third section, which clarifies the objections; it constitutes the formal explanation itself.

It means that when the Sūtra states that the two are mutually conditions for one another, it refers to their mutual dependence within the single moment of the *vijñāna* stage, whereby they are established.
Subsequently, within that stage, there is no separate entity of consciousness external to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), yet within the *vijñāna* stage, there is name external to consciousness.

Because it is a branch of form (*rūpa*), it is called the "form-branch" (*rūpāṅga*); this applies throughout the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Since the consciousness-branch does not extend to the subsequent name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) branch, the status of being a "branch" is established.

After that, in the second moment of mind, there is no further arising of a consciousness-branch. Although they serve as mutual conditions, this is discussed solely in terms of their simultaneous arising.
Nevertheless, because name-and-form exists after consciousness, and consciousness exists before name-and-form, consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.

The statement that "name-and-form conditions consciousness" is based solely on simultaneity; for name-and-form does not exist prior to consciousness, nor does consciousness exist subsequent to name-and-form.
However, the Sautrāntikas maintain that this refers to both temporal sequence and simultaneity, because there can be no cause-and-effect relationship between dharmas that arise simultaneously.
Thus, they use this very proof of simultaneous causality to refute the position [of the Sarvāstivādins] which relies exclusively on temporal sequence.
Furthermore, a sūtra states (up to) "it is not the tenet of the Buddha's Dharma.
[The commentary] says: From here below, he cites evidence; therein, he extracts two sūtras and one parable to form a composite proof.
This is the first [of those]. That sūtra states that, according to the parable of the sheaves of reeds, when they possess substance, they do not even exist simultaneously.
If one dismisses the lack of meaning in both worlds, upon what could there be reliance?
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "...because there is no obstruction.
The commentary says: This cites a second sūtra as proof. Since it speaks of the defiled attention (*manasikāra*) produced by delusion (*moha*), and furthermore—

It is taught that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*), and it is further stated therein that this [ignorance] is proven to arise simultaneously [with its effect].
Furthermore, this is as well-established as the coexistence of a lamp and its light.
The commentary states: This third citation of an analogy serves as proof; that is, the principle that a lamp produces light proves that cause and effect are simultaneous.
Yet there is a rebuttal which claims that the lamp and its light are not distinct.
The commentary states: This records the externalist position that the lamp is itself the light. Since they are not separate entities, how can one speak of cause and effect?
This is not reasonable (up to the point where it says) "it is not separate from the lamp-flame.
[The author] comments: This is a refutation. The lamp and its light differ in various ways:

they differ in contact [with objects], in temperature [hot or cold], in magnitude [small or large], in color [red or white], in location [near or far], and in function [burning or illuminating]. These are common examples in both worldly convention and the sacred teachings (*āgama*).
Because they equally manifest the substance [of light], the lamp and its illumination are distinct in their co-arising substances.
If it is argued that the flame is the cause of the illumination, the commentary states:
this cites the opponent’s defense that illumination does not depend on the lamp-flame, as both the flame and the illumination arise simultaneously from the wick.
This, too, is not logical [up to] "it does not arise from a single conjunction.
The commentary states: This is a refutation because multiple fruits do not arise from a single conjunction.
[Objection: Is it not the case that when struck once, there arises a fruit that is not singular?

The commentary states: Furthermore, the objection that it is like striking iron against stone, where fire and sound arise simultaneously, or like a single wick producing both light and flame, is also illogical (up to the point where it concludes):
because the entities of the causes are distinct.

The commentary states: This master of the treatise refutes [the opponent's position] because fire depends on a few [atoms] while sound depends on many; furthermore, because each of the two has its own distinct homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Thus, it is clarified that the flame and the substance upon which it depends exist simultaneously as distinct entities, thereby establishing a valid example based on shared properties (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
"If consciousness and name-and-form... (up to) consciousness conditions name-and-form.
[Commentary: From here below, he addresses potential objections; first he raises one objection and then provides two responses—this is the raising of the objection.
"Mutually serving as the nature of conditions" (up to "should be known to be likewise").
The commentary states: From here below, there are generally three explanations; this is the first. Although they mutually serve as conditions, because one is superior, it is specifically mentioned.
That which is called "superior" is so because it serves as the support for the mind (*citta*) and because it can sustain the semen and blood (*śukra-śoṇita*).
Furthermore, regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form" (up to the point where there is no distinct stage):
the commentary states that this second explanation may be understood by analogy with the preceding one.
Moreover, regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form," this refers to name-and-form as it exists at the moment [of conception].
The commentary states: This third explanation concerns the stages [of dependent origination]. It specifically explains that moments (*kṣaṇa*) succeed one another and function as mutual conditions.
The Venerable Rāma [states]: "From consciousness arises name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)."
The commentary states: Hereafter follows the refutation of divergent views. First, the view of Rāma is refuted, followed by that of the Sthavira; this passage cites the former.

According to him, the final *nāmarūpa* of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) induces the consciousness that arises immediately thereafter—the consciousness that links rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-vijñāna*).

This consciousness of linking rebirth occurs precisely at the time of birth. However, since the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*) has not yet arisen, this consciousness would have already perished beforehand, and thus it could not coexist with *nāmarūpa*.
Birth arises from name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and from this, [birth] is further induced; therefore, it is called the meaning of being mutual conditions (*anyonya-pratyaya*).
When one investigates in this manner until consciousness (*vijñāna*) is found not to have the nature of a condition, the commentary states:

"This is a critical inquiry. First, when birth occurs from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as a solitary consciousness, if [name-and-form] were taken as a condition in its entirety, what [would be the consequence]?"
Therefore, it is only feeling that [arises] accordingly; as for consciousness, why is it not a condition?
If it is argued that in that state there is no consciousness co-arising with [feeling], the commentary states:
this restates the opponent's defense, asserting that in the final stage of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is no consciousness co-arising, and thus there is no co-arising [of feeling].
This constitutes the fault of being a condition (*pratyaya*).
It would follow that the consciousness at rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*)—up to the point where consciousness arises alone—would arise without any support.
[The author] states: This is the objection; since it results in the fault of a solitary consciousness arising without a basis, mental factors (*caitta*) cannot be [the support].
Because the mind is that upon which mental factors depend; because it is illogical for only a dissimilar type [of consciousness] to arise;
and because as long as one has not abandoned craving for form, form must necessarily exist—by such reasoning, there should be no arising of consciousness alone.
If it is argued that at this stage [only] consciousness (*vijñāna*) is mentioned, the commentary states:
this cites the external opponent’s position that matter (*rūpa*) is not mentioned;
therefore, at this very stage, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) must arise.
The commentary states: This is a refutation. Since form already has a name, how could it not exist? Therefore, one should not say that consciousness alone exists.
Furthermore, this claim that consciousness alone exists arises from false attachments.

The commentary states: This objection—that the state of consciousness alone [exists]—is neither moderate nor logical, as it contradicts both scripture and reasoning; therefore, it is not the correct teaching.
Furthermore, the mind and mental factors arise taking other objects as their conditions.
The commentary states: This further investigates and refutes the doctrine that mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) arise sequentially.
By means of reasoning, it establishes that this contradicts what is asserted in one's own school, thereby demonstrating its invalidity; this constitutes the investigation.

Regarding the statement that "feeling (*vedanā*) arises immediately after visual consciousness," the phrase "produced by eye-contact" indicates that feeling and visual consciousness share the same object. [The question arises: when feeling is present, are there other consciousnesses functioning simultaneously?

If conditioned phenomena were non-existent, they would be beyond expression; yet if there remains some consciousness, is this the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that shares the same object as sensation, or is it another consciousness with a different object and a distinct objective field?
Furthermore, it is not the case that mental consciousness arises [simultaneously] with that which is produced by eye-contact.
The commentary states: This refutes the claim that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) shares the same object as the sensation produced by visual contact (*cakṣu-saṃsparśaja-vedanā*).

While such sensation depends upon the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), the subsequent mental consciousness must necessarily take a present object when depending on the five faculties. If it were to take a preceding form (*rūpa*) as its object, it would necessarily be taking a past object.
Since the times [of the two cognitions] are distinct, there is no possibility for them to share the same object; thus, that sensation cannot belong to the mental faculty (*manas*).
With the mind and mental objects as conditions, the consciousness that arises simultaneously with them— and even the feelings produced by mind-contact and so forth—
do not arise; nor do the various feelings produced by eye-contact arise,
nor does any other consciousness apprehend all objects.
The commentary states: This refutes the notion that distinct cognitions apprehend distinct objects. If they were distinct based on their objects, they could arise simultaneously;
however, not only would there be multiple objects being apprehended at once, but there would also be the implication that they mutually apprehend one another.
Consequently, all objects would have to be apprehended at a single moment, because [distinct cognitions] do not arise together and cannot apprehend themselves.
"If there were no consciousnesses" (up to) "because it contradicts both reason and scripture. The commentary states:

This refutes [the view that] feeling and so forth arise alone without consciousness; for in the interval when there is no consciousness, there would be no basis [for the subsequent mind], resulting in the fault [of a total cessation].

Since consciousness arises again after being interrupted, this is explained as being distinct from the [Sarvāstivāda] school which asserts that [feeling and so forth] exist independently in the desire realm.

The Sautrāntika school does not admit the existence of mindless states in the form and formless realms at all, because they maintain that consciousness continues to arise during the meditative attainments such as cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Therefore, it is impossible for feeling to arise from eye-contact without being concomitant with visual consciousness;
for all minds must necessarily arise simultaneously with mental factors (*caitta*), and all mental factors must likewise be concomitant with consciousness.
Among these, there is no principle whereby the final mind could be without consciousness, nor is it possible for consciousness to arise alone without immediate succession;
otherwise, one would contradict the principles and teachings as previously stated.
Regarding this point, the Sthavira [states that] name-and-form serve as conditions.
The commentary states: The following refutes the position of the Sthavira; this introduces his thesis.

He bases his argument on the meaning of the sequential order of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), wherein it is stated that consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and furthermore, that name-and-form and consciousness serve as mutual conditions.
Since the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* asks whether consciousness could abide without depending upon name-and-form, he raises these two preceding points as a contradictory objection.

Thereafter, you may attempt to reconcile this by means of the third principle, asserting that while consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it serves as the condition for its arising, whereas [name-and-form] serves as the condition for its persistence through successive stages.
This, however, is not the case; [it leads to the fallacy of] mutual dependence.
The commentary states: The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes [the opponent's view] by having the Bodhisattva observe from what condition consciousness arises;

he knows that it arises conditioned by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and thus he knows name-and-form to be the condition for the arising of consciousness. Furthermore, as it is said there, at the very moment name-and-form exists, consciousness takes it as its support-condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*).
However, when the Bodhisattva observes from what name-and-form arises, he knows it is produced by initial consciousness; yet he further asks: from what does that consciousness arise?
Knowing this, one understands that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) arises from consciousness (vijñāna). Thus, it is said that consciousness is the condition for the arising of name-and-form.

To claim otherwise would contradict the subsequent [teaching] regarding consciousness. Furthermore, the *Mahānidānaparyāya-sūtra* states that consciousness abides supported by name-and-form, but does not say that name-and-form abides supported by consciousness;
thus, their mutual dependence is not established. Moreover, that school does not admit that consciousness and name-and-form [are mutually dependent].
If, at that very moment, even simultaneous [entities] do not constitute a reciprocal dependence, how much less so for those who deny the past and future by asserting their non-existence?
How could there be a relationship of mutual dependence among simultaneously arising [phenomena]?
The commentary states: This is an external counter-question regarding the meaning of simultaneous dependence.
"If [the basis] were missing even one [of these factors], it would not be established.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains the principle of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Furthermore, for the Buddha, that [basis] would necessarily fail to be established.

The commentary states: The meaning of the passage from the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* as explained by this master of the treatise is not intended to explain the sequential order of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Rather, it is stated that "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) conditions contact (*sparśa*), and that contact seeks to obtain [feeling].

For this reason, when it says that consciousness (*vijñāna*) abides supported by name-and-form, it means that name-and-form serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), while the support of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is one [of the six bases].

That is to say, the objects of designation (nāma) as focal points (ālambana) pertain to both types [of existence]. The five consciousnesses, conversely, have only one type of object: namely, form (rūpa). Regarding their supports (āśraya), there are two:
first, the name, which is the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya); second, the form, which is one's own physical sense-faculty (indriya).

As for other supports and objects that arise simultaneously with them, among these, the supports of the five consciousnesses necessarily consist of two—namely, those occurring at different times and those occurring at the same time—whereas their objects are only of one kind.
Furthermore, the object of the simultaneous mental consciousness (manovijñāna) pervades this meaning and extends through all the stages of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*);

therefore, one cannot rely on this to explain the mutual dependence between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) within the links of existence. Consequently, the reasoning they have proposed—namely, that these [links] serve as conditions for one another in a reciprocal manner—is necessarily untenable.
Since it is based on the principle of "conditions for arising" (*utpattipratyaya*), the previous explanation is superior.
However, regarding the meaning of the statement in the *Sūtra* [extending to] "...this word," the commentary states:

"The following is the second section, which provides a comprehensive explanation of the contemplation of the forward progression (*pravṛtti*) up to the reversal of consciousness (*vijñāna-pratyāvṛtti*) according to the *Sūtra*.

Within this, first the question is raised, and subsequently the answer is given through its meaning. This is the question: namely, the Blessed One said, "When I was a Bodhisattva, I contemplated conditions (*pratyaya*)."
After the arising of the [twelve] factors, each preceding one serves as the cause for each succeeding one;

up until the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is not said that they arise simultaneously, but rather that consciousness takes name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its condition. Beyond this point, it no longer proceeds toward other minds. What does this indicate?
"At that time, the Bodhisattva... fully manifests the contemplation of the two conditions.
[The commentary] states: This is the answer. It means that the Bodhisattva contemplates in reverse order the conditions from which [the links] arise;

however, those conditions for arising are briefly of two kinds. First, he contemplates from old age and death back to name-and-form, including those that arise prior to and simultaneously with [the result].
Regarding consciousness as a condition, we have only discussed its preceding birth and not its simultaneous arising. Now, wishing to examine the conditions from which consciousness arises:

if the preceding conditions were no different from those previously explained—since the member of "birth" (*jāti*) is itself consciousness and the member of "existence" (*bhava*) is itself formative action (*saṃskāra*)—then for this reason, we shall here cite the simultaneously arising conditions to observe the consciousness that arises together with them;
observing the consciousness that arises together with them serves as an analogy for the rest.

It should be so; for when the mind reaches the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*), it turns back and asks: "Previously, you observed that old age and death have birth (*jāti*) as their condition; has it not already been observed that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises from consciousness?
He replied: "Old age and death should be understood to encompass the four future links (*aṅga*).

Name-and-form refers to one portion of the present life, while old age and death refer to another portion; thus, they are unequal in terms of breadth and brevity. Therefore, one should observe them again. [He asked: "With what is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*) associated? [He replied: "With ignorance (*avidyā*)."

Since ignorance (*avidyā*) is the condition for consciousness (*vijñāna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are subsumed under it, there are both extensive and abbreviated [presentations]. Why, then, is it not further examined? The explanation says:

When examining the gateway of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the principle must follow its proper sequence. Since consciousness arises from formations (*saṃskāra*), one does not examine it;
and since formations arise from ignorance, there is no possibility of an interruption, and thus they are not separately examined.
"How is it that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) has consciousness (vijñāna) as its simultaneous condition?
The commentary states: This question concerns the sense in which name-and-form arises simultaneously with consciousness.
[The text] has already addressed this point here, up until the point where it returns to the discussion of consciousness.
The commentary states: This is the answer. It means that when consciousness arises, it takes that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as its object of attachment and its basis of abiding, which is the body.

Although this passage is cited here to explain the meaning of the "abiding of consciousness" (vijñāna-sthiti), the sense of the "body" is predominant in this context because the Sūtra speaks of the seventh [consciousness] as the support; thus, the Sūtra says that consciousness depends upon name-and-form.
Furthermore, this statement that "craving and delight moisten consciousness" means that through the power of craving,

tainted consciousness becomes attached to the aggregates and attains growth; because name-and-form acts as the co-arising condition for consciousness, that consciousness does not then proceed elsewhere.
"Although the branch of old age and death (up to its point) has consciousness as its condition.

The commentary states: This explains away an anticipated objection. Fearing that there might be an objection saying, "Since you have already observed that old age and death arise with birth as their condition, why do you not further observe that name-and-form arises with consciousness as its condition?
Thus, the meaning of the initial explanation of the text can be understood.
The Vaibhāṣika masters (up to the section on the twelve links). The commentary states:
This records the masters' explanation of the preceding objection. [They argue that] the arising of consciousness and name-and-form are indeed simultaneous with birth;

however, because the desire for revulsion is profound, one observes them again. Because of the desire for revulsion toward the process of saṃsāra, one does not observe everything, but observes birth again. As for the others...
Furthermore, having already understood and aspired toward the cessation of suffering, one therefore observes universally:

"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease," and so on, up to "with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. [Objection: Since one feels revulsion and fear toward birth, one must observe it again;
likewise, one should feel revulsion and fear toward the process of saṃsāra and observe it universally. Why, then, do you say that because of revulsion, one does not observe it universally?
What is the intended meaning of observing this? It is said: suppose a person knows that the flavor and fragrance of food are unbalanced;
wishing to ascertain this for certain, they should briefly smell it. Because they find it disagreeable, they stop as soon as they have recognized it.
Likewise, when one must observe again because of the arising of [defilements], it is due to the depth of one's aversion that one is unable to prevent them entirely.
Having already distinguished the names [up to] "therefore it is called conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*).
The commentary states: From here below is the third explanation of contact (*sparśa*). First, it is explained as six contacts with respect to their basis (*āśraya*);

second, it is divided into two types of contact with respect to the basis and so forth; third, it is divided into eight types of contact with respect to association (*samprayoga*). Thus, contact is said to be tenfold.

The sixfold [contact] is the first of these. The term "contact" (*sparśa*) indicates its essential nature; the "sixfold" refers to its classification according to its basis; and the phrase "arising from the conjunction of three" cites the cause to demonstrate its nature.
In the commentary, the first part explains the verse, while the latter part provides a definitive interpretation. This is the explanation of the verse itself.

Fearing that one might doubt how the sixth [consciousness], the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and mental objects (*dharma*) could be "conjoined" since they do not exist simultaneously, the first section is provided to explain the relationship between cause and effect.
The meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*) is established because they are mutually connected and because they share a single result. As for their being mutually connected as cause and effect:

it is because consciousness arises as the result from the two causes of the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*). As for their sharing a single result: it is because the three together produce contact (*sparśa*).
The distinct nature of contact has already been established within the "Universal Ground" (mahābhūmika) section.

The commentary states: From here below, there is a definitive analysis in six parts: first, clarifying that its substance is real; second, clarifying that it co-exists with consciousness; third, clarifying that it is the condition for sensation;
fourth, clarifying that it is the fruit of the six sense bases; fifth, clarifying that sensation is its fruit; and sixth, distinguishing its causal differences. This is the text.
This demonstrates that its substance is substantially existent; thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that teachers differ in their understanding of this point and do not hold a single view.
One school, such as the Sautrāntikas, asserts that the mere coming together of the three is itself called "contact" (*sparśa*).

Another school asserts that it is a distinct dharma associated with the mind, produced by the coming together of the three, which is called contact. These opposing positions have already been resolved and explained previously.
[The section on] "Discrimination" (Vibhāga). Although [contact] arises from the conjunction of the three, it is produced by two conditions.

The commentary states: From this point downward is the second [section], which clarifies that [contact] co-exists with consciousness; herein, first is the formal analysis of contact (*sparśa*), followed by an analogy regarding feeling (*vedanā*).

To preemptively address this point: in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the Sthavira’s teaching is cited, which holds that the faculties, objects, and consciousness must first exist following contact (*sparśa*), after which consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three is itself termed "contact.
Since the meaning of their conjunction is established in the second moment, it is in the third moment that feeling (*vedanā*) arises conditioned by contact.
Since both [feeling and contact] exist simultaneously, one should ask the Elder: does feeling exist in the second moment? Is consciousness in the third moment not contact?
Having already explained that they are simultaneous, all consciousnesses are indeed contact; yet although there is feeling, it is not the feeling of this specific stage.
This subsequent feeling arises from the contact of this stage. To refute this by means of a different object, [it is said: "the feeling of the subsequent moment."
Regarding whether the consciousness at that stage is identical to or different from the object of cognition: if they were identical, it could not arise from what preceded;

if they were different, there would be no logical connection for their simultaneous arising. To explain: contact does not exist apart from sensation, and the consciousness at the stage of sensation is not itself contact.

Therefore, the reason established here—that contact arises simultaneously with consciousness—serves as a further illustration to establish that sensation and the other [mental factors] likewise arise simultaneously.

Śāriputra asked: "Since it has already been stated that there is no such thing as consciousness arising prior to contact, how can it be established at the outset that consciousness and contact arise simultaneously?

The explanation says: Within the Sautrāntika school, there is no such thing as a simultaneous cause and effect, because they maintain that the essence of contact is simply the convergence of the three [organ, object, and consciousness].

Therefore, they do not say that contact arises subsequent to consciousness. This is refuted by the reasoning previously established, which proves that contact exists as a distinct entity, as it is that which is pressed upon [by the object].

One should understand that there is a fear that, upon hearing of the production [of contact] from the conjunction of the three, one might claim that the first [conjunction] induces the subsequent moment of contact.
To prevent such a misconception, it is established that [contact] arises simultaneously. This is the correct principle for establishing that contact and consciousness arise together;

thus, the formal inference (*prayoga*) is stated: "This sense-faculty and this contact do not arise at a time other than that of this sense-consciousness, because they are the conditions for the arising of that consciousness."
Because there is no distinction, it is as with these faculties and consciousnesses;
that is, as the Sūtra says, "up to" and so forth at length.

[The commentary] states: The following explains the meaning of the non-distinction between causes and conditions, which has two interpretations. The first interpretation follows the faculties and objects.

The second explanation follows the literal meaning of the names; this is the first [point]. "An internal body of consciousness" refers to the six internal bases (*āyatana*), while the term "external name-and-form" refers to the six external objects.

Since it is stated that these two pairs serve as the conditions for the arising of contact, and since other sūtras state that consciousness arises from two conditions, we know that these are identical to the conditions for the arising of consciousness.
"Is it not the case that this [point]—up to 'the reason is not universally established'—is as follows?
The commentary states: This external objection [claims] that the internal body of consciousness can encompass the six consciousnesses;
logically, it should clarify that the condition of contact depends on three factors, and thus the stated condition for arising shares the fault of having an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*).
The meaning of the sūtra is not as [the opponent claims], as has already been explained above.

The commentary states: This citation of two pairs of statements proves that there are not three meanings; furthermore, it cites the previous verse to show that from the two conditions of eye and visible form, all mental factors (caitta-dharma)—namely consciousness, contact, and feeling—are produced.
Since these are subsumed within the category of "mental engagement" (manasikāra), there is a causal proof for the existence of two types of contact.
The establishment [of the sequence] is precluded by the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Furthermore, a sutra states that "consciousness arises from contact" (up to "...because there is nothing to obstruct it").
The commentary says: This second explanation demonstrates that consciousness and contact both take the two factors of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their conditions.
By this, it is proven that [feeling and so forth] are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

The commentary states: the following provides examples and proofs for feeling and the others. First, they are proven by reasoning, because their conditions for arising are identical, as stated in the verse.
Second, they are proven by scripture, because it is taught that they are intermingled. Third, they are proven by the tenets of that school, because within that school’s system, consciousness...

This is precisely contact (*sparśa*). Furthermore, since the Sūtra states that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, by this principle they can all arise simultaneously;
therefore, this is the meaning of the term "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmikadharma*).
They state as follows: [they] are concomitant with all minds.

The commentary states: This passage explains that the Elder’s [Vasubandhu’s] definition of the "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika-dharma) does not require them to be invariably concomitant; how then can their constant concomitance serve as proof for their status as universal mental factors?
If this is so, what then is the meaning of "universal mental factor"?
The commentary states: This poses a question and that provides the explanation.
Regarding the three triads—up to "the remaining as appropriate"—the commentary states:
This explanation by the Venerable Elder [Vasumitra] applies universally across the three triads of those with vitarka and vicāra, the wholesome and so forth, and the trainee and so forth.

The term "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*) refers to those factors that exist in all stages of consciousness. Those factors that exist only in wholesome stages are called "wholesome universal factors" (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).
Those factors that exist only in defiled stages are called "universal factors of affliction" (*kleśamahābhūmika*).

Because these [factors] may arise in this [particular stage] but do not arise in others, they arise according to their respective conditions; it does not mean they are constantly present. This is why [the term "universal"] is not applied [to them].
As for the explanation of the "Great Unwholesome Grounds," the *Mūla-śāstra* (the *Jñānaprasthāna*), in its section on the *Dhātu-pāda*, analyzes the meaning of the various levels (*bhūmi*).

However, it does not explicitly state "Great Unwholesome Grounds"; rather, this was added by later *Vaibhāṣika* masters who, because they were reciting the "Wholesome Grounds," supplemented them with the "Unwholesome Grounds.
Since these were not part of the original treatise, there is no need to further reconcile them; therefore, the "Minor Afflictions" (*upakleśa*) are not explained here.
Because it does not state that [the affliction] pervades all minds, this is merely words that contradict the aforementioned sūtra. The commentary states:
This master of the treatise refutes [the opponent] for deviating from the previously explained *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Sūtra on Interpenetration) by attempting to establish a heterodox position.
This is not logical.
He makes this statement (up to) he speaks thus. [The commentator] says:
This external counter-interrogation further cites the subsequent statement to cause the author of the treatise to explain it, intending to clarify the preceding characteristic.
The meaning of "various" (*miśra*) is as explained below to express the sense of having the same object (*samālambana*).
What remains unclarified? [The point that] its principle is definitive.
The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains that the meanings of the preceding and succeeding [passages] differ.
"How can one know for certain?
[The author] explains: This is the reason for the objection;
it has already been well established in other sūtras.

The commentary states: This master of the treatise cites other scriptural passages that do not exclude the word "together" (*saha*) to prove that the three—contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and cognition (*saṃjñā*)—necessarily arise simultaneously.

Because they are proven to be non-sequential, they lack separate objects of perception (*ālambana*); for contact does not have the same object as its basis, just as vitality (*āyuḥ*) and heat (*uṣman*) lack such objects.
Once this analogy is established, all objections are silenced. If one were to interpret the sutra according to that [opponent's] view, it would imply that they arise without interval (*nirantara*).
As previously stated in the sūtra, it is impossible for non-existence and existence, or existence and non-existence, to stand in a relationship of mutual dependence;

since the principle of mutual dependence does not exist, how could there be a principle of mutual commingling? For two things can only constitute a state of mutual dependence if they both exist in relation to one another.
Thus, by means of the cited sūtra, the meaning of "both" has been well established.
"How is it that contact gives rise to feeling... up to the contact that produces [feeling]? (The commentary states:
From here below is the third section, clarifying that feeling is conditioned by contact, consisting of one question and two answers. This is the question:
based on the principle previously established that contact and feeling arise simultaneously, why is it said only that "feeling arises from contact"? Therefore, two passages are cited to clarify this.
The phrasing is difficult.
Is it not clearly seen that [the same applies] up to contact?

The commentary states: Below this, there are three parts: first, a general explanation; second, resolving objections; third, indicating the thesis. Within the first part, there are three interpretations.
This is the first [point]; the meaning of the three and two examples cited can be understood by extension.
This analogy is not uniform (until the point where it says): "contact is not conditioned by feeling. The commentary states: Furthermore, this is difficult to clarify.
Following the lamp, the shadow moves; following the body, the shadow changes. Length follows the two [factors], and existence follows the two.
It cannot be said that there is a fixed cause for the feeling that arises upon contact;
although there are no manifest signs [of such a cause], there is nonetheless a distinction.

The commentary states: This master of the treatise explains that the mental factor of "contact" (sparśa) takes the mind as its object and functions as "feeling" (vedanā); it is precisely by this principle that [the text] follows [this interpretation].
The meaning of "contact" (sparśa) is established.
If one still does not understand [the passage] up to "not being mutually contradictory," the commentary states:
This second explanation, based on conventional contact, can only produce feeling (vedanā) and does not arise from feeling. If...
Based on the actual facts, although contact is also said to arise from feeling, this is stated because of the mutual relationship of cause and effect;

for fear that one might further claim that consciousness also serves as a reciprocal condition for feeling, it must be understood that contact is merely a designation, and not only gives rise to feeling. Therefore, the commentary states:
"It is not only visual consciousness that constitutes the essence of eye-contact, for feeling and the other factors also arise in dependence upon the eye and visible form."
Furthermore, regarding another meaning [up to] the meaning of revealing distinct categories (*paryāya*), the commentary states:
This third explanation is given in terms of the aspect of experiencing (*anubhava-lakṣaṇa*).

It says that contact (*sparśa*) gives rise to feeling (*vedanā*), but it is not by means of this very feeling that contact can arise, because they do not function as mutual associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*). Therefore, taking the mindfulness directed toward the body (*kāyagatasmṛti*) as an example, they serve as conditions for one another.
One who knows mindfulness of the body contemplates everything from the feet to the crown of the head as impure, thereby producing revulsion toward the object and eliminating defilement.
When one relies on mindfulness and revulsion toward the object, there is nothing further that can be added;
this principle is what is meant by saying that mindfulness of breathing, mindfulness of the Buddha, and the various immeasurable perceptions also sever sensual desire through different methods.
How is it known that feeling (*vedanā*) also has contact (*sparśa*) as its condition?

The commentary states: Furthermore, since this question is posed according to a different perspective—that there is a distinct perspective in which contact arises from feeling—how can it be known that [feeling] arises from contact?
Other sūtras state that [feeling] arises conditioned by bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*).

The commentary states: This citation demonstrates that because there is contact with the body due to bodily sensation, it is thereby proven that there is contact with the body arising from bodily sensation.
This is because [bodily sensation] is a concomitant cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), an associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), or a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) [of such contact].
"Why is it that [the sūtras] do not state that feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth depend on the eye and so forth?
[The author] comments: The following passage addresses the objection within the second explanation. First, the inquiry; second, the explanation; third, the objection;

fourth, the resolution. This is the inquiry. If the aforementioned conventional contact (*saṃsparśa*) has the threefold conjunction as its essence, and if these various threefold conjunctions are capable only of...
Although the contact that arises may be designated by the name of its cause—namely, "contact"—in reality, it also gives rise to sensation and so forth.
For what reason is it not called "sensation" and so on?
Because within the conjunction, all [factors] are induced by contact.
The commentary states: This explanation has three parts. First, if one considers it from the perspective of the result, it should also be called "feeling" (*vedanā*);

however, because the meaning of "contact" (*sparśa*) is more prominent, the name "contact" is established exclusively for it. Second, it clarifies that the term "contact" is based on the sense of "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*), and not on the production of the result that is contact;

therefore, it cannot be objected that feeling and so forth are also contact. If, by necessity, the cause that can produce the result of contact were itself named "contact" based on its conjunction, then it would follow that...

Because sensation (*vedanā*) and the others arise with contact (*sparśa*) as their cause, they all receive the name "contact. However, in reality, sensation and the others all arise from a conventional contact;

one contact gives rise to sensation, while for the others, distinct designations such as "perception" (*saṃjñā*) are established. If it is said that sensation and the others share the common name "contact," there is no fault, as they are designated as "contact" according to the result of the threefold conjunction (*trika-saṃnipāta*).
If it is said that sensation and the others have only distinct names [as results], then since the result does not conform to the cause, the cause likewise [does not conform].

If one does not follow the literal phrasing but relies on the intended meaning, there is no fault even regarding contact (*sparśa*), because it is stated that feeling (*vedanā*) and the other factors all arise from the conjunction of the three.
Thus, another sutra says that "contacted by the mind" (*manaḥ-saṃspṛṣṭa*) is the condition for feeling.
If this is so, [how do you explain] the statement that "conditioned by contact, feeling arises"?

The commentary states: This is an objection. Since you have already admitted that the provisional contact (prajñapti-sparśa) can give rise to perception (saṃjñā) and so forth, why do you say it can only give rise to feeling (vedanā)? [The answer is:
Perception and the others are also mentioned; this is a general statement regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).

The commentary states: This refers to the pervasive [nature of contact]. It is understood that within the sūtras it is taught that contact gives rise to perception (*saṃjñā*), as previously explained.
However, in the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), only feeling (*vedanā*) is mentioned because, in the stage following contact, feeling is the most predominant factor.

Thus, by using the term "feeling" as a general designation for all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), it is logically established that perception and the other factors are implicitly included therein.
"However, regarding dependent origination (up to) cutting off its root.

[The] commentary states: "This indicates the thesis (*siddhānta*). Although the preceding section provided a general explanation so that the meaning might be easily clarified, in reality, it is taught in the context of dependent origination that actual contact (*sparśa*) gives rise to feeling (*vedanā*).
How is this known to be so? Because it is stated only that [feeling] arises from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). If one relies on...

If conventional contact (*prajñapti-sparśa*) not only depends on the sense faculties because it must consist of the synthesis of three factors, how could actual contact (*dravya-sparśa*) arise from the faculties alone?
Although [actual contact] indeed arises from the three, the faculty is preeminent; because the preeminent is emphasized, it is said to arise only from the faculty.
Since the conventional basis lacks such preeminence or inferiority, yet the faculty is emphasized, one knows that the actual is not the conventional. If this is so, what then?

Regarding the statement that contact (*sparśa*) alone gives rise to feeling (*vedanā*), and does not state that they arise together or that contact gives rise to other [factors], one explanation says:

this is because it describes how a superior cause in a prior stage produces a superior effect in a subsequent stage. Alternatively, it may be because the feeling of a subsequent stage serves as the proximate cause for craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth;

thus, in order to ensure that contact—which is the proximate cause of the fruit—does not give rise [to craving], it specifically states that contact is the cause of feeling. In reality, however, feeling also arises from contact.

Perceptions and so forth arise from feeling, and there is likewise the arising of dharmas such as contact; thus, there is no contradiction with the principle of mutual causality or the analogy of the field.
All mental states and mental factors [arise] conditioned by the six sense bases, which in turn condition contact.
The commentary states: The following is the fourth section, which clarifies [the stage of contact] as the fruit of the six sense bases. It consists of a question and an answer; this is the question.

It challenges the view that [contact] is exclusively the fruit in relation to other mental factors, arguing that at this stage, contact is predominant, arising with the six sense bases as its conditions.
The commentary states: This response indicates that, according to the superior principle, this stage should actually be understood as being inclusive [of all].
Furthermore, for what reason does one give rise to superior perceptions and so forth?
The commentary states: From here below is the fifth section, which clarifies that sensation (*vedanā*) is the fruit. It consists of one question and two answers; this is the question.
If, after the excellence of contact (*sparśa*), there is also the excellence of perception (*saṃjñā*), for what reason is it said that only the excellence of feeling (*vedanā*) arises?
Although one should not raise an objection regarding the relationship between contact and those [other factors], the response is as follows:
although at the stage of the excellence of contact it coexists with feeling and the others, within that association (*samprayoga*), it is feeling that experiences [the object].

Because the characteristic of contact is such that its meaning as being "conducive to feeling" (*vedanānukūla*) is predominant, and because it remains particularly conducive to feeling at a later time as well,

it is said that the fruit of contact is exclusively feeling and nothing else. This is just as resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is specifically taught as the cause for certainty, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) for calm (*śamatha*),
and diligence (*vīrya*) for insight (*vipaśyanā*), and so forth.
"What is the distinction between name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), and contact (sparśa) as conditions?
The commentary states: Below this, the sixth section concerns the distinctions among causes; first there is the question, followed by the answer. This is the question.

There are three different distinctions regarding the causes of contact: first, contact conditioned by name-and-form; second, contact arising from two conditions; third, [contact arising from] the six [sense bases].
What is the difference between these three: the sense bases (*āyatana*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and contact (*sparśa*)?
In which sutra is it stated that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the condition for contact?

[The author] states: The following is the answer; first, he sets forth his own view, and subsequently, he recounts divergent opinions. Within the presentation of his own view, he first poses the inquiry.

This consists of: (1) the location of the teaching; (2) citing the scriptural passage; (3) interrogating what the scripture elucidates; and (4) explaining the distinctions through comparison. This [first section] interrogates the location of the teaching:
"Contact arises conditioned by two," as stated in the *Gāthā*: "The eye, visible forms, and so forth. Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
"With the body of consciousness and external name-and-form as the two conditions, various contacts arise."
Regarding "contact conditioned by the six sense bases," as in the case of "name-and-form conditions contact" within the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, which sūtra explicitly states this?
It is the *Mahāpratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*. [The passage] beginning with "that which is called name-and-form" is cited.
The commentary states: This citation of the scriptural text makes it clear that there is a substantial entity (*vastu*) which can be known and designated.
This indicates that what can be described as "contact" (sparśa) arises from contact; that is, it arises with contact as its sequence, contact as its cause, and contact as its condition.

In summary, this indicates that which is capable of producing contact. Alternatively, one may correlate these individually: contact as the sequence, the sense faculty as the basis, and other conditions as the causes, which together produce actual contact.
The remainder is explained in subsequent sections.
What meaning does this cited sūtra intend to clarify?
The commentary states: This interrogates what the sūtra clarifies—namely, that name-and-form (nāmarūpa), up to [the point where it says] "it is also impossible to designate."
The commentary states: From here below, the differences are explained through a comparative analysis. There are two locations where such explanations and analyses occur; this is the first.

That is to say, in that sutra, the object (*ālambana*) is described as the "aspect" (*ākāra*) by means of the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, because it is the aspect traversed by the activity [of consciousness].

Furthermore, the faculties (*indriya*) are described as the "indicative markers" (*uddeśa*) by means of the etymological method (*nirukti*), because names such as "marking" (*lakṣaṇa*) are applied to them. Thus, the five faculties are discussed.
Taking the object as the "form-body" (rūpakāya), according to the interpretation based on a common substratum (*ekāśraya*), form is taken as the essence;

since form is itself the body, this state of conjunction is called "contact with resistance" (*pratighasamsparśa*). Because it is the cause of contact with resistance, the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are designated as the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*).
According to the interpretation based on a common substratum, name is taken as the essence; since name is itself the body, this state of conjunction is called [the contact of non-resistance].

Because the "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) is the cause [of the name], it is designated by way of its effect; this is explained from the perspective of a prolonged duration. Thus, the mind and mental phenomena are established as the "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*).

If there were no designation-contact regarding the mind and mental phenomena, they would not exist; being without a basis, they would be non-existent in the sense that they are merely conventional designations.

By analogy, one should understand that "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is likewise taught as existing [conventionally]. Because of the existence of this conventional contact, actual contact (*bhūta-saṃsparśa*) is able to arise.
If conventional contact (*prajñapti-sparśa*) were unreal, it would likewise lack an essential nature (*svabhāva*); because it lacks existence, its nature cannot be cognized.

Since its nature is thus unascertainable, upon what basis could it be designated? Consequently, it is difficult to establish a name for it across the three periods of time, as the past and future are named by way of the present.

If the present lacks an essential nature, who could be said to have "already" experienced or "will" experience it? To say that conventional contact is unreal is therefore meaningless; this is what is being stated.
Taking conventional contact as the basis for name-and-form (nāmarūpa), that which arises from the conventional is said to be "conditioned by contact.
If it were merely thus [up to] "therefore there is a distinction," [the commentary] states:

this explains the difference in causes relative to the previous interpretation. That is to say, just as in the fourfold explanation of names, they are namely the mind (manas) and mental objects (dharma).
Form (*rūpa*) consists of the five sense faculties and their objects; thus, it is the same as "contact" (*sparśa*), which likewise arises from two conditions.

This is because the term "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), wherein the five faculties and their objects are designated as "form. Furthermore, these two [terms] apply universally to all faculties and objects, whereas the designations "name-and-form" and "six sense bases" differ in their scope:
although "name-and-form" shares the same stage as the six sense bases, it applies only to the faculties and not to the objects.
Because their essential natures possess varying degrees of breadth and narrowness, the three types of causes differ from one another.
Furthermore, there is another distinct meaning (extending to the point where) even actual contact (*sparśa*) does not exist.
[The commentary] states: This second explanation of the modes of activity (*ākāra*) is identical in its general presentation to the previous explanation; it relies upon these two types of...
The "contact of birth" (*jāti-sparśa*) is called the "name-and-form body" (*nāmarūpa-kāya*). Here, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the basis;

"arising from the mind" (*manas-ja*) is explained by the *bahuvrīhi* compound as the "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*), meaning that which is designated by name. This very "name-body" is termed "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-sparśa*).

That which "depends on the five faculties" is explained by the *bahuvrīhi* compound as the "form-body" (*rūpa-kāya*), meaning that which consists of form. This very "form-body" is termed "existence" (*bhava*).

Although contact (*sparśa*) generally applies to all [mental] aspects, it is designated here by its basis; since the sense faculty is the support (*āśraya*), the name is applied according to that support.

Fearing that doubts might arise, it is called "body-contact" (*kāya-sparśa*). As for the statement that it "depends on the mental consciousness," this means that the mental consciousness serves as its support.
If this were the case, it should be called "mental-consciousness-contact" (*mano-vijñāna-sparśa*); yet it is instead called "mind-contact" (*manas-sparśa*). Is this not contradictory?
Now, the meaning of the explanation is that name, mind, and mental consciousness are of one essence and without difference;

therefore, the basis of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is itself the essence of the two conditions, because it takes name and form as its support. Contact (*sparśa*) such as this is called "having a support.

If this were non-existent, there would be no contact without a support. In the explanation of the subsequent section, the absence of contact without a support is used as an analogy for the absence of the two bodies.
In reality, they do not exist. Furthermore, the basis for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is precisely the internal six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);

because name-and-form takes these as its basis, the six bases themselves are metaphorically designated as "six contacts" (*ṣaṭsparśa*). Thus, if these [bases] do not exist as real contacts, then real contact also does not exist.
Since there is no real contact, there can be no contact that lacks a basis. Below, this is illustrated by the example that although the six [bases] exist, there is no metaphorical contact.
Apart from the basis, there is no real contact; the six contacts refer to the six bases.
If one explains it in this way, one understands the profound meaning.

[The commentary] states: This is presented in contrast to the previous explanation to demonstrate the difference in the causes. Since "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) was previously mentioned, it refers only to the basis.

Name-and-form and the six sense bases are not distinct; they are explained through different terminology to make known their distinct meanings, which should be understood as being different from the two [preceding aggregates], as previously stated.
Other masters say that [the remaining aggregates] follow in their respective order.

The commentary states: This passage describes two schools of divergent opinion. According to the former school, the substance of *nāmarūpa* is broad, encompassing both the faculties and their objects, whereas the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) consist only of the faculties.
According to the latter school, *nāmarūpa* subsumes many factors;

therefore, in terms of the elements (*dhātu*), it consists only of the faculties and their objects, while in terms of the bases (*āyatana*), it is explained as a condition in the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The critique states that these divergent opinions do not accord with correct principle.
This is contradictory;
that is, the preceding six types of contact (up to the point mentioned) are established under the name "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).
The commentary states: from here below, the second section, based on the support (*āśraya*) and other factors, divides contact into two types, namely those associated with the five consciousnesses.

It is called "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) because both its basis and its object possess resistance; this is explained through the *tatpuruṣa* or *upapada* compound as "the contact that belongs to resistance" or "the contact proximate to resistance.
Therefore, it is proximate to contact with resistance. Consequently, that which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).

"Designation" (*adhivacana*) refers to a name (*nāman*); it is called "designation" because it is a superior word (*adhika-vacana*), meaning that only when the name has arisen as a superior factor does the subsequent word [function].
It is called "designation" (*adhivacana*) because it increases; or, it is said that it "increases" because it causes speech to increase by means of names.

Alternatively, it is called "superior designation" because it is superior to speech in its capacity to express and signify. Furthermore, because speech is made superior through the power of the name, it is called "proximate. This refers to the object of mental contact;
since the name arises from that [object] and the object serves as the basis for the name, it is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Or...
The *Xiānglín Shì* (Commentary on Adjacent Explanations) states:
Some say that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is designated by the name "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).
