The commentary states: This is an explanation meaning that it praises both the auxiliary factors and the substance; or, it praises what is relinquished and what is received, rather than praising the substance of the food itself.
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously.
The commentary says: "This refers to what was stated before.
What was stated before?
The commentary states: This refers to the locus of the critique.
It means that [the term] "to-be" (bhavya) is used as a designation for what is yet to be; [it asks] what contradiction there is [in this].

The commentary states: This cites the locus of the statement, meaning that within the preceding context, although the substance has not yet actually become food, it is designated by the name "food" based on its future state.
There is no fault in this figurative praise.
Furthermore, the eulogy of the virtues of the food (extending to) "also relying on that which is not a substance" is explained as follows:
this third interpretation of the eulogy of the virtues of the food is likewise applicable to all physicians.
Furthermore, [the sūtra] cites the characteristics of form (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) [up to the point where it says] "therefore it is said thus.
The commentary states: This fourth explanation clarifies that while the excellence of the form is praised, the same applies to the others.
Why does the sūtra not praise the food, the utensils, and the tactile objects?

The commentary states: This critique [argues] that the Sūtra does not praise contact (*sparśa*) and mind (*manas*), but rather praises those possessing form (*rūpa*) and so forth, up to the point where their essence is without deficiency.
The commentary states: This is the explanation. First, regarding the meaning being manifest, it can be understood by analogy; second, regarding the substance of nutriment, this is nutriment.
The statement clarifies that the meaning follows its respective order and that no words have been omitted.
However, regarding the Elder’s statement [up to] "all are called food," the commentary says:
from here below, he refutes divergent views—first stating the opponent's position and secondly providing the formal refutation; this is the statement of that position.
The color, odor, taste, and tangibility that exist within the same aggregate are all termed "nutriment" (āhāra). This is proven by scripture:
the Sūtra speaks of them collectively as "that which enters the mouth, nose, teeth, and is chewed," and so forth at length; it does not say that color is excluded.
Since color, odor, and the rest can all collectively enter [the body], they should all constitute the substance of nutriment. This is also proven by reasoning: for all of them are digested.
"At that time, it can increase blood and so forth.
Their statement is irrational. [This leads to] proving that visible form (*rūpa*) is also nutriment.

The commentary says: From here below, this is refuted. First, the scriptural authority (*sūtra*) is refuted. Although the Sūtra speaks of them collectively, one must distinguish them according to their meaning.

I cite three examples: first, citing a sūtra which states that karma is the cause of birth, yet there are causes of birth that are not karma—namely, tainted (sāsrava) acquisitions (prāpti), possession (samanvāgama), and so forth;
and there is karma that is not a cause of birth—namely, untainted (anāsrava) and neutral (avyākṛta) karma.
Second, citing a sūtra which speaks of karma that is neither black nor white and has no maturation (avipāka), which is capable of exhausting all karma and severing karma.
Only seven [types of karma] can sever black karma; four can sever white karma; one can sever both; and beyond these, none are capable of exhausting them.

Furthermore, among these, the fourth and the karma of the formless realm are excluded. Regarding the scriptural statement that "consciousness arises" and so forth, it should be distinguished as referring to the outflows-free (*anāsrava*) nutriment;

it should likewise be understood that there must be the characteristic of nutriment, namely, that which is capable of being swallowed and consumed. This serves to distinguish [the outflows-free from the other].
Sound and so forth, as well as that which has nutriment, are said to be able to benefit the faculties; this statement excludes visible form, and for this reason there are only three.
Furthermore, as they have stated, [these] are able to sustain the body.
The commentary states: This passage restates the established reasoning and challenges the intended meaning;
since there is only this assertion and no causal proof to establish it, one must incur the fault that what is claimed to exist without a cause cannot be established.
Therefore, the substance of food consists solely of odor, flavor, and tangibility.
The commentary states: This is a general conclusion.
It is because that which is not form cannot provide benefit [up to] "because there is nothing to benefit.

The commentary states: This explains the exclusion of over-extension. While the meaning of other things being non-nutriment is easy to understand, the fact that form is not [necessarily so] is difficult to know.
Therefore, one must distinguish two points: first, by showing that it does not benefit its own sense organ, it lacks the function of immediate benefit;
second, by showing that it does not benefit liberation, it lacks the function of remote benefit.

This means that while the benefit of the organ’s pleasure when seeing a form is evident, the fact that it does not benefit the eye at that time serves as an analogy for its lack of benefit to the organs within the body.
The exposition of the food of morsels (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) has been concluded, up to the point where it was stated that it does not overlap with the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The commentary states: "From here below, the remaining three foods are explained. This consists of two parts: first, the direct explanation of the text; second, the resolution of objections. This is the direct explanation of the text.

Within the section concluding the previous discussion, the food of morsels has already been explained; the summary of its name has already been provided; and its connection to the realms (*dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) has already been explained.
Having already explained the nature of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) bound to the upper realms, one should know that their essential character has been stated.

Having already explained [the fetters] as they pertain to all three locations, regarding the explanation of the three nutriments (*āhāra*), "contact" (*sparśa*) refers to the equal [contact]. This designation of the name is explained; these three are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

Their substance is explained as pervading all three realms. Thus, having explained the bondage to the realms, these four [fetters] and so forth are summarized in sequence; only the final three [nutriments] are [discussed here].
This explains the meaning of the distinction.
For what reason are untainted (*anāsrava*) contact and so forth not considered nutriment?

The commentary states: from here below, the obstacles and difficulties are resolved; first, the obstacle regarding that which is excluded is explained, and subsequently, the obstacle regarding that which is established is explained. This is [the beginning].
This raises the objection that was previously set aside: for what reason are the untainted (*anāsrava*) states excluded from being "nutriments" (*āhāra*)?
The principle that "nutriment" means that which can draw [beings] toward existence is established as certain.
The commentary states: this is the explanation. "Nutriment" refers to that which can draw forth all forms of existence; because it has the sense of "that which leads," it is called nutriment.
The food of this stage can induce the various existences (*bhava*) of this stage in the future;

because it can nourish these existences, it carries the meaning of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*), and is therefore called "nutriment" (*āhāra*). That is to say, the food of this stage sustains these existing existences of this stage.

Because it functions through these two meanings—nourishing and sustaining—it is definitively a nutriment for the outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the perception of revulsion toward food, as it conforms to [the cycle of] existence. This is so.
That which is loathsome and cuts off craving is the place where [craving] grows; the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) can only support others by inducing existence (*bhava*).

This means that when it is present, it nourishes the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, while all other meanings are lacking. Furthermore, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) of other stages also only serves to support, and for this reason it is established as "contaminated.
Regarding the doubt: "What is it that can draw forth a future existence? It refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) that draws forth a future birth.
That is to say, only unwholesome states and already tainted (*sāsrava*) states that accord with the arising of craving for future births possess the power to draw forth other [states];

since they lack this power, they should be identical to untainted (*anāsrava*) states and states belonging to other stages. Furthermore, since edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it lacks the power to induce [such results].

If it is argued that because it sustains others, it enables them to draw forth the untainted and states of other stages, [we reply that] it can also sustain and benefit those [untainted and other-stage states].
Because one has severed the two limits and realized that from which [existence] arises, the following commentary states:

although the untainted (*anāsrava*) can temporarily support the existing conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) to constitute its own basis, it is not for the purpose of inducing a transition toward a different destination; thus, the tainted (*sāsrava*) is not like this and cannot serve as an analogy.

Regarding the binding of future existence (*punarbhava*), the commentary states there are two types: first, exclusively maturation (*vipāka*); second, both tainted and untainted. If it were exclusively...

The dharmas that are *vipāka* (maturation) are those outflows (*sāsrava*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) factors of this stage which are all capable of benefiting this cause of maturation so that it may produce its future fruit.

Within these, if they are neutral by way of maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*), they function as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) in relation to their own future similar types; thus, they share with the cause of maturation the sense of "jointly drawing forth" [the result].
If they are not of the same type, they are nonetheless considered [causes] solely on the basis of being able to provide benefit—both the act of providing and the recipient of such provision.

All [nutriments] that draw [the body] forward are called "attracting" (*āharati*). This cannot be analogized to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states of other stages. If one were to include those with outflows (*sāsrava*), then all would be mutually so. An objection is raised:
"External factors such as fragrance and the like cannot provide sustenance, nor do they have the power to attract;

therefore, they should not constitute nutriment. The following provides the explanation: Nutriment is comprised of three types. External factors are exclusively *niṣyanda* (outflow) results, whereas internal factors consist of three types, which cause [the body] to differ [from its previous state].
By bringing [the body] to maturity, causing the outflow (nisyanda) to arise, and causing it to grow and increase, they are successively designated as "nutriments" (āhāra).

Alternatively, this passage cites their essential categories to clarify that they possess the functional capacity to draw forth existence through successive stages; thus, the principle is established, and the meaning of "nutriment" is made manifest.
"How should this be understood... [it] should not be established"? [The commentary] states:
The following explains the objection to what has been established; this is the raising of the objection itself. Regarding the three types of food established [by you], how can they be distinct?
If their functions were not different, then—just as fragrance, taste, and touch combined constitute a single food—the three would fail to be established as three.
"Just as within a single lump [of food], up to the point where the distinctions are fully established.

The commentary states: This explanation contains three points. First, it clarifies that while the individual and collective aspects of the three [nutriments] are each difficult to discern, they are distinguished by their respective actual functions;
however, the three—contact (*sparśa*) and so forth—can be divided into three nutriments because they are not commonly known to be one.

Because odors and so forth are consumed, they are not like this; it is commonly known that they are one. For this reason, it is logical to divide touch and the others into three, whereas one should not say they are identical, as is the case with odors and the rest.
Next, it is explained that the functions of two or three are equally difficult to discern; likewise, the essential natures of touch and the others are also difficult to understand.
To facilitate understanding, they are distinguished according to principle, while the three natures of odors and the rest are excluded because they are easily understood.

Because this is known, it is simply stated that there is "one" [link]; however, when explaining the subsequent contact (*sparśa*) and so forth, there are also distinctions based on their periods of predominance.

That is to say, the fruits obtained by these three types are distinct, as previously mentioned. Furthermore, regarding the specific timing of the actualization of the supported factors that they benefit and induce:

at the time of generating craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) is actualized; and at the time of inducing future existence, volition (*cetanā*) regarding old age, death, and so forth is actualized.

The food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) manifests at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*). Alternatively, one may distinguish the specific results of these three [foods] in relation to one another;

or, if in this stage the food of contact (*sparśāhāra*) is most predominant, then by taking the others as causes, its superior function is established—namely, that contact is the result while the others are designated as the causes.
If *cetanā* (volition) or *vijñāna* (consciousness) are predominant, the same logic should apply accordingly. This refers to the stage where the preeminent result arises.
Regarding the manifestation of the fruit, there is no lack of distinction at the time this [fruit] functions.
As the Sūtra says (up to): "For what reason? The commentary states:
The following explains away the objection; this refers to raising an objection as a question. This is the meaning of the term *bāhulika*.

Because there are many [variant] explanations, the Sanskrit original is retained here without being translated into the Chinese (Táng) language. In this context, the question is raised based on one specific meaning:
first, it refers to that which is directly manifested by the name; second, because it is the tenet (*siddhānta*) of the treatise (*śāstra*), "already arisen" is cited as the explanation.
This refers to the meaning of "the fruit being drawn forth while [the cause] exists.
The commentary states: The following provides a general explanation to clarify the intent of the phrase "seeking birth.

To prove this point—that there is a substantial entity (*ātman*) existing within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—various sūtras are cited and five names are established. This is the first [of those names], as has already been explained previously.
It is argued that the karma of form in the desire realm cannot act as a projective force; rather, that which projects must necessarily be mental volition (*manas-karman*).
Because it arises from mental volition and is produced by the mind, it is called "produced" (*abhinirvṛtta*).
If this were so, there would be a great fault.

The commentary states: Furthermore, it is difficult to explain how birth from a womb, an egg, or moisture could be induced by projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) unless it necessarily involves mind-made (*manomaya*) existence;
otherwise, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would not exist, as [the body] must be formed [therein].
The commentary states: This response addresses the objection that those who grasp external conditions are not exclusively "mind-made" (*manomaya*).

If it were the case that only those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) are designated as "mind-made," would this not lead to confusion with those born from transformation? It is not so, for it has already been clarified in the preceding text that birth [from other sources] does not share this characteristic.

If that were the case, then since form (*rūpa*) in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) acts as the attractor, it should not be considered "mind-made. This is not so; for although the physical form of those beings in that realm acts as the attractor, [the designation still applies].
Because there must necessarily be volition (*cetanā*).
Second, seeking birth until the fetters of birth (*jāti-saṃyojana*) have not yet been severed.

The commentary states: This cites the latter four [fetters]; the first three are easy [to understand]. Regarding the fifth, two meanings are established, with two sūtras serving as evidence: first, by...
It is called "arising" because it manifests instantaneously; secondly, it is called "arising" because it manifests momentarily.
Regarding those destined for rebirth who are non-retrogressive, the aforementioned sūtra states that the body of birth-and-death is called "ruin," because it is destructible.
This explicitly reveals that it is subject to severance and impermanent extinction; thus, that body is termed "ruin" in its very essence and in its destruction.
Regarding what is called "existence" (bhava) in the world, it is not that there is a body; this existence refers to the world. The World-Honored One said that this exists.
This destruction of the self-substance (*ātman*) arising reveals the meaning of a destructible self-substance suddenly emerging.

It should also be said that there is the destruction of the world's birth. Furthermore, because the *Brahma-voice* (Sanskrit) is often inverted, "birth" (*jāti*) is placed above; another explanation says it is "existence."
"Decaying" (*bhedana*) reveals that the body of birth-and-death has the sense of being subject to destruction; therefore, it is said that its intrinsic nature is decaying.
"The decaying world" (*bhajana-loka*) intends to clarify that once the decaying intrinsic nature has arisen, the decaying world is produced;

thus this statement is made. The arising above and the production below are expressed according to their respective meanings. "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and "world" (*loka*) are general designations for these two.

In order to clarify that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) truly exists, it is designated by its own essence; yet, fearing that one might grasp it as permanent, it is distinguished by the term "worldly" (*laukika*).
This is easily understood after the subsequent sutra passage.
For what reason is it said that [the nutriment] up to the so-called factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are [nourishment]?

The commentary states: The following explains the "Discernment of Superior Function. First is the question, second is the answer, third is the inquiry, and fourth is the explanation. This is the question:
As stated in the *Āhāra-sutta* (Sūtra on Food) within the *Cūḷa-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, it is explained that clear liberation (*vidyā-vimukti*) also has its nutriment;
it is not without nutriment. What is the nutriment of clear liberation? The answer is: The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are its nutriment. Thus, these seven...

The factors of enlightenment, the four foundations of mindfulness, the three types of sublime conduct, the guarding of the sense faculties, right mindfulness, wisdom, and right reflection—these are the practices.

Regarding the question of wholesome qualities, one should approach virtuous friends and good people; these qualities follow the sequence where each preceding factor has the succeeding one as its nutriment.
As for "clearly understanding liberation," this refers to *nirvāṇa*. Since all conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of having a nutriment, why is it [only]...?
[Question: Are the four [nutriments] established as food? [Answer:
Although all conditioned phenomena possess the function of causal conditions, [the author] states:
"This answer is given from the perspective of what is predominant; it does not mean that the others lack the capacity [to serve as conditions]. This can be understood by citing relevant examples.
What are the characteristics of the four nutriments' preeminent functions?
The commentary states: This is an inquiry.
It refers to the first two nutriments [extending] to the beginninglessness of the two types of existence.
The commentary states: The following explains [the four nutriments]. Within this, first my own view is presented, followed by the presentation of divergent opinions.
In presenting my own view, first there is an explanation based on the verses, followed by the discussion of alternative interpretations; this [section] is the explanation based on the verses.

Of the first two nutriments, their capacity to provide benefit is equal, but because the objects of that benefit differ, they are divided into two. As for the latter two nutriments, there is no distinction in the fruit established [by them].
Because their functions differ in terms of being able to project (*ākṣepa*) and being able to produce (*abhinirvṛtti*), volition (*cetanā*) is divided into two types:

volition as projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), since form (*rūpa*) in the desire realm cannot project; and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the seed, because at the time of initial rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), the function of consciousness is predominant.
Thus, the former two nourish the present existence, while the latter two produce the future existence; there is reason for these two principles.
One should first give birth and then nourish; however, when one nourishes first and gives birth later, it is because there is a distinct underlying meaning.
This is intended to clarify that the present basis acts as a cause to trigger the karma that invites the fruits of future lives.

Here, the subsequent cause is the effect and the preceding fruit is the cause; thus, having explained the cause of the preceding fruit, one now shows how the preceding fruit arises from the subsequent cause.
The principle that there is no beginning or end is thus established. If one first speaks of the present life as the cause, its effect has not yet arisen in the future;
if one discusses what is nurtured in the present, its cause has already perished in the past.

Since that which has already perished and that which has not yet arisen are hidden and difficult to discern, and since the effect nurtured in the present is not produced by a present cause, one must therefore rely upon the present effect and the present cause.
The statement that the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) constitutes cause and effect reveals the meaning of beginninglessness; this can be understood by examining the text.
Alternatively, [the passage from] "all sentient beings" [to] "four kinds of nutriment" is explained as follows:
this describes alternative interpretations, which are divided into four types of nutriment because they provide benefit to three categories of persons in both general and specific ways.
Some say that there are four kinds of nutriment, beginning with sensation (*vedanā*).
The commentary states: what follows describes two different schools of interpretation; this is the first school, which itself has two explanations. This is the first [explanation]:
it is understandable that the four [nutriments] are taught in terms of their capacity to act as the remote cause, the object experienced, the object apprehended, and the basis for sensation.
Alternatively, [the four nutriments] range from edible food up to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the two types of existence (*bhava*).

The commentary states: This second explanation clarifies that these four nutriments, in their respective order, serve as the causes for the roots, the great elements, the experience of results, and name-and-form;

they are the objects of craving, sensation, and attachment. Why are craving, sensation, and attachment not established as the nutriments of contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
The *Bie shi ti jie* (Exegesis on the Substance of Separate Nutriment) states that this principle cannot be applied by analogy. It is just as with edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*):
it is called "nutriment" because it can nourish the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), even though one does not expect it to increase craving for further objects.
Since craving for objects arises from contact (*sparśa*) as a condition of conjunction, and is neither direct nor predominant, it is not designated as "nutriment."

Contact (*sparśa*) is proximate and superior to that which is experienced by feeling (*vedanā*), and its manifestation is easy; feeling is remote and inferior to that which is sought by volition (*cetanā*), and its meaning is manifest.
Regarding the future, it is the object not yet sought; regarding the subsequent fruit, it is the preceding cause capable of producing it.

Its meaning is inferior because it arises from volition, being neither superior nor proximate. However, with respect to suffering and pleasure, it is the most excellent cause; for when compared to those [fruits], it is the maturation (*vipāka*).
Because the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*) is established by the fact that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) moistens consciousness (*vijñāna*), yet craving acts only as a secondary condition (*parapratyaya*);

whereas consciousness, being capable of acting as the direct seed (*bīja*) for the arising of existence (*bhava*), is what constitutes nutriment. Therefore, those three [other factors] are not called nutriments. This is demonstrated by citing the Sūtra as proof, showing that the fruit conforms to its cause;
the detailed explanation of the text will be discussed later.
Some say that by contemplating these [objects], one contemplates the four types of inversion (*viparyāsa*).

The commentary states: This second school [asserts this] because: (1) regarding the desire for purity, there is the craving for food; (2) regarding the desire for pleasure, there is the craving for contact; (3) regarding the notion of permanence, there arises volition;

(4) regarding the attachment to existence, there arises volition seeking the future; and (5) regarding the craving for a self, since the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is predominant, many grasp at it as a self.
The Sūtra speaks of the four nutriments (*āhāra*) [up to] "therefore they are called 'sustaining'.

The commentary states: From here on, there are five sections in total that resolve doubts according to specific difficulties: first, explaining the superior functions of the aforementioned four nutriments;

second, explaining the meaning of the aforementioned statement regarding the abandonment and full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the nutriments; third, explaining the reasons why contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are termed nutriments.
Regarding the four conditions, the sutra explains four kinds of nutriment; the fifth explanation states that the name "nutriment" refers to the causes and conditions for sensation (*vedanā*).
This is the first [point]. Within this, there is first an explanation of the meaning of the sutra text, followed by an explanation of the originative cause.

Regarding the explanation of the sutra text, there is first an account of the faultless explanation and subsequently an account of the faulty explanation. Within the faultless explanation, there are briefly three interpretations; this is [the first].

First, the meaning of this explanation is to reveal that the Sūtra contains three senses: namely, it teaches that there are three distinct categories of sentient beings who benefit from the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*);

according to these distinct benefits, they are conditioned by attachment to the three [realms] for a long duration. That is to say, it can cause *bāhujana* (the multitude) to be at peace, it can cause *sattva* (sentient beings) to abide, and it can provide sustenance for those seeking birth.
These three correspond respectively to the root of birth, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and the following [sections], which are discussed here in relation to...

Regarding the section explaining the meaning of "already arisen" (*jātāḥ*): although both "arisen" (*jātāḥ*) and "originally existent" (*pūrvabhava*) are subsumed under "already arisen," the term *bhūta* (being) receives its specific designation based on the distinct meaning of "originally existent.

Thus, the word *bhūta* refers exclusively to the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*). "Peaceful" (*śānta*) signifies temporary peace; "abiding" (*sthita*) signifies long-term duration; and "sustenance" (*puṣṭi*) signifies the support that maintains life.
Furthermore, this nutriment is capable of drawing forth the continuity of the originally existent state, causing it to arise within the realms of existence. This is nutriment.
[This is] its application.
Or again, [it refers to] sentient beings up to the stage where their practice is exhausted.
The commentary states: This is the second explanation; here, the word *bhūta* is explained through the sense of "number," referring to those who possess afflictions (*kleśa*). Number.

Because one proceeds toward [a future state], it is conventionally designated as "sentient being. "Seeking birth" means the capacity to seek; "abiding" (*āśraya*) means dwelling securely; "dwelling" (*vihāra*) means staying for a time;

"sustenance" (*upastambha*) means that which supports and maintains. When these terms are combined, they reveal the convergence of conditions for the future. Fearing that there might be no further distance [to go], it is revealed that in this very life there is the stage where practice is exhausted, which refers to the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa* (the remainderless).
"Or there are classes of sentient beings... up to those seeking birth.
The commentary states: This third explanation interprets the term *bhūta* according to the meaning of the preceding sūtra;

it merely combines the first two [categories] mentioned in the sūtra to manifest those already born, while the last one is cited separately to manifest those about to be born. It shows that past karma is capable of causing [birth].

It establishes the present cause so that it may not be interrupted. Furthermore, "establishing" (*vyavasthāna*) is explained as "not destroying," which means maintaining [the karma] so that it remains;

"arousing its function" (*vṛtti*) means "adding" (*adhi-karaṇa*), which refers to causing the karma to perform its activity. Regarding the phrase "that which is about to arise," the text is explicit and easy to understand.
In the *Abhidharmakośa*, there is an explanation stating that *bhūta* refers to an Arhat; this is an explanation of the meaning of *bhūta* according to ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Some say that *bhūta* refers to [entities] other than the great oceans and so forth.

The commentary states: this passage sets forth two erroneous interpretations; the first is set forth, and the second is refuted. This is the setting forth. It also explains the meaning of *bhūta* as "already arisen.

Since "already arisen" encompasses both the primary existence (*bhava*) and the derivative existence (*upādāya-bhava*), and since "seeking to arise" (*utpitsu*) encompasses these two within the intermediate state, these two constitute the essence.
To clarify that these two do not include non-sentient things, the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) is stated as a qualification to prevent confusion;
for the *Āhāra-sūtra* states that the great oceans, small seas, great rivers, small streams, large channels, small channels, mountain crags, mountain torrents, marshlands,
and heavy rains are, in their respective order, each the food of the one preceding it, with the former being viewed in relation to the latter.
Since the term "possessing food" (āhāraka) is established, this very proof shows that it is not non-sentient things that possess food;
rather, it is to reveal that those who possess food are exclusively sentient beings that the term "sentient beings" (sattva) is used to exclude the previous two [categories].
If that is so, then this statement [extends] to sentient beings who possess volition (cetanā).

The commentary states: This is a refutation. If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "segmented" (piṇḍa) is useless because it merely serves to exclude non-sentient things—since segmented food and so forth are already excluded from being non-sentient—then one might offer this defense:

"Even the various non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) maintain that trees and such things consume 'segmented' food, such as through irrigation and so on; therefore, the term 'sentient' must be included as a qualification."

Nor is it so. If [the position] were that non-Buddhists (tīrthika) also admit that trees and the like are sentient beings—just as gourds and such can see their trellises from afar or near, and extend toward them—then they would be included among sentient beings, and one could not use "sentient being" as a qualification to exclude them.
If one wishes to exclude them, one should explain the meaning of *bhūta* as "real" (*tattvika*). As for "real," it must be...

It is universally established that such [a definition] must be able to exclude forests and the like; thus, it should be understood as being subsumed within the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgṛhīta*), which serves to generally exclude those already produced (*jāta*) and numerous (*bahula*), and this is unobjectionable for the establishment of the meaning.
"Why [is it that] the Sūtra [extends] to these two words? What is their purpose? The commentary states:
The following explains the cause for the arising of the Teaching. First is the question, second is the answer, third is the reprimand, and fourth is the clarification. This is the question:
"Since sentient beings can be satisfied [by this], why rely on further words?"
"Is it not already stated... (up to)... therefore this statement is made"? [The commentary] says:
This is the answer; the preceding [text] may be understood by reference to it.
It merely explains the meaning of "due to food" (up to) "distinctions," and so forth.

The commentary states: This is an external objection. Although you have already distinguished the individual characteristics of the three terms through reasoning, since they collectively refer to sentient beings, for what reason do you contravene this general discussion to speak of their distinctions? What is it that you intend to manifest?
"In other sūtras... [up to] these three phrases. The commentary states:

"This is a general explanation. That nutriment benefits sentient beings has already been taught in other sūtras; the intention of this sūtra is to exclude [the general] and manifest a specific category.
This explains the meaning of the first and third of the two previous schools' interpretations, or it may be intended to clarify the three [nutriments].
Regarding the "distinction of food," this restates the meaning of the second preceding explanation; when compared with the preceding text, its meaning is easy to understand.
It says: "With respect to edible food... therefore it is called 'thorough knowledge'."
The commentary states: The following second section explains the meaning of the aforementioned "abandonment through full knowledge" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Within this, first the meaning of abandonment through full knowledge is explained, and subsequently, the various distinctions are addressed to resolve potential difficulties; this is the former.
To speak directly of "abandonment" means to bring about dissociation (*visamyoga*); whenever one attains dissociation from any given nutriment, that very moment is designated as "abandonment."
That nutriment is for the purpose of distinguishing it from mere cessation; therefore, it is later called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*). "Thorough knowledge" means "comprehensive cognition.

By the power of this comprehensive cognition, nutriment attains dissociation (*visamyoga*); thus, dissociation is dependent upon thorough knowledge. If one refers to the seventh [case], it is "cessation by means of thorough knowledge";

if one refers to the sixth [case], it is "the cessation of thorough knowledge. According to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis of the term, it is named "cessation through thorough knowledge" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).

One may understand this as follows: this "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) are designated by their cause; thus, because it is the cause, it is named "abandonment," and because it is the thorough knowledge, it is named "thorough knowledge.

This is interpreted according to the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound: abandonment itself is thorough knowledge, hence "abandonment-thorough-knowledge" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*). The second interpretation states that the term "abandonment" refers to the stage of suppression (*vibhava-avasthā*), because it is the means for abandonment.
It is named after its result: "uprooting forever" is called "thorough knowledge. Thorough knowledge is that which can uproot forever; it is so named from the perspective of its cause.

If one explains "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) by joining them with their respective opposites, then it would not be appropriate to call [the abandonment] "permanent abandonment.
[The author] states: From here on, he provides specific explanations to resolve various objections; therein, he first addresses the objection regarding substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

Next, the commentary explains the remaining three types of nutriment. Regarding the first [the nutriment of contact], it first raises an objection and then resolves it through reasoning; this constitutes the raising of the objection.

As for the five defilements of sensual desire (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*), they comprehensively encompass the greed that takes the five objects of the desire realm as its object. Greed directed toward the nutriment of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) is limited to three objects;

at first, much of it can be severed, while a little must necessarily remain. There is no possibility of severing the little while leaving the much; rather, one must necessarily sever the much in order to encompass the little.
"Although this principle exists... [up to] ...the substance is termed 'abandoned'. The commentary states:

The following section applies generally to the beginning, while the preceding section applies correctly to the end; it records divergent views. There are two types of "correct general application," and this is the first:
because it is revealed that [the abandonment of the object and the abandonment of the affliction] must occur simultaneously, this statement is made.
"Although this principle exists... because it is not substantial food. The commentary states:
This is an external objection; since the basis [of the argument] is narrow and cannot encompass the broad, it is said that there is no such principle.
This criticism is not valid (up to the point where it says) "therefore this statement is made.

[The author] comments: This is a refutation; based on the fact that [the two] must necessarily be simultaneous, there is no difficulty regarding the lack of temporal extension, nor is there any logical basis for such an objection.
"Alternatively, it is said here that [it refers to] greed for the five objects of the senses.

The commentary states: "This is the second [section]. Its intent is to clarify that all forms of greed existing within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are subsumed under these five defilements of sensual desire;
it is not merely greed directed toward objects within the desire realm. Therefore, this differs from the previous definition."
The principle that "a small [cause] cuts off many [effects]" is also similar to what was stated previously; this initial section merely indicates the quantity of the defiled essence.
If one asks, "How is this so?"—the commentary states: "This is a question."
"Not the affair of the noble ones" (up to) "he speaks thus. The commentary states: This is an objection.

First, desire-taint (*kāmarāga*) is used to subsume the greed of the desire realm; subsequently, the taint of the five exquisite desires (*pañca kāmaguṇa-rāga*) is used to subsume the greed of the desire realm.
This is not the affair of the noble ones, namely sexual intercourse (*maithuna*). It does not depart from the realm of sexuality, or it depends upon the person (*puruṣa*).
Because it explains the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), or because it contains many riches, it is called the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*).

The craving of the Desire Realm is termed "desire-taint" (*kāmarāga*) according to the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound. Based on this, all cravings existing within the Desire Realm are collectively named "desire-taint.
Furthermore, the five objects—form and so forth—are also called "desires" because they are conducive to and increase the provisions for craving.

Because these are objects of delight, they are called "desires" (*kāma*); this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Because they are excellent, they are called "excellent desires" (*sundara-kāma*);
this is an *upapada* (dependent) compound. There are five such excellent desires; this is a *saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa* (numeral-adjective) compound.

Regarding the realm to which these five excellent desires belong, it is an *upapada* compound meaning "the realm of the five excellent desires," and thus it is called the "realm of the five excellent desires" (*pañca-kāma-guṇa-dhātu*). These are the five excellent desires.

Regarding greed within the realm (*dhātu*): if it relies upon the seventh [consciousness] or takes the seventh as its object, because that [seventh consciousness] relies upon and takes the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*) as its objects, it is designated by the *tatpuruṣa* compound as "staining of the five objects of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇarāga*).
Therefore, all greed existing within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) may be termed the staining of the five objects of sensual pleasure.

This staining of sensual pleasure is subject to both abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) and abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); however, at the time of abandoning what is to be abandoned through seeing, it is not [abandoned].

Because edible food has been abandoned, it cannot be said that at the time when the defilement of the five objects of sensual pleasure is permanently severed, the pervasive knowledge of the abandonment of edible food is also attained.

However, since this craving must necessarily be exhausted at the time when edible food is abandoned through pervasive knowledge, one speaks of the attainment of pervasive knowledge regarding the defilement of the five objects of sensual pleasure at the very moment of the pervasive knowledge of the abandonment of edible food.
There is an interpretation which states that the mention of "defilement by the five objects of desire" (*pañca-kāmaguṇa-rāga*) is intended to clarify [the following].

The commentary says: This citation of a divergent view—that defilement by the five objects of desire is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—is made in order to demonstrate that edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) is abandoned through cultivation;
thus, it is stated in this way to show that their abandonment occurs simultaneously, making clear that they are not abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*).
This explanation provided by Śrīlāta is not inconsistent with reason. [The author] comments:

This is a refutation. The term "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) applies exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*); since the tainted (*sāsrava*) cannot be designated as complete knowledge, that which is untainted must necessarily involve neither the combined abandonment of insight (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
It is only when one speaks of the abandonment of the nutriment of physical food (*kavadīkārāhāra*) by means of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) that [the term is used].

To clarify that this refers exclusively to the abandonment of the defilements abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is no ambiguity in the meaning; why then is a distinction necessary? Furthermore, even if such a distinction were made, it would be of no benefit to the meaning.

There is likewise no logical contradiction in including those abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*), because at that time, the defilements abandoned through vision have necessarily already been abandoned.

This is just as the subsequent [states] such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth are all explained by reference to what precedes them; namely, the abandonment of the ninth category of defilement of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is called...
At the time of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of contact (*sparśa*), it is said that the three feelings are also abandoned;

as for the abandonment of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), this is because it has already been abandoned previously upon attaining detachment from the third dhyāna. However, since it is necessarily absent [at that stage], it is said to be "also abandoned.

The abandonment of volition (*cetanā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) occurs at the same time as the abandonment of contact. Furthermore, craving for the desire and form realms, as well as the group of names (*nāmakāya*), have all already been abandoned previously.
Since [the afflictions] have been severed, there is nothing to be excluded; thus, it does not contradict the principle that placing this term of exclusion would be useless.
Is it not the case that [the severance] follows the specific distinctions [of the three types of nutriment]?

The commentary states: "The following [passage] addresses the objection regarding the three nutriments. This refers to raising the objection. Since these latter three nutriments have already been severed...
At the same time, as [the afflictions] are severed, sensation (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates are all simultaneously severed; why then labor to state them separately?
This is because there are sentient beings for whom [the attainment of] the fruit is certain, yet [the cessation of the causes] is not yet present.

The commentary states: this is a general explanation, which contains three interpretations: first, to accord with the capacities of the audience; second, to reveal the relationship between cause and effect; third...

To clarify the meaning: "for the sake of clarifying the meaning" means that food is what leads to the attainment of the goal; because it leads to [the attainment of] both the object and the subject through the objects of craving and grasping, the meaning of "food" is established.
Therefore, the four types of nutriment are led by craving. Furthermore, they lead respectively to the objects of sensual desire (*kāma*), defiled feeling (*vedanā*), and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Since this only refers to three [results], edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is not mentioned as being led by the cause, for it is that which leads.

Because it is a fruit, it fulfills the definition of nutriment (*āhāra*). By this principle, although cessation (*nirodha*) occurs simultaneously [with contact], it is mentioned separately to clarify its difference [from the others].
Furthermore, how is contact (*sparśa*) said to be called "nutriment"?
The commentary states: The following is the third section, which explains contact (*sparśa*), volition (*cetanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the causes and conditions for nutriment.
This passage is divided into three parts; this [first part] addresses the question of contact.
It is because contact has the capacity [to lead to] that which is experienced by feeling (*vedanā*).
The commentary states: This is an explanation based on the fact that the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) possesses the function of providing sustenance and benefit.
"Sustenance" refers to that which is sustained; "benefit" refers to causing growth. Because of contact, [the mind and mental factors] do not perish;

it is contact that draws forth and causes the other mental states and mental factors to arise by sharing its characteristic of leading them forward. Among these, contact is most predominant with respect to sensation (*vedanā*).

That which is produced by the power of conditions such as the faculties and objects is called "nourishing" (*āhāra*) by virtue of its essence being beneficial; furthermore, because it serves as the cause for feeling (*vedanā*), it is termed "that which benefits feeling.

It is explained as having the sense of a "cause" because it is what is experienced by feeling. However, there is no fault of [non-food] items such as the faculties also becoming food, because they are not predominant.
"Not all volition (up to 'is my meritorious function')" — the commentary states:

This explanation of the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*) requires that one grasp it as a volition characterized by aspiration; that is, a volition that looks toward an object conducive to its own nature.
Because of this volitional object, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) necessarily manifests. That this volition of aspiration exists solely within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the proof for this.
Volition is able to accomplish the function of nutriment; it induces the two sons’ longing for a sand-sack, which the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* describes as a sack of ashes.
It also induces those engaged in agriculture and the like who possess hope, whereby they gain strength; this is cited in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.
Furthermore, the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra* states that merchants contemplate the accumulation of foam and so forth, and that there is a great multitude within the great ocean.
When born, they ascend to the shore, lay their eggs within the sand, and return to the ocean. If the mother constantly thinks of them, the eggs do not perish;
if she loses mindfulness, the eggs are destroyed. The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) objects: "This cannot be so, for it contradicts the principle of nutriment (*āhāra*).
How could the thought of another sustain one's own body? In reality, one should say that the egg constantly thinks of the mother."
If one dies while in a state of non-decay and forgetfulness, and then gives rise to the thought of one’s mother, this occurs at the stage of contact (*sparśa*).
This means that upon reaching the stage of contact, one is able to have such an aspiration. Although this principle holds, there is a distinct intention in that treatise:
"If the mother constantly thinks [of her son]" means that if the son can constantly think of the mother, it is like saying "food is always eaten" or "the Buddha is always present."

Mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth may be mutually induced through the causal relationship of mother and child; because the mother thinks of her child, the child immediately thinks of his mother.

Since the text cites the mother as the primary cause, it says that "the mother constantly thinks [of the child]. The Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) did not adopt this intended meaning therein. The Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) did not explain it because it was easily understood.

To provide a comprehensive explanation of the Sūtra’s statement regarding "mental food" (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*), it is said: first, to reveal its association with the mind (*manas*), and second, for...
I refute the Vaiśeṣika position that volition (*cetanā*) is an attribute (*guṇa*) of the self, the Sāṃkhya position that desire (*icchā*) is the function of the self,
or the Sāṃkhya position that volition is the self and the Vaiśeṣika position that volition is an attribute.
The Sūtra speaks of the four nutriments (up to the section on edible food).
The commentary states: This explains the nutriment of consciousness; this first passage generally interprets the Sūtra.
What are the characteristics of consciousness as it functions as a nutriment?
The commentary states: "This is the question.
[It continues: "Because it can maintain the body by perceiving desirable objects.
The commentary states: "This is the explanation."
If that is so, how is it that [the object] is an "indifferent food" (*upekṣā*)?

The commentary states: This is an objection. If a desirable object were established as providing benefit to consciousness both in the present and the future, then there would be no sense in calling it "food" when it is indifferent.
Since that [equanimity] also exists [up to the point mentioned], there is no fault. The commentary states:
This is a general [definition]. Not aspiring for worldly pleasures is called "equanimity"; what contradiction is there in its taking cessation and the path as its objects?
It maintains the body.
The Sūtra says that there are [four kinds of nutriment]... (up to) "what further use would there be?
The commentary states: This section below is the fourth explanation of the Sūtra’s teaching on the four kinds of nutriment; here, the Sūtra is cited to pose a question regarding its meaning.
"To exclude [the notion that] there is a consumer external to the food.

The commentary states: This is the explanation. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that the "consumer" is volition (*cetanā*) or they reckon it is consciousness (*vijñāna*); here, these are collectively referred to as "desire for food" (*āhāra-kāma*).
This is intended to clarify that all foods are themselves the "food of food," and that there is no separate consumer distinct from the food; therefore, it is called "food."
Food. The Buddha taught the four kinds of nutriment (up to) the meaning of their being the causal condition for craving.
The commentary states: Below this is the fifth section, explaining that the four nutriments taught by the Buddha have craving as their causal condition; first, the explanation of the textual meaning.
Second, the explanation of the meaning. Within the explanation of the textual meaning, there is first the question and second the answer;
this is the question. [The reason is that] "the desired and cherished object constitutes the substance of nutriment.
The commentary states: what follows below contains two explanations. In the first explanation, there are four parts: (1) the inquiry, (2) the refutation, (3) the dismissal, and (4) the objection.
The five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are the explanation here: because what is cherished is food, food gives rise to craving.
[Question: For what reason does craving arise toward food?
[Response: This is the objection.
Thus it occurs... [up to] "named the condition of craving. The commentary states: This is the dispelling [of doubt].

From craving arises pleasant feeling; from pleasant feeling arises craving. Craving, in turn, takes food as its object, and because it is sustained by requisites, it is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*).
It is named the "condition of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-pratyaya*) because it is the proximate cause (*āsanna-hetu*) that gives rise to it. Therefore, it is called the "condition of craving."
This is because [some] grasp at it as a requisite for sustenance.
Is it not the case that food arises with eating as its condition?
[The author] comments: This objection should be addressed by noting that [eating] is a cause of suffering and is therefore undesirable.
In principle, it should indeed be so... [up to] "named the causal condition for craving.
The commentary states: This passage has two interpretations. First, regarding those who are deluded, the Sūtra speaks of craving as the cause.

Second, it refers to the craving that arises from food and seeks its cessation; this is precisely the sense of being the cause of craving. Furthermore, with respect to this craving, it serves as the cause once again.

The seeking of food and drink is the meaning of having craving as its causal condition (*pratyaya*). The former [term] is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, while the latter is explained by the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound.
This means that when one is oppressed by the touch of hunger, a craving arises for relief, and one thus seeks out food and drink; this is precisely that meaning.
Alternatively, it is said that the arising of the fruit [up to] is called the causal condition of craving (*tṛṣṇā-pratyaya*).
The commentary states: From here below is the second explanation, which resolves one difficulty and penetrates two points.

This explains that taking the fruit of suffering as the fruit of nutriment and taking craving as the origin (*samudaya*) is also explained according to the sense of "abundance," establishing the meaning of craving as the cause.
"If that were so, then all food should be accompanied by craving.
[The author] states: This objection is not valid;
this criticism is incorrect, for this case should also be understood in the same way.

The commentary states: There are two interpretations of this "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). First, it is said that while it is named according to one part as being caused by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there are also cases where it is not so.
Second, it means that because one previously craved and sought food, there is no fault, as stated in two sūtras.
"Although it is known that based on this... what further use is there? The commentary states:
"The following section explains the underlying intent; therefore, the question is raised first.
It is to demonstrate that all forms of nutriment... are profoundly useful."
The commentary states: This explanation serves two purposes: first, to clarify that nutriment is the cause of saṃsāra;
second, to clarify that nutriment can give rise to all forms of suffering, so as to inspire revulsion toward it and lead one to avoid it—thereby possessing profound utility.
Having extensively explained the types of nutriment [up to the point where it asks], "What is its essential nature?
the commentary states: From here on, the third major section clarifies the meaning of the death of sentient beings through one question and two answers. This is the question itself;
there are six questions in total, as can be seen from the text. Taken as a whole, they are collectively termed the "meaning of the characteristics of death."

Therefore, birth and the other [stages] are explained together; however, while the meaning of the first three questions encompasses all [stages], the latter three questions clarify only the sense of passing away (*cyuti*).
Regarding the *marmans*: they are specific locations within the body of a sentient being, and contact with them leads to death.
In the land of Han, there is no specific name for this, though its meaning is termed "death-veins" (*si-xue*).
The verse says: "The severing of the roots of goodness and their restoration... [up to] the terminal points (*marmaccheda*), etc.
The commentary states: This is the formal explanation. The first three lines answer the first question;
the next line answers the second question; the next line answers the third question; the next line answers the fourth question; and the final three lines answer the fifth question.
The fifth question is answered by the first phrase of the sixth question.
The *Śāstra* says: "Severing the roots of goodness and reconnecting them... [they] lack functional capacity. The *Vyākhyā* states:
These first three phrases answer the first question; [the structure consists of] first, an explanation; second, a reprimand; third, an answer; fourth, a challenge; and fifth, [a further response].
The six points of doubt and seven responses constitute the explanation. The original intent was to clarify which consciousness arises at the moment of death for sentient beings;

since this meaning is consistent with that purpose, the remaining five states are discussed as a digression. The severance of the roots of goodness necessarily occurs through false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Since views do not exist within the five sensory consciousnesses and are severed only by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the severance of the roots of goodness occurs only through doubt (*vicikitsā*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). This [severance] likewise occurs only in the mental consciousness, not in the five sensory consciousnesses.

Regarding the statement that "those abandoned by insight are not [abandoned] by the mind alone," since the term "mind" (*manas*) refers to insight, the abandonment of desire must necessarily occur through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Furthermore, regarding the necessity of birth [in a higher realm],
would it not also be the case that at the very beginning [of such a process], it is likewise only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) [that functions]?
The commentary says: This is the objection.
[Regarding the statement] from "the word 'arising'" up to "is not separate from that which is spoken":
the commentary says: This is the response. Because it is subsumed under "arising," a seventh category is not established.
"This is not [the case] because the statement regarding 'birth' (upapatti) is extremely contradictory.

[The commentary] states: This is an objection. Since the explicit texts of the sūtras and śāstras clarify that there is a distinction between birth and existence, how could the intermediate state (antarābhava) be subsumed within the initial moment of birth?
There is no fault of contradiction [in asserting that] it extends to the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of both realms.

The commentary states: This is a general rule. However, if one considers the distinction between birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) and intermediate existence (*antarā-bhava*), they cannot be mutually inclusive.

Yet, there is no error in saying that birth-existence generally includes them, for the *Mūla-śāstra* states: "The arising of an intermediate existence in the desire realm is called 'birth' in the desire realm."
There is no contradiction or harm.
How could it be that one does not abide in that [state] (the intermediate state) and yet immediately obtain these fetters?

The commentary states: This is a doubt; [it concerns whether] the arising of the intermediate existence of desire and the acquisition of the two classes of fetters bound to the desire realm can occur simultaneously.

Just as the Path of Liberation arises with respect to liberation, so too, at the moment of death in the higher realms, the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) ceases simultaneously with the acquisition of wholesome states belonging to those realms.
This "arising" has the sense of "inducing" [the acquisition];

thus, the Path of Non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) may also be called an "acquisition," because it is identical to the Path of Liberation in its proximity [to the result]. Therefore, this fetter should be abandoned by means of the Path of Non-interruption.
"In the mind at the very moment of death in the upper realms, one first realizes the intermediate state (antarābhava)... [The text continues] "...including the intermediate state.

The commentary states: "This is a refutation. The original intent of citing this passage was to prove that the arising of the intermediate state is also called 'birth' (jāti), and that the term 'birth' includes it."
If one were to explain that passage according to its primary meaning:
although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is present [at the time of death], it is necessarily dull and inferior.
The commentary states: "From here below, the next phrase is explained to answer the second question. This consists of two parts: first, the explanation; second, the proof. This is the explanation.

The original intent also incorporates the preceding examples, which can be understood from before. Because those who are dull and inferior undergo death and birth without any powerful or robust sensation, it is for this reason that it is said [they experience] up to and including neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*). Thus, there is no [other] sensation of abandonment.
The commentary states: This is the citation of scriptural evidence; therefore, it is said that [the state] is identical to the thesis to be established.
Although it is said that [this occurs] in the mental consciousness (until) there is no birth-and-death.
The commentary states: From here below is the explanation of the third phrase, which answers the third question. The verse says: "The second refers to death."
Furthermore, because [the mind] arises in the two states solely as a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), there is certainly no state of non-mind (*acittaka*).
Regarding the two [interpretations], the first explanation is not "certain" (*niyata*) and the second is not "non-existent"; this is precisely what explains why it is not a "certain mind.

If one says it is "certain," it refers to being in a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) or requiring reliance on concentration for the mind to arise. As for being in a concentrated mind, it applies to both one's own and other stages.

Regarding those who abide in a concentrated mind, it is necessary to rely on meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This refers to defiled states of a different level (*bhūmi*) and neutral states of a different level.

As for "defiled states of a different level," this refers to defiled states of a higher level; within this present life, these must necessarily arise based on entering meditative absorption, for they cannot arise spontaneously.

Defiled states of one's own level do not require entry into absorption because they are acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*); even if they are not acquired at birth, they do not [arise] within the present life [without such entry].

Because they arise from entering meditative absorption, the neutral states of other stages—namely, the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) and so forth—do not involve death or rebirth;

this is clear from the text and requires no further analysis. As for the wholesome states of other stages that are not produced through application (*prayoga*), since their meaning is identical to that of the mind in absorption, they are similar to the states acquired at birth in lower or higher stages, which should be examined and reflected upon accordingly.
"Nor is it mindless," and so on, up to the full exposition.

The commentary states: This [passage] explains that it is not mindless. The preceding explanation concerns "not dying," while the subsequent explanation concerns "not being born. Within each of these, there are two parts:
first the principle (*yukti*), then the scripture (*āgama*). These are easy to understand according to the text.
However, regarding the "mind at the moment of death" (up to the point where it says) "one should investigate extensively," the commentary states:
From here below is the explanation of the fourth phrase, answering the fourth question. This consists of: first, the explanation; second, the censure; third, the answer; fourth, the objection;
fifth, the reconciliation; sixth, the doubt; and seventh, the dismissal. This [section] is the explanation. Regarding the two explanations for the desire realm, all treatises are in agreement.
However, since there is no explicit permission [for this], the principle should apply to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
Why would inferior goodness not enter into nirvāṇa?
This is the objection stated [in the text].
"Because that wholesome mind leads to entry into nirvāṇa. [The commentary] states:
This answers the objection that because one is weary of the future fruit, one no longer produces the cause.
If that were so, then while abiding in the maturation (vipāka), one would not enter nirvāṇa.
The commentary states: This is an objection. Since the present is currently being loathed, how can [an aspiration] arise?
If this were not so, it would have already been excluded by the statement that one turns away from the future.
The commentary states: This is a response. It merely says one loathes what is to come and does not say one loathes the present; how, then, can this constitute an objection?
"Why do you not feel revulsion toward the present maturation?
The commentary states: This is a doubt. If one already feels revulsion toward that which has not yet been actualized, why not feel revulsion toward the present?
One should know that [the mind] relies upon the present maturation, up to [the point where it is] restricted to the two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states.
The commentary states: This is a refutation. That which "manifests" possesses volition and thus cannot be loathed; that which is "destined" possesses affliction and thus does not give rise to causes.
From the various consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, up to the point of reaching future existence (*punarbhava*).

The commentary states: This explanation of the fifth threefold phrase answers the fifth question by clarifying that while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has no actual location, it is conventionally described as being of three types based on the place where the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) ceases. These two explanations are taken together without contradiction;
for there is absolutely no case where a homogeneous continuity (*sabhāga-saṃtati*) arises [from such a cessation].
"Only those who die gradually [experience] the suffering of the severance of the *marmaccheda*.
Commentary: The following explains the sixth line of the verse in response to the sixth question.

First, it provides a direct explanation of the verse, clarifying that the severance of the *marmaccheda* is the means by which death occurs for those in the human realm and so forth; subsequently, it discusses animals and provides supplementary arguments regarding the five [types of death] among the gods.
The arising of the signs of decay serves as the preliminary to death. This consists of three parts: first, the explanation; second, the objection; third, the response. This is the explanation.
That which is called a *marman* (vital point) is a death-point of the body; its dimension is extremely small, like a garland of *utpala* flowers or even more minute.
Wherever it is touched, the measure [of the impact] is such that, in the West, there are many who touch upon these *marmans*; for instance, when a thief touches a person with his hand...

Attachment leads directly to death. As for what is called "severance" (*cheda*), it occurs when any one of the three—wind, bile, or phlegm—becomes excessively aggravated and oppresses the vital points (*marman*).
At these vital points, great suffering arises, and from this moment on, one will certainly relinquish life in an instant.

The *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that the meaning of "obstruction" (*vighna*) is not applicable here; because it is like severance, it is designated by the name "severance. This severance of the vital points is induced by sinful karma.

The extensive explanations can be understood according to the text as stated in the *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*. It says that in the hells there is no suffering because [suffering] must be severed;
yet they do not die because karma sustains them. This applies only to the remaining realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and humans—excluding Uttarakuru.
Regarding the "severing of the vital points" (*marmaccheda*), it is explained as the breaking of the joints; this applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*). All of these are possible.
This excludes only the World-Honored One, for among the gods whose suffering is eternally exhausted, there are none who possess [the death-organ] as described below.
For what reason is the earth element not a fatal organ (*marmaccheda*)?
This is the objection stated here.
Because there is no fourth [disaster] (up to the three external disasters of the vessel-world).

The commentary states: This is the answer. Since both the internal and external three disasters lack the suffering of the destruction of the vital points (*marmaccheda*) in the fourth [dhyāna], there are only three stages;
that is, it is not a disaster because it is not harmful. The phrasing used according to what is appropriate indicates that this is not sequential.
Regarding the actual principle: since [the elements] are wind, heat, and moisture respectively, they should arise from wind, fire, and water.
Because these sever the *marmaccheda* (vital points), it is said that there are five. The commentary states:

This ancillary discussion clarifies the stage of imminent death among the various devas, wherein the five signs of decay (*pañcavyasanāni*) appear first in small measure and subsequently in large measure.

Because they arise in succession, they lead to the end of life. This is stated as a general description for all devas; however, regarding these five [faculties], it is not necessarily the case that each one possesses them all.
How is it known that they do not exist in all [beings]?
The commentary states: As for the grounds upon which this critique is based, how is it known to be so?
It is by means of scripture and reasoning (up to the point of) "due to unwholesome karma.
The commentary states: This is the explanation. The scriptural statement "without rising from his seat" indicates that it was not a long duration; furthermore, it says "not at all... [and so forth].
It is also evident from the realization that the five signs do not logically arise simultaneously; for what reason would the marks of decay appear all at once?
Regarding this, the Blessed One stated [in the *Sūtra on the Arising of the Marks*]: "Except for those who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) or other such [heinous acts]..."

The commentary states: From here below is the second major section, which judges the distinctions among the aggregates (*rāśi*). It consists of the headings, the inquiries, and the formal expositions, which may be understood according to the text.
The treatise says: "First, the group of those fixed in the right nature (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*); [up to] third, the group of those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-rāśi*)."
The commentary states: The following explains the initial enumeration of names in the verse.
What is meant by "right nature" (*samyaktva*)?
The commentary states: This is the first question.
It refers to what the World-Honored One said [up to] "this is called right nature" (*samyaktva*).
The commentary states: This answer explains that the unconditioned cessation (*asamskṛta-nirodha*) is right nature.
For what reason is it that only abandonment is designated as right nature?
The commentary states: This is the reason for the inquiry.
It means that because this [state] is eternally exhausted... it is certainly cherished by the wise.
The commentary states: This is the explanation that because the essence of the exhaustion of false dharmas is wholesome and permanent, it is called the "Right Nature" (samyaktva).
The World-Honored One also spoke [of them] up to "the state of rightness and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The commentary states: This second explanation takes the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) as "rightness" (*samyaktva*);
those who are fixed in this state are called "those fixed in rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata-pudgala*). Because such persons are not singular, they are described as a "group" (*rāśi*).
"What is meant by 'wrong nature' (mithyātva)?
The commentary states: This is the second question.
It means that there are three kinds [of wrong nature], which constitute its essence respectively.
The commentary states: From this, the essence of wrong nature (*mithyātva*) can be understood.
Regarding "those established in the two [attainments]" (up to "...therefore it is called 'constructing'"):

the commentary states that this explains the second definition, clarifying that for those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), their meditative attainments inevitably lead to disconnection (*visamyoga*), and thus they do not construct [new karma].
Those who were previously destined for hell are called "sages" (*ārya*) before [their death] and "those in the Uninterrupted Hell" (*avīci*) afterward. If one asks why they are called "sages":

because those in training (*śaikṣa*) are said to be "rightly liberated" and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are "already liberated," they are thus named sages; furthermore, because they have distanced themselves from all evils and because that which they are headed toward is wholesome, they can be understood as sages.
As for the term "Uninterrupted," it carries the meaning of being "without interval," meaning there is no interval between [the end of life and the next state], as there is no death-interruption.
Because there is no interval [between them], they are designated as "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
As for the remaining states—right determination, wrong determination, and so forth—they receive the name "not-empty.
The commentary states: This explains the third point. It intends to clarify that these types [of states] correspond respectively to the conditions of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Because it can become either wholesome or unwholesome and does not belong definitively to one [category], it is called "indeterminate.
*Nyāyānusāra-śāstra-vṛtti* (Exposition of the *Nyāyānusāra*), Fascicle 18, composed by the Śramaṇa Yuanyu.
In years past, I obtained this original manuscript; I cherished its calligraphy and often enjoyed it alongside ancient masterpieces of script.
Upon casually beholding this, the Venerable Yunhua was struck with great amazement, declaring it to be a rare work of our age.
This original treatise is an extremely difficult discourse to read; the contribution of this record is no small matter. Even though it is but a fragment, it is worthy of high esteem.
Far from being merely a calligraphy pleasing to the eye, it required me to transcribe a copy myself, for I feared that its cursive script might be mistaken.
A transcription presented for comparison, with the examination conducted by the Venerable [Master] recorded on the left: Under the *Yitian mulu* (Catalogue of Yi Tian), it states:
*Zhenglilun shuji* (Commentary on the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*), five fascicles, composed by Yuanyu.
The *Dongyu lu* (Record of the Eastern Regions) states: *Zhenglilun shuwenji* (Explanatory Textual Commentary on the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*), twenty-four fascicles, composed by Yuanyu.
The sections from the "Karma-varga" (Gyōhin) onwards have not yet been fully cataloged;
they were compiled by the Master Shinpō. The manuscript held at Ichijō-in contains twenty-four fascicles, while the currently circulating edition held at Saidai-ji contains twenty fascicles.
Seiben’s preface states that there are twenty fascicles, though some say there are twenty-four. [End of] East.

The *Jishiben* (Temple Records) in twenty fascicles states that the *Junzhengli shu* (Commentary on the Nyāyānusāra), consisting of twenty-four fascicles and eight hundred and thirty sheets, was composed by Yuanyu. This is recorded in the *Wuzong zhangshu lu* (Record of the Treatises and Commentaries of the Five Schools).
Alternatively, it was originally present but not transcribed; I have seen only one copy of the ninth fascicle preserved at Chizan, which states that it "expounds the meaning of the text.
This was recorded by Hōshiki on the Qingming Festival in the spring of the Bunsei *eishi* year.
